# rws — Rust Web Server

> A single-binary web server and reverse proxy — automatic HTTPS (ACME / Let's Encrypt),
> HTTP/3, load balancing, auth, rate limiting, configured in one `rws.config.toml` — and
> the same engine as a Rust library (routing, middleware, MCP server, async ORM).

Source: https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server · Website: https://rws8.tech/ ·
API: https://docs.rs/rust-web-server · License: MIT · MSRV: 1.88 · Version: 18.7.0

HTTP/1.1 parsing, routing, middleware, WebSocket, SSE, CORS and JSON are implemented in
the crate — no hyper, Tower or Axum; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 use `h2` and `quinn`/`h3`, TLS uses
`rustls`. Every handler implements one trait,
`Application::execute(&Request, &ConnectionInfo) -> Result<Response, String>`, and every
cross-cutting concern (auth, rate limits, caching, tracing, the reverse proxy) is a
`Middleware` added with `app.wrap(layer)`.

Use it as:
- **a static file server** — `brew install bohdaq/tap/rws && rws`, `cargo binstall rust-web-server`, or `docker run -p 7878:7878 bohdaq/rws`
- **a config-driven proxy** — `[[route]]` / `[[upstream]]` in `rws.config.toml`, no code
- **automatic HTTPS** — an `[acme]` section with `domains = [...]`
- **a library** — `cargo add rust-web-server`

This file is every page of the documentation site in one document, generated from
`docs/src/content/docs/` by `ci/gen_llms.py`. The index with one line per page is
`llms.txt`.

---

# Quick Start

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/quick-start/>

Pick the path that matches your goal. Each ends with a working server you can hit with `curl`.

---

## Path 1 — Static file server (zero code)

Install the binary and point it at a directory. No config file, no code.

```bash
brew install bohdaq/tap/rws      # or: cargo binstall rust-web-server
# create something to serve
mkdir www && echo "<h1>Hello</h1>" > www/index.html
cd www
rws
```

```
Server is up and running at: http://0.0.0.0:7878
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:7878/
# <h1>Hello</h1>
```

`rws` serves every file under the current directory, handles range requests, sets ETags, negotiates gzip, and returns `404` for missing files — all with no configuration. A directory with no `index.html` renders a directory listing page instead of `404` — try `mkdir www/uploads && touch www/uploads/report.pdf && curl http://localhost:7878/uploads/`.

:::note[HTTPS in one flag]
If you have a TLS certificate, pass `--tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem` and the server automatically upgrades to HTTP/2 + HTTP/3:

```bash
rws --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```
:::

---

## Path 2 — First route (library)

Use `rust-web-server` as a Rust library crate and define your own handlers.

### 1. Add dependencies

```toml title="Cargo.toml"
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = "18"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros"] }
```

### 2. Write a handler

```rust title="src/main.rs"
use rust_web_server::prelude::*;

fn hello(_req: &Request, _params: &PathParams, _conn: &ConnectionInfo, _state: &()) -> Response {
    Response::text(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, "Hello, world!")
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let app = routes! {
        App::with_state(()),
        GET "/hello" => hello,
    };
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();
    tokio::join!(
        Server::run_tls(listener, pool, app.clone()),
        Server::run_quic(app),
        Server::run_redirect(),
    );
}
```

### 3. Run and verify

```bash
cargo run
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:7878/hello
# Hello, world!
```

### Handler signature

Every route handler receives four arguments:

| Argument | Type | What it contains |
|---|---|---|
| `_req` | `&Request` | Method, URI, headers, raw body bytes |
| `_params` | `&PathParams` | Named path segments (e.g. `:id`) |
| `_conn` | `&ConnectionInfo` | Client/server IP, port, SNI hostname |
| `_state` | `&S` | Your shared application state |

### Shared state

Replace `()` with any `Send + Sync` type to share state across handlers:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};

struct AppState {
    counter: AtomicU64,
}

fn count(_: &Request, _: &PathParams, _: &ConnectionInfo, state: &Arc) -> Response {
    let n = state.counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
    Response::text(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, &format!("count: {n}"))
}

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let state = Arc::new(AppState { counter: AtomicU64::new(0) });
    let app = routes! {
        App::with_state(state),
        GET "/count" => count,
    };
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();
    tokio::join!(
        Server::run_tls(listener, pool, app.clone()),
        Server::run_quic(app),
        Server::run_redirect(),
    );
}
```

---

## Path 3 — Config-driven proxy (no code)

Drop an `rws.config.toml` next to the `rws` binary and it becomes a reverse proxy and load balancer. No code required.

### Minimal config

```toml title="rws.config.toml"
port = 8080

[[upstream]]
name     = "api"
backends = ["localhost:3000", "localhost:3001"]

[upstream.health_check]
path              = "/healthz"
interval_secs     = 10
healthy_threshold = 2

[[route]]
[route.match]
path = "/api/*"

[route.action]
type     = "proxy"
upstream = "api"

[[route]]
[route.match]
path = "/"

[route.action]
type   = "respond"
status = 200
body   = "Gateway ready"
```

```bash
rws
# Server is up and running at: http://0.0.0.0:8080
```

```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/
# Gateway ready

curl http://localhost:8080/api/users
# proxied to localhost:3000 or localhost:3001 (round-robin, health-checked)
```

### What the config does

- `[[upstream]]` declares a named backend pool with health checking. Dead backends are removed automatically; they re-enter rotation once they pass `healthy_threshold` consecutive checks.
- `[[route]]` rules are evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins. A `path` ending in `*` is a prefix match (`/api/*` matches `/api/users`); without it the path must match exactly. Requests no route matches fall through to the static-file server.
- `type = "proxy"` forwards the request to the named upstream. `type = "respond"` returns a fixed response.

:::note[Add middleware per route]
Rate limiting, Bearer auth, and request rewriting can all be added per-route inside the config file — no code change needed. See the Proxy & Gateway documentation for the full schema.
:::

:::tip[HTTPS in front of the proxy]
Add an `[acme]` section (Path 4) and `rws` gets Let's Encrypt certificates for the proxy itself. To use your own certificates instead, set `tls_cert_file` / `tls_key_file`; per-domain certificates go in `[[virtual_host]]` blocks.
:::

---

## Path 4 — Automatic HTTPS (no code)

On a server whose DNS points at it, with ports 80 and 443 reachable:

```toml title="rws.config.toml"
port               = 443
http_redirect_port = 80

[acme]
domains = ["example.com"]
email   = "you@example.com"
```

```bash
sudo rws     # or grant the binary CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind 80/443 without root
```

On first start `rws` requests a certificate from Let's Encrypt (stored as
`cert.pem` / `key.pem`), then serves HTTPS with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and
redirects HTTP to HTTPS. Renewal runs in the background. Try it against the
Let's Encrypt staging CA first with `staging = true` — see
[Automatic HTTPS](/features/acme/).

```bash
curl -I http://example.com/      # 301 → https://example.com/
curl -I https://example.com/     # 200, valid certificate
```

## Next steps

- **[Dev Workflow](/getting-started/dev-workflow/)** — auto-rebuild and restart on every code change with `cargo-watch`
- **Routing** — named path parameters (`:id`), wildcards, virtual-host routing
- **Middleware** — `RateLimitLayer`, `JwtLayer`, `CacheLayer`, `OtelLayer`, and more via `.wrap(layer)`
- **MCP Server** — expose tools and resources to AI agents over the MCP Streamable HTTP protocol
- **ORM** — `#[derive(Model)]`, `QueryBuilder`, migrations, `HasMany` / `HasOne` / `BelongsTo`

# Examples

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/examples/>

The repository's [`examples/`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/tree/main/examples)
directory holds small, complete apps. Each one runs with `cargo run --example
<name>` from a clone and has a test that `cargo test` runs, so they keep
compiling and working as the crate changes.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server && cd rust-web-server
cargo run --example hello
curl localhost:7878/hello/world      # Hello, world!
```

Without a certificate they serve plain HTTP/1.1 on port 7878; a
`rws.config.toml` in the working directory, environment variables and
command-line flags apply as they do to `rws` (see
[Configuration](/configuration/env-vars/)).

| Example | Shows | Run | Read more |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`hello`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/hello.rs) | Two routes and a path parameter | `cargo run --example hello` | [Routing](/building-apps/routing/) |
| [`rest_api`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/rest_api.rs) | JSON CRUD over shared state, typed errors (400, 404, 422) | `cargo run --example rest_api --features serde` | [JSON](/building-apps/json/), [Error handling](/building-apps/error-handling/) |
| [`static_site`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/static_site.rs) | The working directory as a site, behind request-id and rate-limit middleware | `cargo run --example static_site` | [Static files](/features/static-files/), [Middleware](/building-apps/middleware/) |
| [`reverse_proxy`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/reverse_proxy.rs) | `/api/*` forwarded to a backend, the rest served locally | `cargo run --example reverse_proxy` | [Reverse proxy](/proxy/reverse-proxy/) |
| [`sse_ticker`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/sse_ticker.rs) | Server-sent events written as they are produced | `cargo run --example sse_ticker` | [Server-sent events](/features/sse/) |
| [`upload`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/upload.rs) | Large uploads streamed to disk, not buffered | `cargo run --example upload` | [Forms and uploads](/building-apps/forms-uploads/) |
| [`mcp_inventory`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/mcp_inventory.rs) | One domain served as a REST API (described in OpenAPI 3.1) and as MCP tools for agents | `cargo run --example mcp_inventory --features "macros serde sso openapi"` | [Agent tools](/mcp/agent-tools/) |
| [`tower`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/tower.rs) | A tonic gRPC service and a tower-http layer in an rws app | `cargo run --example tower --features tower` | [Tower interop](/features/tower/) |
| [`mcp_gateway`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/mcp_gateway.rs) | One authenticated MCP endpoint in front of several MCP servers | `cargo run --example mcp_gateway` | [MCP gateway](/mcp/gateway/) |
| [`mcp_conformance`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/examples/mcp_conformance.rs) | The server the official MCP conformance suite tests | `cargo run --example mcp_conformance` | [MCP overview](/mcp/overview/) |

The comment at the top of each file has the `curl` commands to try it.

## Testing an example

Each example builds its app in a function (`app()`) that `main` serves and
its test drives through [`TestClient`](/testing/test-client/) — no socket,
no port. Copy that split into your own app:

```bash
cargo test --example rest_api --features serde
```

## For AI coding agents

[`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/AGENTS.md)
at the repository root tells a coding agent how to build an app on the crate:
which entry point to start from, the handler signature, the conventions that
aren't obvious from the types, and where in these docs each topic lives. The
whole documentation is also available as one file,
[`llms-full.txt`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/llms-full.txt).

# AI coding agents

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/ai-agents/>

Coding agents mostly go wrong on rws by guessing its API — from an older release, or from axum. Three things give them the right context for the release your project uses.

## Start from a starter

Each starter is a standalone project that builds and passes its own tests (CI checks them on every change), with an `AGENTS.md` that tells an agent how the project is laid out and how rws works:

```sh
cargo generate --git https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server starters/api   # JSON API + OpenAPI 3.1, TestClient tests
cargo generate --git https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server starters/mcp   # MCP server: typed tools, a resource, a bearer token
```

([cargo-generate](https://github.com/cargo-generate/cargo-generate): `cargo install cargo-generate`.) Without it, copy the directory and replace `{{project-name}}` in `Cargo.toml`.

## Give the agent the rws skill

[`agents/`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/tree/main/agents) in the repository (also at `https://rws8.tech/agents/`) has the same guidance in each tool's format — the project shape, recipes for routes, JSON, middleware, OpenAPI, MCP tools, tests, and the pitfalls:

| Tool | File | Put it at |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code, Codex and other Agent Skills readers | `agents/skills/rws/SKILL.md` | `.claude/skills/rws/SKILL.md` in the project, or `~/.claude/skills/rws/` for every project |
| Cursor | `agents/cursor/rws.mdc` | `.cursor/rules/rws.mdc` |
| GitHub Copilot | `agents/copilot-instructions.md` | `.github/copilot-instructions.md` |

## Point it at the docs of your release

Every docs page in one file, for pasting into a chat or a system prompt, or for an agent to fetch:

- `https://rws8.tech/llms-full.txt` (and the index, `llms.txt`) — the newest release;
- `https://rws8.tech/<major.minor>/llms-full.txt`, e.g. `/18.7/` — the release your `Cargo.toml` names, kept for every release from 18.7 on.

The library's own conventions for agents working **on** the crate (rather than with it) are in the repository's `CLAUDE.md`.

# Installation

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/installation/>

## Requirements

**Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV): 1.88**

Install or update Rust via [rustup](https://rustup.rs/):

```bash
rustup update stable
rustc --version   # should print 1.88.0 or newer
```

## As a library crate

Add `rust-web-server` to your `Cargo.toml`:

```bash
cargo add rust-web-server
```

Or pin the major version manually:

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = "18"
```

The default feature set (`http3`) pulls in HTTP/3, HTTP/2, TLS, and a tokio async runtime. If you need a lighter build, opt out and select a lower feature tier (see the feature flags table below).

### Prelude

A single glob import covers the types you need in almost every handler:

```rust
use rust_web_server::prelude::*;
// Re-exports: App, Server, ConnectionInfo, Request, Response,
//             STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE, Range, MimeType,
//             PathParams, New, routes!
```

## As a standalone binary

Every release ships prebuilt binaries, so no Rust toolchain is needed:

| Method | Command | Platforms |
|---|---|---|
| Homebrew | `brew install bohdaq/tap/rws` | macOS (Apple Silicon, Intel), Linux (x86_64, arm64) |
| cargo-binstall | `cargo binstall rust-web-server` | everything below, without compiling |
| apt / dnf | `sudo apt install rws`, `sudo dnf install rws` after adding the repository — [systemd: install from a package](/deployment/systemd/#install-from-a-package); installs and starts the `rws` service (since 18.2.0) | Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL and derivatives (x86_64, arm64) |
| Docker | `docker run -p 7878:7878 -v "$PWD:/srv" bohdaq/rws` (also `ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws`) | linux/amd64, linux/arm64 |
| Download | [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/releases/latest) | `x86_64`/`aarch64-unknown-linux-musl`, `x86_64`/`aarch64-apple-darwin`, `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` |
| From source | `cargo install rust-web-server` | anywhere Rust 1.88+ runs |

On Windows, `rws.exe` also runs as a Windows service — see [Windows](/deployment/windows/).

Linux binaries are statically linked against musl, so they run on any distribution regardless of glibc version. Each archive has a matching `.sha256` file.

```bash
rws --version
rws --help      # every option, with its environment-variable equivalent
```

Run it in any directory that contains static files and it will serve them on `http://localhost:7878` with no configuration file needed.

### Verifying a release

From 18.0.0, releases can be checked end to end:

```bash
# The archive was built by this repository's release workflow
gh attestation verify rws-18.0.0-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz --repo bohdaq/rust-web-server

# The image too — attestation, or the keyless cosign signature
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws:18.0.0 --repo bohdaq/rust-web-server
cosign verify ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws:18.0.0 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/.github/workflows/release.yml@.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

# Known vulnerabilities in the dependencies compiled into a binary
# (built with cargo-auditable, so the list travels with it)
cargo audit bin ./rws
```

Each release also has a CycloneDX SBOM (`rws-<version>.cdx.json`) of the
binary's dependency tree. CI checks every change with `cargo audit` and
`cargo deny` (advisories; permissive licenses only; crates.io sources only —
`deny.toml`).

## Build from source

```bash
git clone https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server.git
cd rust-web-server
cargo build --release
# binary is at: target/release/rws
```

To build a specific feature tier from source:

```bash
# HTTP/2 + TLS only (no QUIC)
cargo build --release --no-default-features --features http2

# HTTP/1.1 only — no TLS, no async runtime, smallest binary
cargo build --release --no-default-features --features http1
```

## Feature flags

| Feature | What it adds | Required deps |
|---|---|---|
| `http1` | Synchronous thread-pool server, no async runtime, no TLS | `ctrlc`, `libc` |
| `http2` | tokio runtime, TLS via rustls (aws-lc-rs), HTTP/2 via ALPN | `h2`, `rustls`, `tokio`, `tokio-rustls`, … |
| `http3` *(default)* | QUIC transport and HTTP/3 on top of `http2` | `quinn`, `h3`, `h3-quinn` |
| `http-client` | HTTPS support in the outbound `Client` | `rustls`, `webpki-roots` |
| `serde` | JSON serialization/deserialization via serde | `serde`, `serde_json` |
| `auth` | `BasicAuthLayer`, `JwtLayer` (HS256), `ForwardAuthLayer`, JWT helpers | `hmac`, `sha2` |
| `auth-asymmetric` | RS256 / ES256 in `JwtLayer` (in-crate RSA verification) | `auth`, `p256`, `rand_core` |
| `macros` | `#[derive(Model)]`, `#[derive(FromRequest)]`, `#[derive(Validate)]`, `#[derive(Config)]`, `#[get]`/`#[post]`/… route attributes | `rws-macros` |
| `acme` | Automatic TLS certificate provisioning (ACME/Let's Encrypt) | `http2`, `rcgen`, `aws-lc-rs`, … |
| `mimalloc` | The `rws` binary allocates with mimalloc v3 (about 5% less CPU per request than glibc's allocator; more memory under load); release binaries and images have it. The library never sets a global allocator | `mimalloc` |
| `tera` | Tera template engine integration | `tera`, `serde`, `serde_json` |
| `model-sqlite` | Async ORM backend for SQLite | `http2`, `sqlx` (sqlite) |
| `model-postgres` | Async ORM backend for PostgreSQL | `http2`, `sqlx` (postgres) |
| `model-mysql` | Async ORM backend for MySQL / MariaDB | `http2`, `sqlx` (mysql) |
| `crypto` | Argon2id password hashing, signed (HMAC) and encrypted (AES-GCM) cookies | `argon2`, `rand_core`, `hmac`, `sha2`, `aes-gcm` |
| `csrf` | CSRF token generation and validation | `rand_core` |
| `mailer` | SMTP client (STARTTLS/SMTPS also need `http-client` or `http2`) | — |
| `sso` | OAuth 2.0 / OIDC client (RS256/ES256 `id_token` verification, outbound HTTPS) | `p256`, `sha2`, `rand_core`, `serde`, `serde_json`, `http-client` |
| `sso-server` | `AuthServer`: rws as an OAuth 2.0 authorization server (HS256 tokens) | `sso`, `auth` |
| `sso-saml` | `SamlSp`: SAML 2.0 Service Provider | `sso` |
| `jobs` | In-memory `JobQueue` (`PersistentJobQueue` also needs a `model-*` feature) | — |
| `storage-local` | `LocalStorage` | — |
| `storage-s3` | `S3Storage` (AWS SigV4, no SDK) | `hmac`, `sha2`, `http-client` |
| `storage-azure` | `AzureBlobStorage` (Shared Key / Managed Identity, no SDK) | `hmac`, `sha2`, `http-client` |
| `openapi` | `GET /openapi.json` + `GET /docs` from registered routes | — |
| `webhook` | `verify_webhook_signature` (GitHub, Shopify, Stripe) | `hmac`, `sha2` |
| `rewrite-regex` | `RewriteLayer::request_uri_regex_rewrite` | `regex` |
| `secrets` | `secrets::resolve()` for `vault://`, `aws-sm://`, `azkv://` references | `hmac`, `sha2`, `http-client` |

:::note[Combining features]
Features compose freely. For example, to build HTTP/2 + TLS + JSON + SQLite:

```toml
rust-web-server = { version = "18", default-features = false, features = ["http2", "serde", "model-sqlite"] }
```
:::

## Approximate binary sizes

These measurements are for a release build (`cargo build --release`) of the `rws` binary with only the core transport feature active. Enabling additional features (`serde`, `tera`, ORM backends, etc.) increases the size.

| Feature tier | Approx. binary size |
|---|---|
| `http1` | ~3 MB |
| `http2` | ~8 MB |
| `http3` (default) | ~12 MB |

:::note[No OpenSSL]
TLS uses `rustls` with the `aws-lc-rs` crypto backend. There is no dependency on a system OpenSSL installation. Binaries are fully static with respect to TLS and are compatible with FIPS-validated environments.
:::

## What's built in, and what isn't

HTTP/1.1 parsing, CORS, MIME types, range requests, WebSocket, SSE, and routing are implemented inside this crate. The transitive dependency tree has no `hyper`, `tower`, or `actix-net`.

The HTTP/2 server is rws's own (`h2_server`: framing, HPACK, flow control — conformance-checked with h2spec and fuzzed); the `h2` crate remains a dependency as the HTTP/2 *client* of `H2ReverseProxy`/`GrpcProxy`. HTTP/3 and QUIC use `h3` and `quinn`, and TLS uses `rustls`. `tokio-util` appears transitively in the default build through `h2`.

---

# Auto-Rebuild on Change (cargo-watch)

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/dev-workflow/>

`rws` doesn't need any special support for this — it's the standard Rust dev-loop pattern, using an external file-watcher to rebuild and restart your binary. [`cargo-watch`](https://crates.io/crates/cargo-watch) is the simplest way to get it.

## Setup

```bash
cargo install cargo-watch
```

Run this from your app's project root — the one with a `Cargo.toml` that depends on `rust-web-server`, not inside the `rws` source tree itself:

```bash
cargo watch -x run
```

On every file save, `cargo-watch` kills the currently running process, rebuilds, and restarts it. You never run `cargo run` by hand again — the server you're hitting with `curl` (or a browser) is always built from the latest saved code.

## Useful variants

Fail fast on a compile error before it tries to restart the (now-stale) server:

```bash
cargo watch -x check -x run
```

Scope which paths are watched — useful if your project has directories generating unrelated file-system noise (build scripts, generated files):

```bash
cargo watch -w src -w Cargo.toml -x run
```

If you're developing against a local checkout of `rws` itself via a `path = "../rust-web-server"` dependency (rather than the crates.io release), watch both trees so library changes trigger a rebuild too:

```bash
cargo watch -w src -w ../rust-web-server/src -x run
```

## What to expect

- **Rebuild time** dominates the loop — typically a few seconds for an incremental build, longer the first time or after a `Cargo.toml` change.
- **The process fully restarts** on each change — it isn't a hot code swap. Any in-memory state (counters, caches you built yourself, in-memory `SessionStore`) is reset; state backed by `DbPool`, `RedisSessionStore`, or `DbSessionStore` survives across restarts since it lives outside the process.
- **In-flight requests during a restart** get connection-refused for the brief window between the old process exiting and the new one binding the port again. Fine for iterative development; if this is disruptive enough to matter (e.g. a frontend dev server proxying to your API while you're actively testing), see the note below.

:::tip[Want zero-downtime restarts instead?]
`Server::run()` and `Server::run_tls()` both accept an already-constructed `std::net::TcpListener` rather than always binding their own — which means the [`systemfd`](https://crates.io/crates/systemfd) + [`listenfd`](https://crates.io/crates/listenfd) pattern works with `rws` as-is: `systemfd` holds the listening socket open across restarts and hands it to each new process via `listenfd`, so there's no "address already in use" and no gap where the port stops accepting connections. This is a bigger setup than plain `cargo-watch` and only worth it if the restart gap is actually causing friction.
:::

---

# Frontend Dev Server Proxy (React / Vite / webpack)

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/frontend-dev-proxy/>

`rws` is a production HTTP server, not a bundler — it has no built-in dev-mode HMR/asset-compilation story. During local development you run your frontend's own dev server (Vite, webpack-dev-server, etc.) for fast hot-module-reload, and `rws` as your API backend on a separate port. This page covers the two ways to wire the two together, and which one to reach for.

## Recommended: point the dev server's own proxy at rws

This is the standard pattern for every JS frontend tooling ecosystem, and the simplest option here — the frontend dev server proxies API requests to `rws`; everything else (the app bundle, HMR's own WebSocket) stays entirely inside the dev server, which already handles it correctly. The browser only ever talks to one origin (the dev server's port), so **no CORS configuration is needed at all**.

### Vite

```js
// vite.config.js
export default {
  server: {
    proxy: {
      '/api': {
        target: 'http://localhost:7878',
        changeOrigin: true,
      },
    },
  },
};
```

```bash
# Terminal 1
rws  # backend on :7878 (RWS_CONFIG_PORT, default 7878)

# Terminal 2
npm run dev  # Vite dev server on :5173, proxies /api/* to rws
```

Your React code just calls `fetch('/api/users')` — Vite transparently forwards it to `http://localhost:7878/api/users` and the response looks like it came from the same origin.

### webpack-dev-server (Create React App / custom webpack)

```js
// webpack.config.js
module.exports = {
  devServer: {
    proxy: {
      '/api': {
        target: 'http://localhost:7878',
        changeOrigin: true,
      },
    },
  },
};
```

Create React App reads the same shape from a `"proxy"` key in `package.json` instead, if you haven't ejected:

```json
{
  "proxy": "http://localhost:7878"
}
```

## Alternative: call rws directly, cross-origin

If you'd rather not proxy through the dev server — e.g. you're testing against a shared staging backend rather than a local `rws` instance — call it directly from the browser at its own origin instead. A fresh `rws` sends no CORS headers (since 18.0.0), so list the dev server's origin:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=false
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=true   # only if you send cookies
rws
```

See [CORS & Security](/features/cors-security/) for the full set of `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_*` variables.

This works with no bundler-side config, but every request now does a real cross-origin fetch — mutating requests will trigger a CORS preflight `OPTIONS` round-trip, and cookie-based auth needs `credentials: 'include'` in `fetch`.

## Alternative: rws as the single front door

You can flip the direction — run `rws` as the one port you point your browser at, and have it reverse-proxy through to the dev server instead. `ReverseProxy`'s `.path_prefix()` is shaped for the opposite split from what you'd want here, though, so it's worth understanding before reaching for it:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::proxy::ReverseProxy;

// path_prefix("/api") means /api/* is what gets FORWARDED to the given
// backend — everything else falls through to the wrapped App instead.
let app = App::new()  // serves everything that ISN'T /api locally
    .wrap(ReverseProxy::new(["http://backend-api:8080"]).path_prefix("/api"));
```

That's the right shape for *production* — `App` serves your built, static frontend and `/api` is proxied to a real backend service (see [Reverse Proxy](/proxy/reverse-proxy/)). For the *dev-time* case on this page — proxy everything **except** `/api` to the dev server, and answer `/api` locally — there's no built-in "exclude prefix" on `ReverseProxy` (unlike `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK_EXCLUDE_PREFIXES`'s exclude-list for the static-file fallback), so it isn't a one-line `.wrap()`. You'd need a small custom `Application` that checks the path itself and dispatches to either your local API handler or `ReverseProxy` explicitly — meaningfully more code than the [recommended approach](#recommended-point-the-dev-servers-own-proxy-at-rws) above for the same result.

:::caution[HMR's WebSocket does not pass through `ReverseProxy`, either way]
`ReverseProxy` strips the `Upgrade` header on every forwarded request (it's a plain buffered request/response HTTP/1.1 proxy, not a WebSocket-aware one — see [Reverse Proxy](/proxy/reverse-proxy/)). Vite's HMR client opens a WebSocket back to the dev server for live updates; proxied through `ReverseProxy` that connection simply won't upgrade, and Vite falls back to full-page reloads instead of true HMR — regardless of which direction the proxying goes.

This is the real reason the [recommended approach](#recommended-point-the-dev-servers-own-proxy-at-rws) above has the dev server proxy *to* rws, not the other way around: the dev server keeps serving its own bundle and HMR socket directly, so none of its WebSocket handling is ever in rws's path.
:::

Given both the extra composition work and the HMR limitation, reach for this direction only if you specifically need rws's own middleware (auth, rate limiting, IP filtering) sitting in front of the dev bundle for a test — otherwise the recommended approach above gets you the same local dev loop with far less setup.

## Production has none of this

In production there's no separate dev server at all — build your frontend (`npm run build`), point `rws` at the output directory, and let `StaticResourceController` serve it directly, with `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK` handling client-side-router deep links. See [Static Files, Directory Listing & SPA Fallback](/features/static-files/).

---

# All Features

<https://rws8.tech/getting-started/features/>

This page is a single-page reference for everything the crate ships. Items that require an opt-in feature flag are annotated with the flag name in backticks.

---

## Server / Protocol

- **HTTP/1.1** — keep-alive, chunked transfer encoding, gzip compression, ETags, range requests, 30-second idle read timeout, 30 s to receive a whole request head (`408`)
- **HTTP/2** — ALPN negotiation, full multiplexing, forbidden-header stripping, `Alt-Svc` advertisement — `http2`
- **HTTP/3 / QUIC** — UDP listener via `quinn`, `h3` + `h3-quinn`, QUIC connection-level SNI — `http3` *(default)*
- **TLS** — `rustls` with `aws-lc-rs` crypto backend; no system OpenSSL dependency; FIPS-compatible — `http2`
- **mTLS** — client certificate verification via `WebPkiClientVerifier`; set `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE` — `http2`
- **Virtual-host routing** — per-domain TLS certificates via `SniCertResolver`; `.with_host("example.com")` on any `Router` — `http2`
- **HTTP → HTTPS redirect** — `Server::run_redirect()` listens on a second port and issues `301` responses — `http2`
- **ACME / automatic TLS** — automatic certificate provisioning compatible with Let's Encrypt — `acme`
- **Hot reload** — `SIGHUP` (or `POST /admin/config/reload`) reloads CORS rules, rate limits, log format, and TLS certs without restarting — `http2`
- **Graceful shutdown** — `SIGINT` / `SIGTERM` drain in-flight requests before exit; `SERVER_READY` flag cleared on shutdown
- **Gzip compression** — applied automatically based on `Accept-Encoding` to text bodies of at least 512 bytes (`compression::MIN_COMPRESS_SIZE`)
- **Static file serving** — a directory with no `index.html` renders a dark/light-adaptive directory listing page by default; files over 256 KiB streamed (`sendfile(2)` on plain TCP); ETag + `Last-Modified` with `304` revalidation, `Cache-Control: no-cache` by default (`RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL`)
- **SPA fallback** — `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK=index.html` serves a fallback file for unmatched routes instead of `404`, for React Router/Vue Router/etc. deep links; opt-in, scoped by an extension heuristic and `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK_EXCLUDE_PREFIXES`
- **Thread pool** (http1 only) — hand-rolled `ThreadPool`; connection-per-thread; no tokio — `http1`
- **Tokio async runtime** — used for `http2` and `http3` builds; `http1` is fully synchronous
- **Request framing** — heads up to 64 KiB across any number of reads (`431` beyond), pipelining, chunked request bodies; `Content-Length` + `Transfer-Encoding` or conflicting lengths are rejected (`400`) so a proxy in front can't be desynced (request smuggling)
- **`Expect: 100-continue`** — `100 Continue` is sent before the body is read, after the body-size check
- **Max request body size** — `RWS_CONFIG_MAX_BODY_SIZE_IN_BYTES` rejects oversized bodies with `413` before buffering, on HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
- **Outbound HTTP client** — `Client` (sync) and `AsyncClient` (`http2`); HTTPS with `http-client` or `http2`; redirects, `.form()`, `.body_json()`
- **WebSocket** (RFC 6455) — handshake and frame codec built in
- **WASM guest component** — `rws-wasm-shim` runs `App`/`Router`/middleware inside a `wasi:http/proxy` component (Wasmtime, Spin, Fastly Compute); see [WASM](/deployment/wasm/)

---

## Routing & App Building

- **`App`** — zero-config entry point; wraps all built-in controllers (static files, CORS, health, metrics, MCP, …)
- **`App::with_state(S)`** — state-aware dynamic router; `Arc` shared across all handlers; builder methods `.get()`, `.post()`, `.put()`, `.patch()`, `.delete()`
- **`App::with_async_state(S)`** — same API with `async fn` handlers — `http2`
- **`routes!` macro** — ergonomic route registration: `GET "/path" => handler` — `macros`
- **`Router`** — standalone path-based router with named parameters (`:name`) and trailing wildcards (`*name`); `PathParams::get(name)`
- **`Controller` trait** — low-level `is_matching` / `process` interface; register in `App::execute` for maximum control
- **Typed extractors** — `Body` (raw bytes), `BodyText` (UTF-8), `Query` (parsed query string), `RequestHeaders` (case-insensitive header map)
- **Typed errors** — `AppError` enum (`BadRequest`, `Unauthorized`, `Forbidden`, `NotFound`, `Conflict`, `UnprocessableEntity`, `TooManyRequests`, `Internal`) with `IntoResponse` trait
- **`Middleware` trait** — `handle(request, connection, next) -> Result`; compose via `.wrap(layer)`
- **`WithMiddleware`** — wraps any `Application`; layers applied in push order (first-pushed is outermost)
- **JSON (de)serialization** — `serde` / `serde_json` integration (e.g. `http_client::Response::json::()`) — `serde`
- **Tera templates** — render `.html` templates with a `serde_json::Value` context via `tera::render` — `tera`
- **In-process test client** — `TestClient::new(app)` dispatches requests without opening a TCP socket; use in unit and integration tests
- **WebSocket** — RFC 6455 handshake and frame codec built in; no third-party WebSocket library
- **SSE (Server-Sent Events)** — `Sse` builder for streaming events; ideal for streaming AI model output
- **Background scheduler** — `Scheduler::new().every(duration, fn).cron("…", fn).start()`
- **Background job queue** — `JobQueue` (in-memory) or `PersistentJobQueue` (crash-safe, model-backed); retry with exponential backoff — `jobs`
- **File / object storage** — `Storage` trait; `LocalStorage` (disk), `S3Storage` (AWS S3, R2, MinIO via AWS SigV4, no SDK), or `AzureBlobStorage` (Azure Blob via Shared Key/Managed Identity, no SDK) — `storage-local` / `storage-s3` / `storage-azure`
- **OpenAPI / Swagger** — `.openapi(OpenApiConfig)` generates `GET /openapi.json` + `GET /docs` (Swagger UI) from registered routes — `openapi`
- **Email / SMTP** — `mailer` module, plain SMTP; STARTTLS/SMTPS also needs `http-client` or `http2` — `mailer`
- **Outbound HTTP client** — `http_client::Client` (always compiled for plain HTTP); HTTPS without the server TLS stack — `http-client`
- **Per-route timeouts** — `with_timeout`/`with_timeout_state`/`with_timeout_async` wrap a handler with its own deadline; `TimeoutLayer` for a whole app; config-driven proxy's `timeout_ms`
- **Request ID middleware** — `RequestIdLayer` injects/echoes `X-Request-Id` on every request and response; `RequestId` extractor to read it

---

## Proxy & Gateway

- **`ReverseProxy`** — HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy middleware; round-robin backend selection
- **`H2ReverseProxy`** — HTTP/2 upstream proxy; bridges sync middleware into async via an isolated-runtime helper (works under any tokio runtime flavor) — `http2`
- **`GrpcProxy`** — wraps `H2ReverseProxy`; filters on `Content-Type: application/grpc*` — `http2`
- **`TcpProxy`** — standalone L4 TCP proxy; bidirectional `std::io::copy` relay; round-robin backends
- **`UdpProxy`** — standalone UDP datagram proxy; per-datagram ephemeral socket; round-robin backends
- **`WsProxy`** — standalone WebSocket proxy; relays raw bytes after upgrade handshake
- **Config-driven proxy mode** — `rws.config.toml` with `[[upstream]]` + `[[route]]` sections; no code required
- **Health checking** — per-upstream background health checker; dead backends removed automatically; configurable thresholds and intervals
- **Load balancing** — `round_robin`, `random`, `ip_hash`, or `least_connections` across live backends
- **`RewriteLayer`** — rewrite request headers, URI, and response headers / body / status code per route; regex URI rewrites via `request_uri_regex_rewrite` — `rewrite-regex`
- **Per-route rate limiting** — `PerRouteRateLimit` in config-driven mode; `RateLimitLayer` in code
- **Per-route Bearer auth** — `BearerAuthMiddleware` in config-driven mode; `JwtLayer` in code
- **Route matching** — host, path prefix, exact path, HTTP method, `Content-Type` prefix; first-match wins
- **Service discovery** — `BackendPool` with `Static`/`EnvPrefix`/`File`/`Dns`/`DnsSrv` (weighted)/`Consul`/`Docker` (label value as address) sources on a poll loop, plus `EtcdWatch` on a dedicated live watch stream
- **Circuit breaker + retries** — `CircuitBreaker` (Closed → Open → HalfOpen, capped probes), `RedisCircuitBreaker` (state shared across instances), `RetryLayer` on 502/503/504; `ReverseProxy::with_circuit_breaker`; `rws_circuit_breaker_state` metric
- **Canary / traffic splitting** — `CanaryLayer` with smooth weighted round-robin, live weight updates, `BackendPool` groups
- **Kubernetes Ingress** — `KubernetesIngressWatcher` watches the API (Exact/Prefix `pathType`, `ingressClassName`), `.from_service_account()` in-cluster
- **Private-CA upstreams** — `[[upstream]] tls_ca_file` / `ReverseProxy::tls_ca_file`
- **Non-blocking proxying** — config routes without middleware forward on the event loop, holding no thread

---

## Security

- **`RateLimitLayer`** — sliding-window rate limiter keyed by client IP; global singleton via `rate_limit::global()`; returns `429` when budget exceeded
- **`RedisRateLimiter`** — fixed-window limiter in Redis for a budget shared across instances
- **`BasicAuthLayer`** — HTTP Basic authentication middleware — `auth`
- **`JwtLayer`** — JWT Bearer token validation middleware (HS256) — `auth`; RS256/ES256 against a static public key via `::rs256`/`::es256` — `auth-asymmetric`
- **`ForwardAuthLayer`** — delegates the allow/deny decision to an external HTTP service (Traefik/nginx `auth_request` style) — `auth`
- **`IpFilter`** — allowlist / denylist middleware keyed by client IP
- **`crypto`** — Argon2id password hashing and verification; `signed_cookie`/`verify_signed_cookie` (HMAC-SHA256) and `encrypted_cookie`/`decrypt_cookie` (AES-256-GCM) — `crypto`
- **CSRF tokens** — secure random token generation and validation — `csrf`
- **SSO / OAuth 2.0 / OIDC** — `OidcAuth` login flow, RS256/ES256 `id_token` verification via JWKS, outbound HTTPS token exchange — `sso`
- **OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server** — `AuthServer`: rws issues its own HS256 tokens (`/oauth/token`, `/oauth/authorize`) — `sso-server`
- **SAML 2.0 Service Provider** — `SamlSp`: metadata, login, ACS, logout — `sso-saml`
- **Webhook verification** — `verify_webhook_signature` for GitHub, Shopify, Stripe — `webhook`
- **Secrets manager references** — `secrets::resolve()` for `vault://`, `aws-sm://`, `azkv://` — `secrets`
- **CORS** — built-in CORS controller; configurable origins, methods, and headers; hot-reloadable
- **mTLS** — mutual TLS client certificate verification — `http2`
- **No OpenSSL** — TLS via `rustls` + `aws-lc-rs`; fully static binaries

---

## Observability & Ops

- **`/healthz`** — liveness probe; always `200 OK` while the server is up
- **`/readyz`** — readiness probe; returns `503` after graceful shutdown begins (`SERVER_READY` flag)
- **`/metrics`** — Prometheus text-format scrape endpoint
- **`MetricsLayer`** — per-route `rws_route_requests_total{method,path,status}` counters and `rws_route_duration_seconds{method,path}` histograms
- **Global metrics** — `record_request()`, `record_error()`, `connection_open()` / `connection_close()` counters
- **`OtelLayer`** — OpenTelemetry trace propagation middleware
- **`CacheLayer`** — response caching middleware
- **Structured logging** — `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=json` (default), `combined`, or `off`; hot-reloadable
- **Config hot reload** — `SIGHUP` or `POST /admin/config/reload` reloads CORS, rate limits, log format, TLS certs; no restart required
- **Kubernetes-ready** — `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/metrics` all built in; graceful `SIGTERM` drain; static binary with no system dependencies
- **`rws --check`** — validates `rws.config.toml` (unknown keys, bad values, TLS files, undeclared upstreams, unset auth secrets) and exits 1 on errors, like `nginx -t`; `--format=json`
- **Helm chart** — `helm/rws/`
- **Background scheduler** — fixed-rate, fixed-delay and 6-field cron tasks
- **Job queue** — `JobQueue` (in-memory) and `PersistentJobQueue` (model-backed); retries with exponential backoff — `jobs`
- **Email** — `Mailer` over SMTP, STARTTLS or SMTPS; text + HTML — `mailer`

---

## AI & MCP

- **`McpServer`** — implements `Application`; serves the MCP Streamable HTTP protocol (`POST /mcp`, JSON-RPC 2.0)
- **Tool registration** — `.tool(name, description, schema, handler)` — any function returning a string
- **Resource registration** — `.resource(uri_template, name, description, handler)`
- **Prompt registration** — `.prompt(name, description, handler)`
- **Bearer auth gate** — `.require_bearer(token)` gates all MCP requests behind a static token
- **Fallthrough** — `.wrap(app)` passes non-MCP requests to another `Application`
- **20 built-in rws tools** in the binary — config, metrics, routes, cache, rate limits, CORS, static files, reload, maintenance mode, IP blocklist, feature flags, recent requests/errors (see [MCP](/mcp/overview/))
- **SSE streaming** — `Sse` builder for streaming AI tokens to browser clients
- **Protocol coverage** — session context (`.tool_with_context`), tool annotations, image/embedded content, JSON-RPC batches, list pagination, `GET /mcp` SSE push, `logging/setLevel`, dynamic registration with `list_changed`, progress, `completion/complete`, cancellation, `resources/subscribe`, server-side sampling, `roots/list`, async tools (`http2`), OAuth (`.require_oauth`, `sso`)

---

## Database / ORM

All ORM features require at least one of `model-sqlite`, `model-postgres`, or `model-mysql` (async, backed by `sqlx`; several can be compiled in, pick one with `RWS_DB_BACKEND`).

- **`#[derive(Model)]`** — generates `impl Model`, `Struct::repository()`, `Struct::query()` — `macros`
- **Table and column mapping** — `#[table(name = "…")]`, `#[column(name = "…")]`, `#[primary_key]`, `#[primary_key(auto_increment)]`, `#[ignore]`
- **`DbPool`** — async `sqlx` pool: `execute`, `query_rows`, `query::`, `query_raw`, `begin` (→ `DbTransaction` with `commit`/`rollback`), `transaction(closure)`, `migrate`
- **`Repository`** — `save` (INSERT or UPDATE by primary key), `save_all`, `find_by_id`, `find_all`, `delete_by_id`, `delete_all_by_id`, `count`, `exists_by_id`
- **`QueryBuilder`** — fluent `where_eq`, `filter`, `order_by`, `limit`, `offset`, `paginate`, `fetch_all`, `fetch_one`, `count`, `delete`, `update`; placeholder tokens auto-converted to `?` (SQLite/MySQL) or `$N` (PostgreSQL)
- **Migrations** — reads `*.sql` files in lexicographic order; `_schema_migrations` table tracks applied versions; each migration wrapped in a transaction
- **Relations** — `HasMany`, `HasOne`, `BelongsTo` with explicit `.load(&pool)`; no lazy loading, no hidden N+1 queries
- **SQLite** — `sqlx` SQLite driver — `model-sqlite`
- **PostgreSQL** — `sqlx` Postgres driver — `model-postgres`
- **MySQL / MariaDB** — `sqlx` MySQL driver — `model-mysql`

---

## Sessions & Cookies

- **`CookieJar` / `SetCookie`** — parse request cookies, write every RFC 6265 attribute
- **Sessions** — `SessionStore` (in-memory TTL), `DbSessionStore` (model-backed), `RedisSessionStore`

---

## File / Object Storage

- **`Storage` trait** — `put` / `get` / `delete` / `url`; swap backends without touching handlers
- **`LocalStorage`** — local disk — `storage-local`
- **`S3Storage`** — AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO via SigV4; static keys or EKS IRSA / ECS task role / EC2 IMDSv2; no AWS SDK — `storage-s3`
- **`AzureBlobStorage`** — Shared Key or Managed Identity; no Azure SDK — `storage-azure`

---

## Secrets

- **`secrets::resolve`** — `vault://path#field`, `aws-sm://name[#field]`, `azkv://vault/secret` resolved over HTTPS — `secrets`
- **Any `RWS_CONFIG_*` can be a reference** — `resolve_env_vars()` runs in `Server::setup()`; a broken reference fails startup instead of running with the literal string

---

## Dependency Injection

- **`Container`** — `TypeId`-keyed service store for concrete types and `dyn Trait` objects
- **`register::(value)`** — wraps in `Arc`, keyed by `TypeId::of::()`
- **`provide::(Arc)`** — stores trait objects directly
- **Named services** — `get_named::(name)` / `register_named::(name, value)` for multiple instances of the same type
- **`App::with_state(container)`** — pass the container directly as state; it's `Send + Sync + 'static` like any other state type, no wrapping needed
- **`into_arc()`** — for sharing one container across multiple hand-built `Application`s outside of `with_state`
- No external dependencies

---

# Configuration Overview

<https://rws8.tech/configuration/overview/>

`rust-web-server` uses a four-layer configuration system. Each layer can override
the one below it. All resolved values are stored as process environment variables
under the `RWS_CONFIG_*` namespace and read at request time — there is no config
struct passed through the call stack.

## Priority order (lowest to highest)

| Priority | Source | Notes |
|----------|--------|-------|
| 1 | Built-in defaults | Hardcoded in `src/entry_point/mod.rs` |
| 2 | System environment variables | Set before the process starts |
| 3 | `rws.config.toml` | Optional file in the working directory |
| 4 | CLI arguments | Flags passed on the command line |

A value set at a higher priority layer always wins. For example, `--port=9000` on
the command line overrides `port = 8080` in `rws.config.toml`, which in turn
overrides `RWS_CONFIG_PORT=8888` in the environment.

## How startup loading works

`Server::setup()` first calls `set_default_values()`, which gives the core
settings (IP, port, thread count, request allocation size, CORS, TLS paths, …)
their compiled-in default when no environment variable is set. Then
`bootstrap()` in `src/entry_point/mod.rs` runs three steps in order:

```rust
read_system_environment_variables();       // step 1: read existing env vars
override_environment_variables_from_config(None); // step 2: apply rws.config.toml
override_environment_variables_from_command_line_args(); // step 3: apply CLI flags
```

Settings without a default there fall back to the default in the code that
reads them. Per-request settings (CORS, CSP, client hints, static
`Cache-Control`, log format, …) are read through `ServerConfig::current()`, a
snapshot rebuilt only after something writes `RWS_CONFIG_*`.

The config file path can be overridden at the OS level:

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/rws/production.toml rws
```

## Hot reload

Some settings can be changed while the server is running without a restart.
Trigger a reload with either:

```bash
# Unix signal
kill -HUP $(pidof rws)

# HTTP endpoint (no body required)
curl -X POST http://localhost:7878/admin/config/reload
```

### What reloads

| Setting | Environment variable |
|---------|---------------------|
| CORS — all fields | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_*` |
| Rate-limit thresholds | `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS`, `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS` |
| Log format | `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT` |
| Request allocation size | `RWS_CONFIG_REQUEST_ALLOCATION_SIZE_IN_BYTES` |
| Security headers, CSP, client hints, nanosecond timestamps, static `Cache-Control` | `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS`, `RWS_CONFIG_CSP`, `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS`, `RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS`, `RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL` |
| Proxy routes and upstreams | `[[route]]`, `[[upstream]]`, `[middleware]` (kept as before if the new file has errors) |
| Tera templates | re-globbed from `RWS_CONFIG_TEMPLATE_DIR` (`tera` feature) |

On TLS builds, `SIGHUP` also rebuilds the `TlsAcceptor` from the updated
certificate files for all virtual hosts — no restart needed to rotate certs.

### What requires a restart

| Setting | Reason |
|---------|--------|
| IP / Port | The bound socket cannot be moved |
| Thread count | The thread pool is fixed at startup |
| Enabling the global rate limit | Decided once at startup (changing its numbers reloads) |
| `[[tcp_proxy]]`, `[[udp_proxy]]`, `[[ws_proxy]]` | Listeners start once |
| TLS cert / key paths (plain HTTP build) | The acceptor is built once |

:::note[Rate-limit changes are instant]
When a reload fires, the live global `RateLimiter` is updated in place via
`set_limits()`. Existing per-IP counters are preserved — only the limit values
change. The new limits apply to the very next request.
:::

## Reading config in handler code

`config_reload::current()` returns a typed `ConfigSnapshot` containing all
hot-reloadable values. It takes a brief read lock and clones a handful of
strings — safe to call on every request.

```rust
use rust_web_server::config_reload;

let cfg = config_reload::current();
if cfg.cors_allow_all {
    // allow any origin
}
println!("log format: {}", cfg.log_format);
```

The `ConfigSnapshot` fields map directly to environment variables:

| Field | Environment variable |
|-------|---------------------|
| `cors_allow_all` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` |
| `cors_allow_origins` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` |
| `cors_allow_credentials` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS` |
| `cors_allow_methods` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS` |
| `cors_allow_headers` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS` |
| `cors_expose_headers` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS` |
| `cors_max_age` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_MAX_AGE` |
| `rate_limit_max_requests` | `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` |
| `rate_limit_window_secs` | `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS` |
| `log_format` | `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT` |
| `request_allocation_size` | `RWS_CONFIG_REQUEST_ALLOCATION_SIZE_IN_BYTES` |

For settings that are not in `ConfigSnapshot` (IP, port, thread count, TLS
paths) read them directly:

```rust
let port = std::env::var("RWS_CONFIG_PORT").unwrap_or_else(|_| "7878".to_string());
```

## Memory

`rws` reads each request in chunks of `request_allocation_size_in_bytes`
(default 10000 bytes); larger bodies span several reads, and
`max_body_size_in_bytes` caps them (`0` = unlimited). Static files over
256 KiB are streamed from disk rather than buffered, and so are proxied
upstream bodies over 1 MB.

---

# Environment Variables

<https://rws8.tech/configuration/env-vars/>

All configuration in `rust-web-server` is ultimately stored as process
environment variables. The variables below can be set before the process starts
(e.g. in a shell, a `docker run -e` flag, a Kubernetes `env:` block, or a
`systemd` unit file). Settings in `rws.config.toml` and CLI flags map to the
same variables and will override anything set in the environment.

See the [Configuration Overview](/configuration/overview) for the full priority
order.

## Server

| Variable | Default | Type | Description |
|----------|---------|------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_IP` | `0.0.0.0` | string | IP address the server binds to. `0.0.0.0` makes the server reachable from any interface, including inside containers and Kubernetes pods. Override to `127.0.0.1` for local-only development. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_PORT` | `7878` | integer | TCP port the server listens on. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT` | `200` | integer | Size of the worker thread pool (synchronous HTTP/1.1 build only). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_REQUEST_ALLOCATION_SIZE_IN_BYTES` | `10000` | integer | Size in bytes of each individual socket read. Bodies larger than this are accumulated across multiple reads automatically (as long as `Content-Length` is present) — this tunes read-syscall chunk size, not the maximum accepted body size. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_SERVE_DOTFILES` | `false` | boolean | Serve files and directories whose name starts with `.` (`.git/`, `.env`). Off by default since 17.113.1; `.well-known/` is always served. Read at startup. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_OPEN_FILE_CACHE_SECS` | `1` | integer | How long an open static file is reused before its path is checked again (like nginx's `open_file_cache`). `0` turns the cache off. Edits in place are always served correctly; a replaced or deleted file is noticed within this many seconds. At most 128 files are held open. Read at startup; Unix only. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_OPEN_FILE_CACHE_STRICT` | `true` | boolean | `true`: every static request checks the cached file's size and modification time (one `fstat`), so an edit in place is served at once. `false`: that check is reused for `RWS_CONFIG_OPEN_FILE_CACHE_SECS`, like nginx's `open_file_cache_valid` — about 0.7 µs less per request, but a file edited in place can be served stale (old size or bytes) for up to that long. Read at startup. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME` | `per-core` (`rws` binary; `shared` for library apps) | string | Async builds, Unix only. The `rws` binary runs `per-core` since 18.0.0 (`shared` before); an application built on the library stays `shared` unless it sets this. `shared`: one multi-threaded tokio runtime (`TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS` workers) takes every connection. `per-core`: one single-threaded runtime per worker, each accepting on its own `SO_REUSEPORT` socket on the same port, like nginx's worker processes — a connection stays on one thread, with no work stealing or cross-thread wake-ups. On fast CPUs that's more throughput (on the benchmark's fastest runners +12–16% requests per second, and 4% less CPU per proxied request); on slower ones it costs about 12% more CPU per small request for a few percent more throughput. HTTP/3, the redirect listener and ACME stay on the main runtime; SIGHUP and shutdown work as usual. Read at startup. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL` | `no-cache` | string | `Cache-Control` sent with static files (since 18.0.0; other responses keep `no-store, …`). The default lets browsers keep a file and revalidate it with `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since`, which costs a `304` instead of the whole file. Set e.g. `public, max-age=3600` for assets with versioned names; an empty value sends the `no-store` default for static files too. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS` | `false` | boolean | Send `Accept-CH`, `Critical-CH` and the client hints in `Vary` on every response (always on before 18.0.0). Off by default: they add ~700 bytes to every response, and `Critical-CH` makes Chromium retry a request that arrived without the hints. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_MAX_BODY_SIZE_IN_BYTES` | `0` | integer | Maximum accepted request body size in bytes. `0` means unlimited. When set, a request whose `Content-Length` exceeds this is rejected with `413 Payload Too Large` before any body bytes are read, and the connection is closed. Applies to HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CSP` | unset | string | `Content-Security-Policy` header value, sent on every response. Unset: `default-src 'self'` with `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true`, otherwise no header (18.0.0; was always `default-src 'self'`). An empty value suppresses the header. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS` | `false` | boolean | Send `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, `Permissions-Policy: geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()` and the default CSP on every response (always sent before 18.0.0). `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` is always sent. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS` | `false` | boolean | Send `Date-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` on every response and `Last-Modified-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` on static files (always sent before 18.0.0). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK` | `` (empty) | path | File (e.g. `index.html`) served for a `GET`/`HEAD` that matches no file or directory, instead of `404` — for client-side routers. Paths whose last segment contains a `.` still get `404`. Empty disables it. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK_EXCLUDE_PREFIXES` | `` (empty) | string | Comma-separated path prefixes (e.g. `/api,/healthz`) that never get the SPA fallback. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_FILE` | `rws.config.toml` | path | Config file to load (settings and proxy routes) instead of `./rws.config.toml`. |

:::note[Thread count and the async build]
`RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT` only applies to the `http1`-only build, which uses a
hand-rolled `ThreadPool`. The `http2` / `http3` builds run on tokio and manage
concurrency differently — this variable is read but ignored at runtime.
:::

## TLS

| Variable | Default | Type | Description |
|----------|---------|------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE` | `` (empty) | path | Path to the PEM-encoded certificate chain file. When non-empty, enables HTTPS, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE` | `` (empty) | path | Path to the PEM-encoded private key file. Must match `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE` | `` (empty) | path | Path to a PEM-encoded CA certificate used to verify client certificates (mTLS). When set, the TLS handshake requires a valid client certificate signed by this CA. Connections without a valid cert are rejected before any HTTP processing. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT` | `` (empty) | integer | When non-empty, a plain-HTTP listener is started on this port that issues `301 Moved Permanently` redirects to HTTPS. Set to `80` when running on standard ports. Requires TLS to be configured. |

### Virtual hosts

Per-domain TLS is configured through indexed variables. The server reads entries
sequentially, stopping at the first missing index.

| Variable | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_0_DOMAIN` | Domain name for virtual host 0 (e.g. `example.com`) |
| `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_0_CERT_FILE` | Certificate file for virtual host 0 |
| `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_0_KEY_FILE` | Private key file for virtual host 0 |
| `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_DOMAIN` | Domain name for virtual host 1 |
| `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_CERT_FILE` | Certificate file for virtual host 1 |
| `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_KEY_FILE` | Private key file for virtual host 1 |

Continue the pattern (`_2_`, `_3_`, …) for as many domains as needed. The
`SniCertResolver` selects the correct certificate at TLS handshake time.

### ACME (Automatic Certificate Management)

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DOMAINS` | `` (empty) | Comma-separated list of domain names. Setting this activates ACME at startup. Example: `example.com,www.example.com`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_EMAIL` | `` (empty) | Contact email sent to the CA. Recommended but not required by all CAs. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_STAGING` | `false` | Set to `true` to use the Let's Encrypt staging environment for testing. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DIRECTORY` | `` (empty) | Custom ACME directory URL. Defaults to Let's Encrypt production when empty. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CERT_PATH` | `` (empty) | Where to write the provisioned certificate chain (PEM). Defaults to `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE`, else `.rws/acme/cert.pem` (since 17.113.1; was `cert.pem` in the web root). When TLS paths are unset, ACME also points the TLS listener at this file. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_KEY_PATH` | `` (empty) | Where to write the certificate's private key (PEM). Defaults to `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE`, else `.rws/acme/key.pem`; written `0600`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE_PORT` | `80` | Port the CA connects to for HTTP-01. A temporary listener answers at startup; once the redirect listener (`RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT`) runs on this port it answers renewal challenges. Must be reachable from the internet on port 80. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_BEFORE_DAYS` | `` (empty) | Renew this many days before expiry. Empty (the default since 18.0.0; it was `30`): at two-thirds of the certificate's lifetime, or earlier when the CA's renewal information (RFC 9773) says so. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_PROFILE` | `` (empty) | Certificate profile to order, e.g. `shortlived` (6-day certificates) or `tlsserver` at Let's Encrypt. Empty: the CA's default. A profile the CA doesn't offer stops provisioning with the list it offers. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ACCOUNT_KEY_PATH` | `.rws/acme/account.key` | Path to persist the ACME account key between restarts (written `0600`). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CA_FILE` | `` (empty) | PEM file of extra root CAs to trust for the ACME directory, on top of the public roots — for private ACME CAs (step-ca, Pebble). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE` | `http-01` | How the CA checks you control the domains: `http-01` (port 80), `tls-alpn-01` (on the HTTPS port, RFC 8737), `dns-01` (a TXT record; needed for wildcards) or `dns-persist-01` (a TXT record you publish once). Since 18.4.0. See [Challenge types](/features/acme/#challenge-types). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_PROVIDER` | `` (empty) | DNS-01: `rfc2136` (a DNS UPDATE), `cloudflare`, `route53` (credentials from `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` / `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`) or `exec` (a program). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_TOKEN` | `` (empty) | DNS-01 `cloudflare`: the API token (DNS edit). No command-line flag; never printed. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_ZONE_ID` | `` (empty) | DNS-01 `cloudflare` / `route53`: the zone's id instead of looking it up. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_URL` | `` (empty) | DNS-01 `cloudflare` / `route53`: another API base URL (a proxy, a test double). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_SERVER` | `` (empty) | DNS-01: `rfc2136`'s primary server, `host[:port]` (port 53); with `exec`, optional: where to check that the record is visible (else the system resolver). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_ZONE` | `` (empty) | DNS-01: the zone holding `_acme-challenge` records; found by an SOA lookup when empty. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_KEY` | `` (empty) | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: the TSIG key name. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_SECRET` | `` (empty) | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: the TSIG secret, base64. Set it here or in `rws.config.toml` — there is no command-line flag — and it is never printed. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_ALGORITHM` | `hmac-sha256` | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: `hmac-sha256` or `hmac-sha512`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_EXEC` | `` (empty) | DNS-01 `exec`: run as `<program> present <fqdn> <value>` and `<program> cleanup <fqdn> <value>`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_PROPAGATION_SECS` | `120` | DNS-01: how long to wait for the record to be visible before the CA checks it. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND` | `false` | `true`: order a certificate at the first TLS handshake for a name `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND_ASK` allows. Since 18.4.0. See [On-demand TLS](/features/acme/#on-demand-tls). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND_ASK` | `` (empty) | URL asked `?domain=<name>` before each on-demand order; a 2xx answer allows it. Required with `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS` | `` (empty) | Redis `host:port` shared by replicas: one orders each certificate, all install it, and any answers the CA's challenges. Since 18.4.0. See [Several replicas](/features/acme/#several-replicas). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PASSWORD` | `` (empty) | Password for `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS`. No command-line flag; never printed. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PREFIX` | `rws:acme` | Key prefix in that Redis, for several sites in one. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_CHECK_INTERVAL_SECS` | `43200` | Longest time between renewal checks (sooner when renewal is due earlier or the CA's renewal information asks). After a failed renewal the next attempt comes within an hour. |

## CORS

Off by default (since 18.0.0). When `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` is `true` the server sets permissive CORS
headers on every response — any origin, with credentials — and the more specific `CORS_ALLOW_*` variables are
ignored.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` | `false` | When `true`, allows all CORS requests from any origin, with credentials. Was `true` before 18.0.0. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` | `` (empty) | Comma-separated list of allowed origins. Example: `https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com`. Ignored when `CORS_ALLOW_ALL` is `true`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS` | `` (empty) | Comma-separated list of allowed HTTP methods. Example: `GET,POST,PUT`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS` | `` (empty) | Comma-separated list of allowed request headers (lowercase). Example: `content-type,x-api-key`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS` | `` (empty) | Set to `true` to allow cookies and credentials to be sent with cross-origin requests. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_EXPOSE_HEADERS` | `` (empty) | Comma-separated list of response headers the browser may expose to JavaScript (lowercase). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_MAX_AGE` | `86400` | How long (in seconds) the browser may cache a preflight response. Default is 24 hours. |

All CORS variables are hot-reloadable. Send `SIGHUP` or `POST /admin/config/reload`
to apply changes without restarting.

## Rate limiting

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` | `` (unset) | Maximum number of requests allowed per client IP within the window. The `rws` binary enforces the global limit only when this is set above `0` (decided at startup). `rate_limit::global()` in library code defaults to `1000`. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS` | `60` | Sliding window length in seconds. |

Rate-limit values are hot-reloadable. Existing per-IP counters are preserved when
limits change — only the allowed maximum and window size are updated.

## Circuit breaker

Read by `RedisCircuitBreaker::from_env()` (with `RWS_REDIS_HOST`/`_PORT`/`_PASSWORD`;
see [Circuit breaker](/proxy/circuit-breaker/)). Config-driven proxy routes
don't use them.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_THRESHOLD` | `5` | Consecutive failures before the circuit opens. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_RECOVERY_SECS` | `30` | Seconds the circuit stays open before a half-open probe. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_CIRCUIT_BREAKER_MAX_HALF_OPEN_PROBES` | `1` | Probe requests allowed while half-open. |

## Logging

| Variable | Default | Options | Description |
|----------|---------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_PROXY_PROTOCOL` | `false` | boolean | Every connection to the main listener starts with a PROXY protocol v1 or v2 header (HAProxy `send-proxy`, AWS NLB, GCP); its source address becomes the client address. Connections without one are closed. Since 18.3.0; read at startup. See [Behind a load balancer](/proxy/overview/#behind-an-l4-load-balancer-proxy-protocol). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_WATCH` | `false` | boolean | Reload when `rws.config.toml` (or `RWS_CONFIG_FILE`) or a configured TLS certificate or key changes — the same validated reload as `SIGHUP`, checked once a second (since 18.1.0). Read at startup. See [Hot reload](/features/hot-reload/#reloading-when-the-file-changes). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACCESS_LOG` | (stdout) | path | Append access-log lines to this file instead of stdout (since 18.1.0). Opened at the first line; `SIGUSR1` reopens it (for logrotate). Read at startup. See [Logs](/deployment/observability/#writing-to-a-file). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACCESS_LOG_MAX_SIZE` | `0` | bytes (`K`/`M`/`G` suffixes) | Rotate the access-log file when the next lines would take it past this size: `access.log` → `access.log.1` …. `0` never rotates (leave it to logrotate). |
| `RWS_CONFIG_ACCESS_LOG_KEEP` | `5` | integer | Rotated access-log files to keep; `0` empties the file instead of keeping any. |
| `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT` | `json` | `json`, `combined`, `off` | Log format for access logs. `json` writes structured JSON. `combined` writes Combined Log Format (Apache/nginx-compatible). `off` (or `none`) writes no per-request line — e.g. behind a proxy that already logs. Hot-reloadable. |

The log format is hot-reloadable.

## Templates

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_CONFIG_TEMPLATE_DIR` | `templates` | Directory containing Tera HTML templates. Only relevant when the `tera` Cargo feature is enabled. |

## Database

Database variables are only used when the `model-sqlite`, `model-postgres`, or
`model-mysql` Cargo feature is enabled. They are not part of the `RWS_CONFIG_*`
namespace — they use a shorter `RWS_DB_*` prefix.

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `RWS_DB_BACKEND` | inferred | `sqlite`, `postgres`, or `mysql`. Inferred when exactly one `model-*` feature is compiled in; required otherwise. |
| `RWS_DB_HOST` | `localhost` | Database server hostname or IP address. |
| `RWS_DB_PORT` | `5432` | Database server port. The default matches PostgreSQL; MySQL uses `3306`. |
| `RWS_DB_USER` | `` (empty) | Database user name. |
| `RWS_DB_PASSWORD` | `` (empty) | Database password. |
| `RWS_DB_NAME` | `` (required) | Database name. No default — the server will fail to start if this is unset when the model feature is active. |
| `RWS_DB_POOL_SIZE` | `10` | Number of connections to pre-create in the connection pool at startup. |

:::caution[SQLite path]
For `model-sqlite`, `RWS_DB_NAME` is the file path of the SQLite database, for
example `RWS_DB_NAME=./data/app.db`. Use `:memory:` for an in-memory database
(useful in tests).
:::

## Example: production environment

```bash
# Server
export RWS_CONFIG_IP=0.0.0.0
export RWS_CONFIG_PORT=443
export RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT=500

# TLS
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/certs/server.pem
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE=/etc/ssl/private/server.key
export RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT=80

# CORS — restrict to known origins
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=false
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_METHODS=GET,POST,PUT,DELETE
export RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_HEADERS=content-type,authorization

# Rate limiting
export RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS=500
export RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_WINDOW_SECS=60

# Logging
export RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=json
```

---

# Config File (rws.config.toml)

<https://rws8.tech/configuration/config-file/>

`rws.config.toml` is an optional TOML file placed in the server's working
directory. It provides a convenient alternative to environment variables and CLI
flags. Any key set here overrides the built-in default and any system environment
variable, but can be overridden by a CLI flag.

The file is auto-detected at startup. Override the path with the
`RWS_CONFIG_FILE` environment variable (used for both server settings and
proxy routes):

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/rws/prod.toml rws
```

### Check the file before you deploy

`rws --check` validates the configuration without starting the server and
exits `0` if it has no errors, `1` otherwise — like `nginx -t`:

```bash
rws --check                       # the file rws would load
rws --check=/etc/rws/prod.toml    # a specific file
rws --check --format=json         # machine-readable, for CI and editors
```

With `--format=json` the report is one JSON object —
`{"path":…,"ok":…,"errors":[…],"warnings":[…]}` — with the same exit codes.

```text
error: [route.action] upsteam: unknown key — ignored
error: route 'api': upstream 'missing' is not a declared [[upstream]]
warning: [acme] without http_redirect_port: nothing answers the HTTP-01 challenge on port 80; set http_redirect_port = 80
rws.config.toml: 2 errors, 1 warning
```

It reports unknown keys anywhere in the file, values of the wrong type,
certificate and key files that are missing or don't load, ACME mistakes,
proxy routes that point at undeclared upstreams, unknown action types, IP
filter entries that aren't addresses, and auth secrets that aren't set.
Secrets and files are checked in the current environment, so run it where the
server runs. Proxy problems are also printed when the server starts.

The same checks are a library call, e.g. in a test that keeps a deployment's
config honest:

```rust
use rust_web_server::config_check;

#[test]
fn production_config_is_valid() {
    let report = config_check::check_file("deploy/rws.config.toml");
    assert!(report.is_ok(), "{}", report.render("deploy/rws.config.toml"));
}
```

`report.render_json(path)` gives the `--format=json` output.

### How keys map to settings

Every setting has an `RWS_CONFIG_*` environment variable. In the file, a key's
variable is its table name plus the key, upper-cased:

| In `rws.config.toml` | Setting |
|---|---|
| `port = 443` (top level) | `RWS_CONFIG_PORT` |
| `[cors]` `allow_all = false` | `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL` |
| `[rate_limit]` `max_requests = 500` | `RWS_CONFIG_RATE_LIMIT_MAX_REQUESTS` |
| 2nd `[[virtual_host]]` block, `domain = ...` | `RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_DOMAIN` |

Strings keep their exact contents (`csp = "default-src 'self'; img-src *"`
works); arrays become comma-separated lists. A key that doesn't correspond to
any setting is reported at startup — `Warning: unknown setting '[server] port'
in rws.config.toml — ignored` — rather than silently dropped. `[[route]]`,
`[[upstream]]`, `[[tcp_proxy]]`, `[[udp_proxy]]`, `[[ws_proxy]]`, and
`[middleware]` tables configure the proxy (below) and aren't settings.

An inline table is the same as a sub-table, here and in the proxy sections:

```toml
rate_limit = { max_requests = 1000, window_secs = 60 }
# same as
[rate_limit]
max_requests = 1000
window_secs  = 60
```

:::note[Proxy mode]
When the file contains at least one `[[route]]` or `[[upstream]]` section, the
server starts in **proxy mode** (`ConfigDrivenApp`). The built-in static-file and
controller stack is used only as a fallback for unmatched requests.
:::

## Server settings (top level)

Basic server settings go at the top of the file, before any `[section]`
header. Each key maps to the `RWS_CONFIG_*` environment variable and the
`--flag` of the same name (`rws --help` lists them all).

```toml
ip                 = "0.0.0.0"   # RWS_CONFIG_IP (default: 0.0.0.0)
port               = 443         # RWS_CONFIG_PORT (default: 7878)
thread_count       = 200         # RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT (default: 200, http1 build only)
tls_cert_file      = "cert.pem"  # RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE — enables HTTPS, HTTP/2, HTTP/3
tls_key_file       = "key.pem"   # RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE
http_redirect_port = 80          # RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT — HTTP → HTTPS redirect listener
request_allocation_size_in_bytes = 10000  # RWS_CONFIG_REQUEST_ALLOCATION_SIZE_IN_BYTES — per-read chunk size
```

:::caution
Don't wrap these in a `[server]` table: keys are prefixed with their table's
name, so `[server] port = 443` becomes `--server-port`, which doesn't exist
and is ignored.
:::

## `[acme]`

Automatic HTTPS from Let's Encrypt or another ACME CA (`acme` feature,
included in the prebuilt binaries). Setting `domains` enables it. See
[Automatic HTTPS](/features/acme/) for how it works.

```toml
[acme]
domains        = ["example.com", "www.example.com"]  # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DOMAINS
email          = "ops@example.com"                   # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_EMAIL
staging        = false             # Let's Encrypt staging CA (testing)
directory      = ""                # ACME directory URL of another CA
ca_file        = ""                # extra root CA PEM for a private ACME CA
challenge      = "http-01"         # or "tls-alpn-01" (port 443 only), "dns-01" (wildcards),
                                   # "dns-persist-01" (a TXT record you publish once)
challenge_port = 80                # port the CA connects to for HTTP-01
# dns_provider = "rfc2136"         # dns-01: rfc2136, cloudflare, route53 or exec; dns_server, dns_zone,
#                                  # dns_tsig_key, dns_tsig_secret, dns_tsig_algorithm,
#                                  # dns_exec, dns_api_token, dns_zone_id, dns_api_url,
#                                  # dns_propagation_secs — see Automatic HTTPS
# redis        = "10.0.0.20:6379"  # replicas share certificates and challenges
#                                  # (redis_password, redis_prefix)
# on_demand     = true             # certificates for names on_demand_ask allows,
# on_demand_ask = "http://127.0.0.1:9000/allowed"   # at their first handshake
cert_path      = ""                # default: tls_cert_file, else cert.pem
key_path       = ""                # default: tls_key_file, else key.pem
profile        = ""                # certificate profile, e.g. "shortlived"
# renew_before_days       = 30                  # default: at 2/3 of the lifetime
renew_check_interval_secs = 43200               # longest time between checks
account_key_path          = "acme_account.key"  # ACME account key, kept between restarts
```

## `[cors]`

CORS policy applied to every response. All fields are hot-reloadable.

```toml
[cors]
# Allow every origin, with credentials (default false since 18.0.0). When
# true, the specific allow_* fields below are ignored.
allow_all         = false

# Restrict to specific origins (comma-separated). Used when allow_all = false.
allow_origins     = "https://app.example.com,https://admin.example.com"

# Allowed HTTP methods (comma-separated).
allow_methods     = "GET,POST,PUT,DELETE,OPTIONS"

# Allowed request headers, in lowercase (comma-separated).
allow_headers     = "content-type,authorization,x-api-key"

# Whether to allow cookies and credentials with cross-origin requests.
allow_credentials = "true"

# Response headers the browser may expose to JavaScript (comma-separated, lowercase).
expose_headers    = "x-request-id,x-rate-limit-remaining"

# Preflight cache duration in seconds (default: 86400 = 24 hours).
max_age           = 86400
```

## `[rate_limit]`
