`check`, unlike `RateLimiter::check`, returns `Result<bool, std::io::Error>` — the network call to Redis can fail. Callers decide whether an unreachable Redis server should fail open (allow the request) or fail closed (reject it); `RedisRateLimiter` does not pick one for you.

### API

- `RedisRateLimiter::new(addr, password, max_requests, window_secs)` — connect to `addr` (e.g. `"127.0.0.1:6379"`).
- `RedisRateLimiter::from_env()` — build from the environment variables above.
- `check(key) -> Result<bool, io::Error>` — atomically increments the shared counter for `key` and returns whether the call is within budget.
- `remaining(key) -> Result<u32, io::Error>` — requests `key` may still make in the current window.
- `set_limits(max_requests, window_secs)` — update limits on a live limiter; takes effect on the next `check`/`remaining`.
- `reset(key) -> Result<(), io::Error>` — deletes the Redis key for `key`. Useful in tests.

Cloning a `RedisRateLimiter` is cheap — all clones share the same underlying TCP connection, mirroring `RedisSessionStore`'s connection-sharing model (see [Sessions](/features/sessions/)).

---

# Compression

<https://rws8.tech/features/compression/>

`rust-web-server` compresses text responses automatically, in the coding the
client prefers: `br` (brotli), `zstd` or `gzip` (brotli and zstd since
18.1.0). No middleware registration, no configuration.

## Which coding

The request's `Accept-Encoding` decides: the coding with the highest `q`
wins, `*` stands for any coding not listed, and `q=0` refuses one. When
several are equally acceptable — a browser sends
`gzip, deflate, br, zstd` — the server's order breaks the tie:

| Response | Order | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Static files (compressed once, then cached) | `br`, `zstd`, `gzip` | brotli's output is smallest, and it is paid for once |
| Everything else (compressed per response) | `zstd`, `br`, `gzip` | zstd costs the least CPU at a similar ratio |

A request without `Accept-Encoding` gets the response uncompressed.

Brotli and zstd are the `brotli` and `zstd` Cargo features, both on by
default (`zstd` builds the C libzstd). Without them only gzip is offered;
the `http1`-only build (`--no-default-features --features http1`) has
gzip only.

## What gets compressed

`compression::apply_compression(request, response)` runs after your
handler, before the response is written (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3). It
compresses when:

1. The response has no `Content-Encoding` already — a backend's compressed
   response is passed through, never compressed twice.
2. The body is at least 512 bytes (`compression::MIN_COMPRESS_SIZE`, the
   same minimum Caddy uses).
3. The client accepts a coding (above).
4. The `Content-Type` is compressible (below).
5. The response isn't partial: a `206` is a slice of the file and is sent as
   is (since 17.113.2).

Levels are the fast ones peers use for per-response compression: brotli 4,
zstd 3, gzip 6 (`compression::Level::Dynamic`; brotli's default, 11, is
about a hundred times slower than gzip). If the result isn't smaller than
the original, the original is sent. A compressed response gets:

- `Content-Encoding: br`, `zstd` or `gzip`
- `Vary: Accept-Encoding` (appended to an existing `Vary`, or added)
- its own `ETag` when it had one: `"x"` becomes `"x-br"` (since 18.1.0;
  each representation needs a different strong ETag)

`compression::apply_gzip` still exists and only ever uses gzip.

## Compressible content types

Only responses whose `Content-Type` starts with one of these are compressed:

| MIME type |
|-----------|
| `text/html` |
| `text/css` |
| `text/javascript` |
| `text/plain` |
| `text/xml` |
| `application/json` |
| `application/javascript` |
| `application/xml` |
| `application/xhtml+xml` |
| `image/svg+xml` |

Images, audio, video, fonts and archives are already compressed.

## Static files are compressed once

A static file is compressed once per version per coding, not on every
request: the open-file cache keeps the brotli, zstd and gzip forms of each
file up to 1 MiB, keyed by its size and modification time, within the same
8 MiB memory budget, at the higher `Level::Static` (brotli 6, zstd 6,
gzip 6). An edit is picked up at once; a file modified less than 2 seconds
ago isn't cached yet. The `ETag` carries the coding (`"<mtime>-<size>-br"`),
so a client revalidating gets a `304` for the representation it holds.

### Precompressed files

If `app.js.br`, `app.js.zst` or `app.js.gz` sits next to `app.js`, is a
regular file (not a symlink) and is at least as new as `app.js`, its bytes
are sent for that coding instead of compressing — as nginx's `gzip_static`
does. Build them once with the best settings (`brotli -q 11`,
`zstd -19`):

```bash
brotli -q 11 -k static/app.js       # static/app.js.br
zstd -19 -k static/app.js           # static/app.js.zst
gzip -9 -k static/app.js            # static/app.js.gz
```

A sibling older than the file (the file was edited since) is ignored, and
the file is compressed instead. Like the cached forms, this applies to
files up to 1 MiB.

## Large files

Static files larger than **256 KiB** are sent without being read into
memory — `sendfile(2)` over plain HTTP, chunked otherwise — except that a
client accepting a coding gets a compressible file of up to **1 MiB**
compressed from the cache. Larger files are sent uncompressed.

:::note[Range requests]
Byte-range requests (`Range: bytes=N-M`) are answered with the slice,
uncompressed: compressing a slice would describe bytes that don't exist.
:::

## Checking it

```bash
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "Accept-Encoding: br" http://localhost:7878/app.js
# content-encoding: br
# vary: Accept-Encoding
# etag: "1793007086216830266-26624-br"
```

## No configuration needed

There are no `rws.config.toml` keys, environment variables or middleware
layers for compression.

---

# HTTPS / TLS

<https://rws8.tech/features/https-tls/>

## Feature requirements

TLS is available when you build with the `http2` or `http3` (default) feature.
The `http1`-only build has no TLS support.

```bash
# Default build — HTTP/3 + HTTP/2 + TLS
cargo build

# HTTP/2 + TLS only, no QUIC
cargo build --no-default-features --features http2
```

## Generating a self-signed certificate

Use `openssl` to create a certificate and key for local development:

```bash
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem \
  -days 365 -nodes -subj "/CN=localhost"
```

## Starting the server with TLS

Pass the certificate and key on the command line:

```bash
cargo run -- --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```

Alternatively, set environment variables or add them to `rws.config.toml`:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE=cert.pem
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE=key.pem
cargo run
```

```toml
# rws.config.toml
tls_cert_file = "cert.pem"
tls_key_file  = "key.pem"
```

## TLS implementation

`rust-web-server` uses [rustls](https://github.com/rustls/rustls) with the
`aws-lc-rs` cryptography backend. There is no dependency on OpenSSL.

## ALPN negotiation

When a TLS certificate is configured, the server advertises both `h2` and
`http/1.1` via ALPN in the TLS handshake. A single port handles HTTP/2 and
HTTP/1.1 simultaneously — no extra configuration is required.

```
alpn_protocols = ["h2", "http/1.1"]
```

The HTTP/2 server (`h2_server`) turns HTTP/2 streams into the same `Request` /
`Application::execute` / `Response` pipeline that HTTP/1.1 uses.

## HTTP → HTTPS redirect

Set `RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT` to have the server also listen on a plain
HTTP port and issue `301 Moved Permanently` redirects to HTTPS:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT=80
```

```toml
# rws.config.toml
http_redirect_port = "80"
```

`Server::run_redirect()` binds the redirect listener and sends every incoming
request to the HTTPS port with a `301` response.

## Alt-Svc advertisement

HTTP/1.1 TLS responses include an `Alt-Svc` header so clients learn that a
faster protocol is available:

- HTTP/3 build: `Alt-Svc: h3=":7878"`
- HTTP/2-only build: `Alt-Svc: h2=":7878"`

Browsers that support HTTP/3 will upgrade automatically on subsequent requests.

## Configuration reference

| Variable | Config key | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE` | `tls_cert_file` | Path to the PEM certificate chain |
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE` | `tls_key_file` | Path to the PEM private key |
| `RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT` | `http_redirect_port` | Plain HTTP port that issues 301 → HTTPS |

:::note[Hot reload]
Send `SIGHUP` or `POST /admin/config/reload` to reload the TLS certificate
from disk without restarting the server. This also rebuilds the TLS acceptor
for all configured virtual hosts.
:::


## Upstream TLS (proxy mode)

When using the config-driven proxy (`rws.config.toml`), prefix backend addresses with `https://` to connect to upstream services over TLS:

```toml
[[upstream]]
name     = "secure-api"
backends = ["https://api.internal:443", "https://api2.internal:443"]
```

Certificate verification uses the WebPKI root store (same trust anchors as browsers). To trust a private CA instead, set `tls_ca_file` on the `[[upstream]]` (since 18.0.0). Requires the `http-client` or `http2` feature — included in all builds except `--no-default-features --features http1`.

See [Config-Driven Proxy → TLS upstreams](/proxy/config-driven/#tls-https-upstreams) for the full reference.

---

# Automatic HTTPS (ACME)

<https://rws8.tech/features/acme/>

`rws` obtains certificates from Let's Encrypt (or any ACME CA) by itself and
keeps them renewed. Point a domain's DNS at the server, then:

```toml
# rws.config.toml
port               = 443
http_redirect_port = 80     # HTTP → HTTPS redirects; also answers ACME challenges

[acme]
domains = ["example.com", "www.example.com"]
email   = "you@example.com"
```

```bash
rws
```

On first start `rws` requests a certificate, stores it in `.rws/acme/`
(`cert.pem`, `key.pem`, `account.key` — keys `0600`, the directory `0700`,
and never served: the working directory is the web root), and starts serving HTTPS, HTTP/2, and
HTTP/3 with it. Later starts reuse the stored certificate. Renewal happens in
the background and is hot-swapped without dropping connections.

:::note[Which binaries include ACME]
The prebuilt binaries (Homebrew, `cargo binstall`, Docker, GitHub Releases)
include it. When building from source, enable the `acme` feature:
`cargo install rust-web-server --features acme,auth`. A binary built without
it prints a warning if `[acme]` is configured instead of silently serving
plain HTTP.
:::

## Requirements

- **DNS** for every domain in `domains` points at this server.
- **One way for the CA to check you control the domains**: port 80 reachable
  from the internet (HTTP-01, the default), or port 443 (TLS-ALPN-01), or
  write access to the domain's DNS (DNS-01, also for wildcards) — see
  [Challenge types](#challenge-types).
- **Binding ports 80/443 on Linux** needs root or the capability:
  `sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep "$(which rws)"`.

IPv6 is handled: when a domain has an AAAA record, Let's Encrypt validates
over IPv6, so the challenge and redirect listeners accept both IPv4 and IPv6.

## How it works

1. **Startup.** If no certificate exists, or it is due for renewal (see 4),
   `rws` runs the ACME flow before opening the HTTPS
   port: account (key saved to `.rws/acme/account.key`), order, HTTP-01 challenge,
   ECDSA P-256 key + CSR, finalize, download.
2. **Challenges.** At startup a temporary listener on the challenge port
   (default 80) answers them. Once the HTTP → HTTPS redirect listener is
   running on that port, it answers challenges itself — so renewals never
   compete with it for port 80.
3. **First-time failures are retried**, e.g. while DNS for a new domain is
   still propagating: after 30 s, doubling up to every 15 minutes, until a
   certificate is issued.
4. **Renewal** (since 18.0.0). A certificate is renewed at two-thirds of its
   lifetime — day 60 of 90, day 30 of 45, day 4 of 6 — or earlier when the
   CA's ACME Renewal Information ([RFC 9773](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9773.html))
   suggests a window that opens sooner, e.g. after a revocation. `rws` asks
   for it at every check (every 12 hours at most, every 6 when the CA has
   renewal information, sooner when renewal is due earlier or the CA's
   `Retry-After` says so) and picks a point in the window that's fixed per
   certificate. The renewal order names the certificate it replaces, so the
   CA can exempt it from rate limits. A failed renewal is retried within an
   hour. After renewing it reloads the TLS certificate in place (on Unix, via
   the same `SIGHUP` reload used for config). `renew_before_days`, if set,
   replaces the two-thirds point (a CA window that opens earlier still wins).
5. **Profiles.** `profile` orders a certificate profile the CA offers —
   Let's Encrypt has `classic`, `tlsserver` and `shortlived` (6-day
   certificates). A name the CA doesn't list stops provisioning with the list
   it offers. Unset, the CA picks its default.

The ACME client (RFC 8555) is implemented in-crate. It has been tested end to
end against [Pebble](https://github.com/letsencrypt/pebble), Let's Encrypt's
test CA, including a `shortlived` profile and renewal on Pebble's renewal
information through the redirect listener.

## Testing with the staging CA

Let's Encrypt production has strict
[rate limits](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/). Try your setup
against staging first — its certificates aren't browser-trusted, but the
limits are generous:

```toml
[acme]
domains = ["example.com"]
staging = true
```

Delete `.rws/acme/` before switching back to production.

Before 17.113.1 the defaults were `cert.pem`, `key.pem` and `acme_account.key`
in the working directory — the web root, so the keys could be downloaded.
On upgrade, files found there are moved into `.rws/acme/` (when the default
paths are in use), and the static server no longer serves `*.pem`, `*.key`
or `rws.config.toml` anywhere. Rotate a key that was exposed.

## Private ACME CAs

To use step-ca, an internal Boulder, or Pebble, set the directory URL and
trust the CA's root certificate (in addition to the public roots):

```toml
[acme]
domains   = ["internal.example"]
directory = "https://ca.internal.example:9000/acme/acme/directory"
ca_file   = "/etc/rws/internal-root.pem"
```

## Challenge types

`challenge` picks how the CA checks that you control the domains (since
18.4.0; HTTP-01 before):

| `challenge` | The CA checks | Needs | Wildcards |
|---|---|---|---|
| `http-01` (default) | `http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/…` | port 80 reachable | no |
| `tls-alpn-01` | a TLS handshake on port 443 with ALPN `acme-tls/1` (RFC 8737) | port 443 reachable — nothing else | no |
| `dns-01` | a TXT record `_acme-challenge.<domain>` | a way to change the domain's DNS | yes |
| `dns-persist-01` | a TXT record `_validation-persist.<domain>` you publish once | nothing on the server: no port, no DNS credentials | yes |

### TLS-ALPN-01

For a server that only listens on 443 — no port 80 at all:

```toml
port = 443

[acme]
domains   = ["example.com"]
challenge = "tls-alpn-01"
```

rws answers on its HTTPS port: at startup, before it has a certificate, a
temporary acceptor on the same socket serves the challenge; afterwards the
TLS listener does, beside the normal traffic. A challenge handshake gets a
special self-signed certificate and is then closed; other clients never
see it. If a port mapping forwards 443 elsewhere, set `port` to where it
lands.

### DNS-01

The CA looks up a TXT record, so nothing needs to reach the server — and it
is the only way to get a wildcard certificate (`*.example.com`). rws adds
the record, waits until the zone's server answers with it, lets the CA check,
and removes it.

```toml
[acme]
domains   = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge = "dns-01"
dns_provider        = "rfc2136"            # DNS UPDATE (RFC 2136) to the primary server
dns_server          = "ns1.example.com"    # host[:port], port 53
dns_tsig_key        = "rws-acme"           # TSIG key name the server knows
dns_tsig_secret     = "base64secret=="     # better in RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_SECRET
# dns_tsig_algorithm  = "hmac-sha256"      # or hmac-sha512
# dns_zone            = "example.com"      # found by SOA lookup when not set
# dns_propagation_secs = 120               # how long to wait for the record
```

| `dns_provider` | Adds and removes the record by |
|---|---|
| `rfc2136` | a DNS UPDATE to `dns_server`, signed with the TSIG key — BIND, Knot, PowerDNS, Windows DNS, and many DNS hosts' "dynamic DNS" endpoints |
| `cloudflare` | Cloudflare's API, with an API token (`dns_api_token`) |
| `route53` | Amazon Route 53's API, signed with the credentials in `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (and `AWS_SESSION_TOKEN`) |
| `exec` | running `dns_exec` as `<program> present <fqdn> <value>` and `<program> cleanup <fqdn> <value>`: any DNS API, in a script (exit status 0 = done) |

A BIND key and the zone permission it needs:

```text
key "rws-acme" { algorithm hmac-sha256; secret "base64secret=="; };
zone "example.com" { type primary; file "example.com.zone";
    update-policy { grant rws-acme name _acme-challenge.example.com. TXT; }; };
```

(`tsig-keygen rws-acme` prints a new key.) The secret is never printed in
rws's startup log.

#### Cloudflare

```toml
[acme]
domains      = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge    = "dns-01"
dns_provider = "cloudflare"
# dns_api_token = "..."     # better in RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_TOKEN; never printed
# dns_zone_id   = "023e105f4ecef8ad9ca31a8372d0c353"
```

Create the token under *My Profile → API Tokens* with **Zone → DNS → Edit**
for the zone. rws finds the zone by asking for `example.com`'s parents in
turn, which also needs **Zone → Zone → Read** — or set `dns_zone_id` (the
zone's overview page shows it) and the DNS permission is enough. rws
replaces the `_acme-challenge` TXT records and deletes its own afterwards.

#### Route 53

```toml
[acme]
domains      = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge    = "dns-01"
dns_provider = "route53"
# dns_zone_id = "Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ"
```

Credentials come from the environment the AWS tools use —
`AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and, for temporary ones,
`AWS_SESSION_TOKEN` (instance roles and profiles in `~/.aws` aren't read:
export them, e.g. `eval "$(aws configure export-credentials --format env)"`).
The IAM policy needs `route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets` and
`route53:GetChange`, plus `route53:ListHostedZonesByName` unless
`dns_zone_id` is set:

```json
{"Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [
  {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets"], "Resource": "arn:aws:route53:::hostedzone/Z0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ"},
  {"Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["route53:GetChange", "route53:ListHostedZonesByName"], "Resource": "*"}]}
```

rws waits for Route 53 to report the change `INSYNC`, then for the record
to be visible, as with every provider (`dns_server`, or the system resolver
— set `dns_server` to one of the zone's name servers to skip resolver
caches).

CI tests both against a stand-in API that writes into BIND, with the
request signatures checked independently, and Pebble validating
(`ci/e2e/acme_dns_api.sh`).

### DNS-PERSIST-01

The CA looks up one TXT record that you publish once and leave in place:
it names the CA and your ACME account, so nothing on the server needs DNS
credentials or an open port, and renewals need no DNS change at all
(draft-ietf-acme-dns-persist; Let's Encrypt is rolling it out — Pebble has
it).

```toml
[acme]
domains   = ["example.com", "*.example.com"]
challenge = "dns-persist-01"
# dns_server = "ns1.example.com"   # where to look for the record (else the system resolver)
```

The first time, rws creates its ACME account and logs the record to
publish (one line):

```text
[ACME] Provisioning failed: dns-persist-01: publish this TXT record once (it stays; rws retries until it's visible): _validation-persist.example.com. TXT "letsencrypt.org; accounturi=https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/acme/acct/123456; policy=wildcard"
```

Publish it at your DNS host; rws retries on its own and issues as soon as
it sees the record. `policy=wildcard` is there because `*.example.com` is
in `domains`. The record belongs to the ACME account, so keep
`account_key_path`'s file (`.rws/acme/account.key`) — with a new key comes a
new account, and a new record to publish. Before asking the CA, rws checks
that the record is visible, so a missing one never costs a failed
validation. `dns_provider` is ignored: rws never changes this record.

## On-demand TLS

For a SaaS whose customers point their own domains at it: rws orders a
certificate at the first TLS handshake for a name nobody configured, once
your *ask* endpoint allows that name (since 18.4.0).

```toml
http_redirect_port = 80                  # answers HTTP-01

[acme]
domains       = ["saas.example.com"]     # rws's own certificate, the default
on_demand     = true                     # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND
on_demand_ask = "http://127.0.0.1:9000/allowed"   # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND_ASK
```

- Before each order rws asks `GET <on_demand_ask>?domain=<name>`; a 2xx
  answer allows it, anything else (or no answer in five seconds) refuses
  it. Answer from your list of customer domains. `on_demand` without
  `on_demand_ask` is refused: anyone could make rws order certificates for
  every name they point at it.
- The first handshake for a new name waits for its certificate (up to 90
  seconds; with Let's Encrypt usually a few). A refused name gets the
  default certificate and isn't asked about again for a minute; a failed
  order isn't retried for ten. At most four orders run at once, and one per
  name however many clients arrive together.
- Certificates are kept in `.rws/acme/on-demand/<name>/` (next to the
  `cert_path`), loaded at startup and renewed like the main one; with
  [`redis`](#several-replicas) replicas share them too.
- HTTP-01 or TLS-ALPN-01 (DNS-01 would need every customer's zone). Over
  HTTP/3 a name is served once a TCP handshake has ordered it.

CI checks it against Pebble with an ask endpoint (`ci/e2e/acme_on_demand.sh`):
an allowed name is served its certificate on the first request, a refused
one the default, five simultaneous first requests make one order, and a
restart orders nothing.

## Several replicas

Replicas of one site behind a load balancer each run ACME for the same
domains. On their own they would each order a certificate — hitting the
CA's rate limits — and each answer only the challenges they presented,
while the CA's request may reach another replica. Give them one Redis
(since 18.4.0):

```toml
[acme]
domains = ["example.com"]
redis   = "10.0.0.20:6379"       # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS
# redis_password = "..."         # RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PASSWORD; never printed
# redis_prefix   = "rws:acme"    # several sites in one Redis
```

- One replica orders each certificate (a lock in Redis, held up to five
  minutes); the others wait for it and install it.
- A renewal by any replica reaches the rest at their next renewal check,
  which they hot-swap like their own.
- HTTP-01 and TLS-ALPN-01 challenges are answered by every replica, from
  Redis, wherever the CA's request lands.
- Redis down: each replica carries on alone with its own files, and says so
  in its log.

The certificate's private key is stored in Redis: keep Redis on a private
network (and set a password). CI runs two replicas against one Redis and
Pebble (`ci/e2e/acme_shared.sh`): one order per certificate, both serving
the same one before and after a renewal.

## Configuration reference

Every setting can go in the `[acme]` section of `rws.config.toml`, on the
command line (`--acme-domains=...`; not the last three), or in the environment.

| `[acme]` key | Environment variable | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `domains` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DOMAINS` | — | Domains for the certificate. Setting this enables ACME. |
| `email` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_EMAIL` | — | Contact email for expiry notices from the CA |
| `staging` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_STAGING` | `false` | Use the Let's Encrypt staging CA |
| `directory` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DIRECTORY` | Let's Encrypt | ACME directory URL of another CA |
| `ca_file` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CA_FILE` | — | Extra root CA(s) to trust for the directory (private CAs) |
| `challenge` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE` | `http-01` | `http-01`, `tls-alpn-01`, `dns-01` or `dns-persist-01` — see [Challenge types](#challenge-types) |
| `challenge_port` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CHALLENGE_PORT` | `80` | Port the CA connects to for HTTP-01 |
| `dns_provider` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_PROVIDER` | — | DNS-01: `rfc2136`, `cloudflare`, `route53` or `exec` |
| `dns_server` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_SERVER` | — | DNS-01: `rfc2136`'s primary server, `host[:port]`; otherwise optional: where to look for the record (else the system resolver) |
| `dns_api_token` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_TOKEN` | — | DNS-01 `cloudflare`: the API token (no command-line flag; never printed) |
| `dns_zone_id` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_ZONE_ID` | looked up | DNS-01 `cloudflare` / `route53`: the zone's id |
| `dns_api_url` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_API_URL` | the provider's | DNS-01 `cloudflare` / `route53`: another API base URL (a proxy, a test double) |
| `dns_zone` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_ZONE` | SOA lookup | DNS-01: the zone of the records |
| `dns_tsig_key` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_KEY` | — | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: TSIG key name |
| `dns_tsig_secret` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_SECRET` | — | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: TSIG secret, base64 (no command-line flag; never printed) |
| `dns_tsig_algorithm` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_TSIG_ALGORITHM` | `hmac-sha256` | DNS-01 `rfc2136`: `hmac-sha256` or `hmac-sha512` |
| `dns_exec` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_EXEC` | — | DNS-01 `exec`: the program |
| `dns_propagation_secs` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_DNS_PROPAGATION_SECS` | `120` | DNS-01: how long to wait for the record to be visible |
| `redis` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS` | — | Redis `host:port` shared by replicas — see [Several replicas](#several-replicas) |
| `redis_password` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PASSWORD` | — | Its password (no command-line flag; never printed) |
| `redis_prefix` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_REDIS_PREFIX` | `rws:acme` | Key prefix in that Redis |
| `on_demand` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND` | `false` | Order certificates at the first handshake — see [On-demand TLS](#on-demand-tls) |
| `on_demand_ask` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ON_DEMAND_ASK` | — | URL asked `?domain=<name>` before each such order; 2xx allows it |
| `cert_path` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CERT_PATH` | `tls_cert_file`, else `.rws/acme/cert.pem` | Where the certificate chain is stored |
| `key_path` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_KEY_PATH` | `tls_key_file`, else `.rws/acme/key.pem` | Where the certificate key is stored (`0600`) |
| `renew_before_days` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_BEFORE_DAYS` | — | Renew this many days before expiry instead of at two-thirds of the lifetime (was `30` before 18.0.0) |
| `profile` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_PROFILE` | — | Certificate profile to order (`classic`, `tlsserver`, `shortlived`, … as the CA offers) |
| `renew_check_interval_secs` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_CHECK_INTERVAL_SECS` | `43200` | Longest time between renewal checks |
| `account_key_path` | `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ACCOUNT_KEY_PATH` | `.rws/acme/account.key` | Where the ACME account key is stored (`0600`) |

Top-level `http_redirect_port` (`RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT`) starts the
HTTP → HTTPS redirect listener; set it to the challenge port (80) in
production.

## Using ACME from Rust

The `rws` binary does all of the above. In your own binary built on the
library, the equivalent is:

```rust
use rust_web_server::acme::{AcmeConfig, AcmeManager};
use rust_web_server::prelude::*;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();

    if let Some(cfg) = AcmeConfig::from_env() {
        // Serve the issued certificate unless TLS paths were set explicitly.
        cfg.install_as_tls_certificate();
        let mgr = AcmeManager::new(cfg);
        mgr.provision_until_ready().await;   // retries until issued
        tokio::spawn(mgr.run_renewal_loop());
    }

    let app = App::new();
    tokio::join!(
        Server::run_tls(listener, pool, app.clone()),
        Server::run_quic(app),
        Server::run_redirect(),               // answers renewal challenges
    );
}
```

`AcmeManager::provision_if_needed()` (single attempt, returns the error) is
also available if you want to handle failures yourself.

---

# Mutual TLS (mTLS)

<https://rws8.tech/features/mtls/>

## Overview

Mutual TLS (mTLS) enforces two-way authentication: the server presents its
certificate to the client as usual, and the client must also present a
certificate signed by a CA that the server trusts. Connections that do not
present a valid client certificate are rejected at the TLS handshake layer,
before any HTTP traffic is exchanged.

## Enabling mTLS

Set `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE` to the path of a PEM file containing the
CA certificate (or certificate chain) whose signatures you trust:

```bash
export RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE=/etc/ssl/client-ca.pem
```

```toml
# rws.config.toml
tls_client_ca_file = "/etc/ssl/client-ca.pem"
```

No other configuration is needed. When this variable is set,
`create_tls_acceptor_from_vhosts()` builds a `WebPkiClientVerifier` and
attaches it to the `rustls::ServerConfig`. The same CA applies to both the
HTTPS (TCP/TLS) listener and the QUIC listener used for HTTP/3.

## How the verifier is built

```rust
// src/tls/mod.rs (simplified)
let verifier = WebPkiClientVerifier::builder(Arc::new(root_store))
    .build()
    .unwrap();

ServerConfig::builder()
    .with_client_cert_verifier(verifier)
    .with_cert_resolver(Arc::new(resolver))
```

The CA certificate is loaded into a `RootCertStore`. Every TLS `ClientHello`
that follows must include a certificate chain rooted in that store.

## Generating test client certificates

Create a self-signed CA and a client certificate signed by it:

```bash
# 1. Generate a CA key and self-signed certificate
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:4096 -keyout ca-key.pem -out ca.pem \
  -days 3650 -nodes -subj "/CN=MyTestCA"

# 2. Generate a client key and certificate signing request
openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout client-key.pem -out client.csr \
  -nodes -subj "/CN=test-client"

# 3. Sign the client certificate with the CA
openssl x509 -req -in client.csr -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca-key.pem \
  -CAcreateserial -out client.pem -days 365
```

## Testing with curl

```bash
curl --cert client.pem --key client-key.pem \
     --cacert cert.pem \
     https://localhost:7878/healthz
```

`--cacert cert.pem` tells curl to trust the server's self-signed certificate.
`--cert` / `--key` provide the client certificate and key that the server
validates against `client-ca.pem`.

## Scope

mTLS applies globally to all connections on the TLS port. There is no per-route
or per-virtual-host granularity at the TLS layer; use application middleware
(e.g., `JwtLayer` or a custom `Middleware`) for finer-grained access control
within a single TLS session.

:::note[Plain HTTP connections]
mTLS only applies to TLS connections. Plain HTTP/1.1 connections (when no cert
is configured, or connections on a redirect port) are not affected.
:::

## Configuration reference

| Variable | Config key | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CLIENT_CA_FILE` | `tls_client_ca_file` | Path to the CA PEM file whose signatures are trusted for client certificates |

---

# Virtual Hosting

<https://rws8.tech/features/virtual-hosting/>

## Overview

A single `rust-web-server` instance can host multiple domains simultaneously.
At the TLS handshake, the client sends its target hostname via SNI (Server Name
Indication). `SniCertResolver` reads that hostname and selects the matching
certificate before any HTTP traffic is exchanged. The negotiated hostname is
then available in every request handler as `ConnectionInfo::sni_hostname`.

Virtual hosting requires the `http2` or `http3` (default) feature for TLS
support.

## Configuring virtual hosts in `rws.config.toml`

Add one `[[virtual_host]]` block per domain. The top-level `tls_cert_file` /
`tls_key_file` pair is used as a fallback when no SNI hostname matches (or when
the client sends no SNI):

```toml
# Default certificate — used when no virtual host matches
tls_cert_file = "/etc/ssl/default.pem"
tls_key_file  = "/etc/ssl/default.key"

[[virtual_host]]
domain    = "example.com"
cert_file = "/etc/ssl/example.pem"
key_file  = "/etc/ssl/example.key"

[[virtual_host]]
domain    = "api.example.com"
cert_file = "/etc/ssl/api-example.pem"
key_file  = "/etc/ssl/api-example.key"
```

## Configuring virtual hosts via environment variables

The same configuration is available through numbered environment variables,
which is convenient in container environments:

```bash
RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_0_DOMAIN=example.com
RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_0_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/example.pem
RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_0_KEY_FILE=/etc/ssl/example.key

RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_DOMAIN=api.example.com
RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/api-example.pem
RWS_CONFIG_VIRTUAL_HOST_1_KEY_FILE=/etc/ssl/api-example.key
```

## How SNI resolution works

`SniCertResolver` implements `rustls::server::ResolvesServerCert`. It holds a
`HashMap>` keyed by the exact SNI hostname, plus an
optional default. The resolver is built once at startup (or after SIGHUP) by
`create_tls_acceptor_from_vhosts()`:

```rust
// src/tls/mod.rs (simplified)
pub fn create_tls_acceptor_from_vhosts(
    vhosts: &[VirtualHostConfig],
    default_cert: &str,
    default_key: &str,
) -> Result```

HTTP/3 (QUIC) uses the same `SniCertResolver` via
`create_quinn_server_config_from_vhosts()`, so virtual hosting works
transparently across all protocols.

## Reading the SNI hostname in handlers

After the TLS handshake, `ConnectionInfo::sni_hostname` carries the negotiated
hostname as `Option`. For plain HTTP/1.1 connections (no TLS) this
field is `None` and the `Host` header should be used instead.

```rust
fn process(&self, request: &Request, response: Response, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response {
    match &connection.sni_hostname {
        Some(host) => println!("Serving request for: {}", host),
        None       => println!("No SNI — plain HTTP or no matching vhost"),
    }
    response
}
```

## Host-restricted routing with `Router`

Call `.with_host("hostname")` before registering routes to restrict a `Router`
to requests whose SNI hostname (TLS) or `Host` header (plain HTTP) matches:

```rust
use rust_web_server::router::Router;

let api_router = Router::new()
    .with_host("api.example.com")
    .get("/v1/users", |_req, _params, _conn| { /* ... */ });

let www_router = Router::new()
    .with_host("example.com")
    .get("/", |_req, _params, _conn| { /* ... */ });
```

`router.handle(request, connection)` returns `None` when the host or path
doesn't match, so an `Application` can try each domain's router in turn and
fall through to the built-in `App` (static files, `/healthz`, …):

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::application::Application;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::{Response, STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE};
use rust_web_server::router::Router;
use rust_web_server::server::ConnectionInfo;

pub struct VhostApp {
    example: Router,
    other: Router,
    fallback: App,
}

impl VhostApp {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        VhostApp {
            example: Router::new().with_host("example.com").get("/", |_req, _p, _c| {
                Response::text(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, "example.com home")
            }),
            other: Router::new().with_host("other.com").get("/", |_req, _p, _c| {
                Response::text(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, "other.com home")
            }),
            fallback: App::new(),
        }
    }
}

impl Application for VhostApp {
    fn execute(&self, request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result {
        if let Some(r) = self.example.handle(request, connection) { return Ok(r); }
        if let Some(r) = self.other.handle(request, connection)   { return Ok(r); }
        self.fallback.execute(request, connection)
    }
}
```

## Hot reload

Send `SIGHUP` (or `POST /admin/config/reload`) to hot-reload all virtual host
certificates from disk without restarting the server:

```bash
kill -HUP $(pidof rws)
```

`Server::run_tls` rebuilds `TlsAcceptor` with updated certificates for all
virtual hosts on every SIGHUP. New connections immediately use the refreshed
certificates; existing connections are not interrupted.

---

# HTTP/2

<https://rws8.tech/features/http2/>

## Feature requirements

HTTP/2 support is included in the `http2` feature and the default `http3`
feature:

```bash
# HTTP/2 + TLS only (no QUIC)
cargo build --no-default-features --features http2

# Default build — also includes HTTP/3
cargo build
```

HTTP/2 is only available over TLS. A valid certificate must be configured.
See [HTTPS / TLS](/features/https-tls) for setup instructions.

## ALPN negotiation

No extra configuration is required to serve HTTP/2. The server advertises both
`h2` and `http/1.1` in the TLS handshake via ALPN. The client's preference
determines which protocol is selected for each connection:

```
alpn_protocols = ["h2", "http/1.1"]
```

Both protocols share the same port. Browsers, `curl`, and other HTTP/2-capable
clients negotiate HTTP/2 automatically.

## Cleartext HTTP/2 (h2c)

Without TLS, a client can still speak HTTP/2 by sending the HTTP/2
connection preface straight away ("prior knowledge") — gRPC clients and
`grpcurl -plaintext` do. Since 18.3.0 rws's plain-HTTP listener recognises
the preface and serves the connection as HTTP/2; anything else is HTTP/1.1
as before. The `Upgrade: h2c` handshake (removed from HTTP/2 in RFC 9113)
isn't supported.

```bash
curl --http2-prior-knowledge http://localhost:7878/healthz
grpcurl -plaintext -proto echo.proto localhost:7878 echo.Echo/Unary
```

## Request pipeline

`rws` has its own HTTP/2 server (`h2_server`, since 18.0.0 — the `h2` crate is
now only the HTTP/2 client of the proxies). Per connection it:

1. Exchanges the connection preface and SETTINGS (at most 250 concurrent
   streams, header lists up to 64 KiB — larger ones get `431`).
2. Reads frames, decodes HPACK header blocks and assembles each stream's
   `Request` (body included), validating it as RFC 9113 §8.3 requires.
3. Calls your `Application` — inline for a quick bodiless request the app
   says it can answer inline (`runs_inline`, as on HTTP/1.1), otherwise in its
   own task.
4. Encodes the `Response` (headers seen before become one-byte HPACK indexes)
   and sends it within the client's flow-control windows; file and streamed
   bodies go out in chunks. Everything ready at once is written in one go.

It passes h2spec's 146 conformance tests and is fuzzed (frames and HPACK).
Abusive clients are cut off: rapid stream resets, CONTINUATION floods and
oversized frames end the connection with `GOAWAY`.

Your application code is unchanged between HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

## Forbidden headers

The HTTP/2 specification (RFC 9113 §8.2.2) prohibits certain connection-level
headers in responses. The following headers are stripped automatically before
sending any H2 response:

- `connection`
- `keep-alive`
- `transfer-encoding`
- `upgrade`
- `proxy-connection`
- `te`

You do not need to remove these headers from `Response` objects yourself.

## Alt-Svc advertisement

When built without HTTP/3, HTTP/1.1 TLS responses include:

```
Alt-Svc: h2=":7878"
```

This tells HTTP/1.1 clients that HTTP/2 is available on the same port. With
the default `http3` build the header advertises `h3` instead.

## HTTP/2 reverse proxy

`H2ReverseProxy` provides an upstream proxy that connects to backends over
HTTP/2. It is available as middleware and wraps the normal
`Middleware` / `Application` stack:

```rust
use rust_web_server::proxy::H2ReverseProxy;

let proxy = H2ReverseProxy::new(vec!["h2://backend:8080".to_string()]);
let app = App::new().wrap(proxy);
```

`H2ReverseProxy` bridges between the synchronous middleware calling
convention and the async tokio runtime via an internal `block_on_isolated`
helper — a scoped OS thread running its own single-threaded tokio runtime,
rather than `tokio::task::block_in_place`. This works under any tokio
runtime flavor (including `current_thread`, where `block_in_place` would
panic) and even with no runtime active at all.

## Async handlers

The `http2` feature enables `App::with_async_state(S)`, which accepts `async fn`
handlers. This lets you `await` futures (database calls, outbound HTTP requests,
etc.) directly inside route handlers:

```rust
let app = App::with_async_state(my_state)
    .get("/data", |_req, _params, _conn, state| async move {
        let rows: Vec<u8> = state.db.fetch_all_json().await;
        Response::json(STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE.n200_ok, rows)
    });
```

:::note[SNI in HTTP/2]
The SNI hostname is extracted from the TLS handshake and available in
`ConnectionInfo::sni_hostname` for every HTTP/2 request, the same as for
HTTP/1.1 TLS connections.
:::

## Limits and conformance

Each HTTP/2 connection advertises `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS = 250`
(the same limit as Go's `net/http`), so one client can't open unbounded
simultaneous streams, and `SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE = 64 KiB`, so one
request can't make the server buffer megabytes of headers (HTTP/3 uses the
same 64 KiB field-section limit; an HTTP/1.1 request head is capped at
64 KiB, else `431`). CI runs [h2spec](https://github.com/summerwind/h2spec)
against a live server on every commit and requires all 146 tests to pass
with none skipped (`ci/e2e/h2spec.sh`).

---

# HTTP/3 / QUIC

<https://rws8.tech/features/http3-quic/>

## Feature requirements

HTTP/3 is included in the default build. No flags are needed:

```bash
cargo build
cargo run -- --tls-cert-file=cert.pem --tls-key-file=key.pem
```

HTTP/3 requires a valid TLS certificate. Without one, the QUIC listener is
silently skipped and the server continues to serve HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 over TLS.

## How it works

The `http3` feature (which implies `http2`) starts two listeners on the same
port number:

- A TCP listener for HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 (via `Server::run_tls`).
- A UDP listener for QUIC / HTTP/3 (via `Server::run_quic`).

Both share the same port. Clients that support HTTP/3 connect via UDP; others
fall back to TCP transparently. `main()` runs both listeners concurrently:

```rust
tokio::join!(
    Server::run_tls(listener, pool, app.clone()),
    Server::run_quic(app.clone()),
    Server::run_redirect(), // optional HTTP→HTTPS redirect
);
```

## Dependencies

HTTP/3 is built on the following crates:

- `quinn` — async QUIC transport
- `h3` — HTTP/3 framing over QUIC streams
- `h3-quinn` — bridge between `quinn` and `h3`

All parsing and protocol handling is contained in `src/h3_handler/mod.rs`.

## SNI from the QUIC handshake

The SNI hostname is extracted from the QUIC connection's TLS handshake data
and placed in `ConnectionInfo::sni_hostname`, exactly as it is for HTTP/2:

```rust
// src/h3_handler/mod.rs
let sni_hostname: Option = conn
    .handshake_data()
    .and_then(|d| d.downcast::<quinn::crypto::rustls::HandshakeData>().ok())
    .and_then(|d| d.server_name.clone());
```

Virtual host routing via `Router::with_host()` and direct access in handlers
via `connection.sni_hostname` work the same way for HTTP/3 as for HTTP/2.

## Alt-Svc advertisement

HTTP/1.1 TLS responses include:

```
Alt-Svc: h3=":7878"
```

This header tells clients — including browsers — that HTTP/3 is available on
the same port number over UDP. No client configuration is required; browsers
such as Chrome and Firefox will upgrade to HTTP/3 automatically on subsequent
requests after seeing this header.

## Forbidden headers

Like HTTP/2, HTTP/3 (RFC 9114 §4.2) prohibits connection-level headers.
The same set is stripped automatically before sending H3 responses:

- `connection`
- `keep-alive`
- `transfer-encoding`
- `upgrade`
- `proxy-connection`
- `te`

## Request pipeline

`h3_handler::handle_connection` mirrors the HTTP/2 handler:

1. Extracts SNI from the QUIC handshake.
2. Wraps the `quinn::Connection` in an `h3::server::Connection`.
3. Resolves each request stream with `resolver.resolve_request()`.
4. Assembles a `Request`, calls `app.execute()`, applies gzip compression, and
   sends the `Response` back as H3 frames.

Your `Application` implementation is called identically for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2,
and HTTP/3.

:::note[Firewall requirements]
HTTP/3 uses UDP. Ensure your firewall or cloud security group allows UDP
traffic on the server port (default 7878) in addition to TCP.
:::

---

# WebSocket

<https://rws8.tech/features/websocket/>

## WebSocket routes

Since 18.5.0 a WebSocket endpoint is an ordinary route. The handler gets a
`WebSocketConnection` once the `101 Switching Protocols` response is out,
and runs on a thread of its own for the connection's life:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::websocket::Message;

let app = App::with_state(()).websocket("/chat/:room", |mut ws, params, _state| {
    let room = params.get("room").unwrap_or("lobby").to_string();
    while let Ok(Some(message)) = ws.recv() {
        let _ = match message {
            Message::Text(text) => ws.send_text(&format!("{room}: {text}")),
            Message::Binary(data) => ws.send_binary(&data),
        };
    }
});
```

`Router::websocket(pattern, |ws, params| ...)` does the same in a `Router`,
and inside any handler `WebSocket::upgrade(request, |ws| ...)` returns the
`101` response and runs the closure with the connection. A request that
isn't a WebSocket upgrade gets `426 Upgrade Required`.

`ws.recv()` returns `Ok(Some(Message::Text | Message::Binary))` per message,
`Ok(None)` after the closing handshake, and `Err` when the client
disappeared or broke the protocol. Along the way it

- joins fragmented messages (text is checked to be UTF-8 once whole),
- answers pings with pongs and drops pongs,
- answers the client's close frame, and finishes one you started with
  `ws.close(code, reason)`,
- fails the connection with the right close code: 1002 for an unmasked
  frame, reserved bits or a bad fragment, 1007 for invalid UTF-8, 1009 for
  a message over `max_message_size` (16 MiB by default).

To send while `recv` waits, take a `WebSocketSender` — cloneable, usable
from any thread:

```rust
.websocket("/ticker", |mut ws, _params, _state| {
    let sender = ws.sender();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        for n in 1.. {
            if sender.send_text(&format!("tick {n}")).is_err() { return; }
            std::thread::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(1));
        }
    });
    while let Ok(Some(_)) = ws.recv() {}
})
```

`sender.send_text`, `send_binary`, `ping` and `close` all return `Err` once
the connection is closed.

Notes:

- HTTP/1.1 only, plain or TLS. Browsers open WebSockets over HTTP/1.1
  unless the server offers RFC 8441 (WebSocket over HTTP/2), which rws
  doesn't, so this is what they use.
- Each connection holds a thread while it's open: tokio's blocking pool
  in async builds (up to 512 by default), a new thread in the `http1`
  build.
- No idle timeout: send pings yourself if connections can go quiet
  behind a proxy that drops them.
- `Server::process` called directly, on a stream it can't hand over,
  answers an upgrade with `500`.

`examples/realtime.rs` has both routes above. `ci/e2e/realtime.sh` drives
them from Node's WebSocket client over plain HTTP and TLS, on the shared
and per-core runtimes: echo with a 400 KB message, server-pushed messages
from another thread, and clean closes started by either side.

## Frame-level API

The building blocks below are for connections you manage yourself, in a
custom accept loop:

```rust
use std::io::{Read, Write};
use std::net::TcpListener;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::websocket::{WebSocket, Frame};

let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:7878").unwrap();

for stream in listener.incoming() {
    let mut stream = stream.unwrap();

    // Read the HTTP upgrade request.
    let mut buf = vec![0u8; 4096];
    let n = stream.read(&mut buf).unwrap();
    let request = Request::parse(&buf[..n]).unwrap();

    if WebSocket::is_upgrade_request(&request) {
        // Send 101 Switching Protocols.
        let mut response = WebSocket::handshake_response(&request).unwrap();
        stream.write_all(&response.generate()).unwrap();

        // Enter the frame loop.
        loop {
            match WebSocket::read_frame(&mut stream) {
                Ok(Frame::Text(msg)) => {
                    WebSocket::write_frame(&mut stream, Frame::Text(msg)).unwrap();
                }
                Ok(Frame::Ping(data)) => {
                    WebSocket::write_frame(&mut stream, Frame::Pong(data)).unwrap();
                }
                Ok(Frame::Close(code, reason)) => {
                    WebSocket::send_close(&mut stream, code.unwrap_or(1000), &reason).ok();
                    break;
                }
                Ok(_) => {}
                Err(_) => break,
            }
        }
    }
}
```

`read_frame` returns frames as they come — fragments, pings and all; use
`WebSocketConnection` (above) for whole messages.

## Detecting upgrade requests

```rust
WebSocket::is_upgrade_request(request: &Request) -> bool
```

Returns `true` when the request has all three required headers:

- `Upgrade: websocket`
- `Connection: Upgrade` (or any value containing "upgrade")
- `Sec-WebSocket-Key: <base64>`

## Handshake response

```rust
WebSocket::handshake_response(request: &Request) -> Result```

Builds an HTTP `101 Switching Protocols` response with the correct
`Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value. The accept value is computed as:

```
base64(SHA-1(client_key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11"))
```

Both SHA-1 and base64 are implemented from scratch in `src/websocket/mod.rs`
with no external dependencies.

If the request includes a `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` header, the first listed
sub-protocol is echoed back in the response.

## Frame types

`Frame` is an enum covering all RFC 6455 opcodes:

| Variant | Opcode | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Frame::Text(String)` | `0x1` | A complete UTF-8 text message |
| `Frame::Binary(Vec<u8>)` | `0x2` | A binary message |
| `Frame::Ping(Vec<u8>)` | `0x9` | Ping — respond with a matching Pong |
| `Frame::Pong(Vec<u8>)` | `0xA` | Pong |
| `Frame::Close(Option<u16>, String)` | `0x8` | Close with optional status code and reason |
| `Frame::Continuation { fin, data }` | `0x0` | Continuation fragment for fragmented messages |

## Reading frames

```rust
WebSocket::read_frame(stream: &mut impl Read) -> Result```

Reads one complete frame. Client-to-server masking (required by RFC 6455) is
handled automatically — the payload is unmasked before being returned. Extended
payload lengths (16-bit and 64-bit) are supported.

A frame whose declared payload is larger than `WebSocket::MAX_FRAME_PAYLOAD`
(16 MiB) is an error, returned before any of the payload is read, and the
payload is read as it arrives rather than allocated at the size the client
claims (since 18.1.0; before, a frame claiming an enormous length made the
process abort). For another limit:

```rust
WebSocket::read_frame_limited(stream: &mut impl Read, max_payload: u64) -> Result```

## Writing frames

```rust
WebSocket::write_frame(stream: &mut impl Write, frame: Frame) -> Result<(), String>
```

Writes one frame. Server-to-client frames are sent unmasked per the RFC.
Payload length encoding (7-bit, 16-bit, 64-bit) is chosen automatically.

## Convenience methods

```rust
// Send a text message
WebSocket::send_text(&mut stream, "hello")?;

// Send a close frame
WebSocket::send_close(&mut stream, 1000, "normal closure")?;

// Reply to a Ping with a Pong
WebSocket::send_pong(&mut stream, ping_payload)?;
```

:::note[WebSocket proxy]
`src/ws_proxy/mod.rs` provides `WsProxy` — a standalone WebSocket proxy that
forwards upgrade requests and relays raw bytes bidirectionally between the
client and a backend server.
:::

---

# Server-Sent Events

<https://rws8.tech/features/sse/>

## Streaming

`Sse::stream()` gives a handler the response to return and an `SseSender`
that pushes events to the client as they are sent — AI tokens, progress,
live updates — over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 (since 18.5.0):

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::sse::{Sse, SseEvent};

let app = App::with_state(()).get("/tokens", |_req, _params, _conn, _state| {
    let (events, response) = Sse::stream();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        for (n, token) in ["Hello", ",", " world"].iter().enumerate() {
            let event = SseEvent::data(*token).id(n.to_string()).event_type("token");
            if events.send(event).is_err() {
                return; // the client went away
            }
        }
        // Dropping the last sender ends the stream.
    });
    response
});
```

| `SseSender` | |
|---|---|
| `.send(event)` | waits while the buffer is full: a slow client slows the sender, memory stays bounded |
| `.try_send(event)` | `Ok(false)` and the event dropped when the buffer is full |
| `.send_async(event).await` | `send` for async handlers (`http2` builds) |
| `.data(text)`, `.comment(text)` | shortcuts |
| `.clone()` | several producers; the stream ends when the last clone is dropped |

Every method returns `Err(SseClosed)` once the client is gone. When nothing
is sent for 15 seconds a `: keep-alive` comment goes out, which keeps
proxies from timing the connection out and notices a client that left. To
change the buffer (32 events) or the interval:

```rust
use std::time::Duration;
use rust_web_server::sse::SseStream;

let (events, response) = SseStream::new().buffer(256).keep_alive(Duration::from_secs(5)).start();
```

The MCP server's `GET /mcp` stream is built on the same writer.
`examples/realtime.rs` serves one, and `ci/e2e/realtime.sh` checks that its
events arrive as they are sent, over plain HTTP, TLS and HTTP/2.

## Buffered

For a sequence known up front, `Sse` builds the whole body at once:

```rust
use rust_web_server::sse::{Sse, SseEvent};

fn handle_updates(_req: &Request, _conn: &ConnectionInfo) -> Response {
    Sse::new()
        .event("connected", "ready")
        .push(SseEvent::data(r#"{"count":1}"#).id("1").event_type("update"))
        .push(SseEvent::data(r#"{"count":2}"#).id("2").event_type("update"))
        .comment("keep-alive")
        .into_response()
}
```

### `Sse` builder

`Sse::new()` creates an empty builder. Every method takes `self` and returns `Self` for chaining. Call `.into_response()` at the end to get a `Response`.

| Method | Wire output |
|---|---|
| `.event(event_type, data)` | `event: <type>\ndata: <data>\n\n` |
| `.data(data)` | `data: <data>\n\n` (no `event:` field — client sees `"message"`) |
| `.push(SseEvent)` | fully configured event |
| `.retry(ms)` | `retry: <ms>\n\n` — overrides client reconnect timer |
| `.comment(text)` | `: <text>\n\n` — ignored by browsers, used as keep-alive ping |

`.into_response()` sets:

- `200 OK`
- `Content-Type: text/event-stream`
- `Cache-Control: no-cache`
- `X-Accel-Buffering: no` — disables nginx proxy buffering

## `SseEvent`

Build with `SseEvent::data(payload)` and chain optional setters:

```rust
let event = SseEvent::data(r#"{"token":"Hello"}"#)
    .id("42")
    .event_type("token")
    .retry(3000);
```

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `data` | `String` (required) | Payload; multi-line strings split into multiple `data:` lines |
| `id` | `Option` | Event ID; client sends `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect |
| `event_type` | `Option` | Event type; client listens with `addEventListener("type", fn)` |
| `retry_ms` | `Option<u32>` | Reconnect delay in milliseconds |

### Multi-line data

Line breaks in the `data` string (`\n`, `\r\n` or a lone `\r`) are split into separate `data:` lines per the SSE specification; the client joins them with `\n`. Line breaks in `id` and the event type are dropped, so a value can't add fields of its own:

```rust
SseEvent::data("line one\nline two\nline three")
// Wire: data: line one\ndata: line two\ndata: line three\n\n
```

## Client-side JavaScript

```js
const source = new EventSource("/updates");

// Default handler — fires for events with no `event:` type field
source.onmessage = (e) => {
    console.log("message:", e.data);
};

// Named event handler
source.addEventListener("update", (e) => {
    const payload = JSON.parse(e.data);
    console.log("update count:", payload.count);
});

// Reconnection — browser retries automatically; Last-Event-ID is sent
source.onerror = () => console.warn("SSE connection lost, retrying…");
```

---

# Authentication

<https://rws8.tech/features/auth/>

The `auth` Cargo feature adds `BasicAuthLayer`, `JwtLayer`, and `ForwardAuthLayer` middleware, plus standalone helpers for building and verifying HS256 JWTs. The `auth-asymmetric` feature (on top of `auth`) adds `JwtLayer::rs256`/`::es256` for verifying RS256/ES256 tokens against a static public key.

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["auth"] }
# or, for RS256/ES256 support too:
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["auth-asymmetric"] }
```

The `auth` feature pulls in `hmac` and `sha2` (RustCrypto) as additional dependencies. `auth-asymmetric` additionally pulls in `p256` (also RustCrypto) for ES256; RS256 is verified in-crate (`rust_web_server::rsa_key::RsaPublicKey`), with no `rsa` crate.

## HTTP Basic Auth

`BasicAuthLayer` validates `Authorization: Basic <base64>` credentials against a caller-supplied closure. It issues `401 Unauthorized` with a `WWW-Authenticate: Basic realm="Protected"` challenge when the header is absent or malformed.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::auth::BasicAuthLayer;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let app = App::new()
    .wrap(BasicAuthLayer::new(|user, pass| {
        user == "admin" && pass == "s3cret"
    }));
```

The closure signature is `Fn(&str, &str) -> bool + Send + Sync + 'static`. Passwords containing `:` are handled correctly — only the first `:` splits username from password, per RFC 7617.

Credential check outcomes:

| Condition | Response |
|---|---|
| `Authorization` header absent or malformed | `401` + `WWW-Authenticate` challenge |
| Header present but closure returns `false` | `401` (no challenge) |
| Closure returns `true` | Request forwarded to next layer |

### Validating against an htpasswd-style file

`BasicAuthLayer::from_htpasswd_file(path)` loads credentials from a file instead of a closure — the file is read once, at construction time:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::auth::BasicAuthLayer;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let app = App::new()
    .wrap(BasicAuthLayer::from_htpasswd_file(".htpasswd").expect("failed to read htpasswd file"));
```

Each non-empty, non-comment (`#`-prefixed) line is `username:credential`, where `credential` is one of:

- a plain-text password (Apache's `htpasswd -p` format), or
- `{SHA256}` followed by the base64-encoded SHA-256 digest of the password — **rws's own scheme**, not Apache's.

```
# .htpasswd
alice:s3cret
bob:{SHA256}9S+9MrKzuG/4jvbEkGKChfSCrxXdyylUH5S89Saj9sc=
```

Generate a `{SHA256}` entry with `openssl` (no need to write Rust code):

```bash
printf '%s' 'hunter2' | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | openssl base64
# -> 9S+9MrKzuG/4jvbEkGKChfSCrxXdyylUH5S89Saj9sc=
```

:::caution[Not compatible with real Apache htpasswd files]
Apache's actual `{SHA}` scheme is SHA-1 (not SHA-256), and modern `htpasswd` tool versions default to bcrypt or `$apr1$` (iterated MD5) when no flag is given. None of `{SHA}`, `$apr1$`, or bcrypt are supported here — this crate has no third-party crypto dependencies beyond the audited RustCrypto hash crates it already uses (`hmac`, `sha2`), and hand-rolling SHA-1, MD5, or bcrypt from scratch isn't a risk worth taking for an authentication check. A real Apache-generated htpasswd file will **not** verify against `from_htpasswd_file`.

If you need genuine Apache-hash compatibility, use [`BasicAuthLayer::new`](#http-basic-auth) with your own closure backed by the `bcrypt`/`sha1` crate of your choice, or regenerate the file with `htpasswd -p` (plain text) or the `{SHA256}` scheme above.
:::

## JWT — HS256

`JwtLayer` verifies `Authorization: Bearer <token>` JWTs signed with HMAC-SHA256.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::auth::JwtLayer;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let app = App::new()
    .wrap(JwtLayer::new(b"my-signing-secret"));
```

Tokens with a past `exp` claim are rejected. Any token that fails format validation, algorithm check, or signature verification returns `401 Unauthorized`.

### Building tokens

Use `build_jwt` in a login handler to issue a signed token:

```rust
use rust_web_server::auth::build_jwt;

fn login_handler(/* ... */) -> String {
    let claims = r#"{"sub":"42","role":"admin","exp":9999999999}"#;
    let token = build_jwt(claims, b"my-signing-secret");
    // return token to client
    token
}
```

`build_jwt(claims_json, secret)` always produces an HS256 JWT with the `alg` and `typ` header set. The `claims_json` argument is any valid JSON object string.

### Verifying tokens and reading claims

Call `verify_jwt` directly inside a handler when you also need the decoded claims. The verification is cheap (~1 µs) so double-calling is fine.

```rust
use rust_web_server::auth::{verify_jwt, extract_bearer_token};
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;

fn protected_handler(req: &Request) -> Response {
    let token = extract_bearer_token(req).expect("JwtLayer already validated this");
    let claims = verify_jwt(&token, b"my-signing-secret").unwrap();

    println!("subject: {:?}", claims.sub);
    println!("expires: {:?}", claims.exp);
    // parse custom claims from claims.raw (raw JSON string)

    Response::new()
}
```

### `Claims` struct

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sub` | `Option` | Subject (user ID), if present |
| `exp` | `Option<u64>` | Expiration as Unix seconds, if present |
| `raw` | `String` | Raw UTF-8 JSON payload — inspect for custom claims |

`claims.is_valid_at(now_secs)` returns `true` when the token is not yet expired. Returns `true` when `exp` is absent (no expiry set).

### `extract_bearer_token`

Extracts the raw token string from `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Returns `None` when the header is absent or does not start with `Bearer `.

```rust
use rust_web_server::auth::extract_bearer_token;

if let Some(token) = extract_bearer_token(&request) {
    // token is the raw JWT string
}
```

## Login handler pattern

A typical login flow: verify credentials, issue a JWT, return it to the client.

```rust
use rust_web_server::auth::build_jwt;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;
use rust_web_server::body::form_urlencoded::FormUrlEncoded;
use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};

fn login(req: &Request) -> Response {
    let form = FormUrlEncoded::parse(req.body.to_vec()).unwrap_or_default();
    let username = form.get("username").map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("");
    let password = form.get("password").map(String::as_str).unwrap_or("");

    if username != "admin" || password != "s3cret" {
        let mut r = Response::new();
        r.status_code = 401;
        return r;
    }

    let exp = SystemTime::now()
        .duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)
        .unwrap()
        .as_secs() + 3600; // 1 hour

    let claims = format!(r#"{{"sub":"{username}","exp":{exp}}}"#);
    let token = build_jwt(&claims, b"my-signing-secret");

    let mut r = Response::new();
    // set body to JSON with token
    r
}
```

:::note[Algorithm support]
`build_jwt` and `verify_jwt` only support HS256. For RS256/ES256 against a static public key, see the next section. For public-key JWTs from an identity provider that rotates keys behind a live JWKS endpoint, use the `sso` feature's `JwksCache` instead.
:::

## JWT — RS256 / ES256 (`auth-asymmetric` feature)

A common pattern: a separate auth server issues JWTs signed with its RSA or P-256 *private* key, and your service only ever needs the corresponding *public* key to verify them — no OAuth login flow, no JWKS endpoint, no key rotation to track. `JwtLayer::rs256` and `JwtLayer::es256` cover exactly this, without pulling in the full `sso` feature (OIDC login/callback handlers, PKCE, JWKS fetching):

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["auth-asymmetric"] }
```

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::auth::JwtLayer;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

// public_key_pem is SubjectPublicKeyInfo PEM (RS256 also accepts PKCS#1 `BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY`), e.g.:
//   openssl rsa -in key.pem -pubout   (RS256)
//   openssl ec  -in key.pem -pubout   (ES256)
let app = App::new().wrap(JwtLayer::rs256(&rsa_public_key_pem).expect("invalid RSA public key"));
// or:
let app = App::new().wrap(JwtLayer::es256(&ec_public_key_pem).expect("invalid P-256 public key"));
```

Both reject a token whose header `alg` doesn't actually match what was verified — an RS256 key can't wave through a token whose header claims `"alg":"HS256"` just because the bytes happen to parse as something. ES256 signatures are validated in the raw 64-byte `r || s` form JWTs specify, not the ASN.1 DER encoding OpenSSL produces by default when signing outside of a JWT library.

If a handler also needs the decoded claims, call the standalone verify functions directly — same code `JwtLayer` uses internally:

```rust
use rust_web_server::auth::{verify_jwt_rs256, verify_jwt_es256};
use rust_web_server::rsa_key::RsaPublicKey;

let rsa_public_key = RsaPublicKey::from_public_key_pem(PEM)?;   // or from_components(n, e)
let claims = verify_jwt_rs256(&token, &rsa_public_key).unwrap();
let claims = verify_jwt_es256(&token, &ec_public_key).unwrap();
```

RSA keys are 2048–8192 bits. Since 18.0.0 RSA verification is implemented
in-crate (`rust_web_server::rsa_key`) rather than with the `rsa` crate, whose
RUSTSEC-2023-0071 advisory has no fixed release; `verify_jwt_rs256` takes an
`rsa_key::RsaPublicKey`.

`RsaPublicKey` loads a key with `from_public_key_pem` (`BEGIN PUBLIC KEY` or
`BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY`), `from_public_key_der` (SPKI), `from_pkcs1_der`, or
`from_components(n, e)` (a JWK's `n`/`e`). It also verifies any
RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 / SHA-256 signature directly, not just a JWT:

```rust
use rust_web_server::rsa_key::RsaPublicKey;

let key = RsaPublicKey::from_public_key_pem(&std::fs::read_to_string("issuer.pub.pem")?)?;
let ok: bool = key.verify_pkcs1v15_sha256(b"message", &signature);
```

:::note[Upgrading from 17.x]
`verify_jwt_rs256` and `SamlIdpMetadata.signing_key` used `rsa::RsaPublicKey`.
Build an `rsa_key::RsaPublicKey` instead (`from_public_key_pem`,
`from_public_key_der`, or `from_components(n, e)`).
:::

:::note[When to use `sso::JwksCache` instead]
`JwtLayer::rs256`/`::es256` pin a single static public key at construction time. Use `sso::JwksCache` when the signing key can rotate and you need to fetch current keys from a live JWKS URL (`.well-known/jwks.json`), keyed by `kid` — the right fit for a full OIDC identity provider, not a service-to-service integration with one known signer.
:::

## Forward-auth (delegate to an external service)

`ForwardAuthLayer` delegates the allow/deny decision to an external HTTP service — the same pattern as Traefik's `forwardAuth` or nginx's `auth_request`. Use it to gate requests behind a centralized policy engine (OPA, Casbin) or a shared SSO/session service, without embedding that logic in your app.

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::auth::forward::ForwardAuthLayer;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

let app = App::new()
    .wrap(ForwardAuthLayer::new("http://auth.internal/verify")
        .copy_header("X-User-Id")
        .copy_header("X-Roles")
        .timeout_ms(2000));
```

On every request, the layer sends a `GET` to the configured URL with every incoming request header copied onto it (so the auth service can inspect a session cookie or an existing `Authorization` header):

1. **`2xx`** — the request proceeds to the next layer/handler. Any header named via `.copy_header(name)` that's present on the *auth service's response* **replaces** the same-named header on the forwarded request. This is deliberate: if it merely appended, a client could send its own `X-User-Id` and have it coexist with the trusted value.
2. **Any other status** — the auth service's response is returned to the client **verbatim**: status code, headers (minus hop-by-hop and body-framing ones), and body. This preserves a `WWW-Authenticate` challenge or a `Location` redirect into an OAuth login flow without `rws` needing to understand either.
3. **Auth service unreachable** (connection refused, timeout, DNS failure) — `502 Bad Gateway`. This fails *closed*: an unreachable auth service is never treated as "access granted."

Redirects from the auth service itself are not followed (`max_redirects(0)` internally) so a `3xx` response reaches step 2 intact instead of being silently resolved to whatever it points to.

No new Cargo dependency — `ForwardAuthLayer` reuses the existing `crate::http_client::Client`, the same synchronous outbound HTTP client used elsewhere in the framework.

:::note[Builder options]
| Method | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `ForwardAuthLayer::new(url)` | — | Auth service URL, e.g. `"http://auth.internal/verify"` |
| `.copy_header(name)` | none | Copy `name` from the auth response onto the forwarded request on `2xx`; call multiple times for multiple headers |
| `.timeout_ms(ms)` | `5000` | Auth service call timeout |
:::

## No-code auth in the config-driven proxy

`rws.config.toml`'s `[route.middleware.auth]` wires directly into `JwtLayer` and `BasicAuthLayer` — no Rust code required. Both need the `auth` feature enabled at build time (`cargo build --features auth`; the default build doesn't include it).

```toml
[[route]]
name = "api"

[route.match]
path = "/api/*"

[route.action]
type = "proxy"

[route.action.proxy]
upstream = "backend"

[route.middleware.auth]
type = "jwt"
secret_env = "JWT_SECRET"
```

```toml
[route.middleware.auth]
type = "basic"
htpasswd_file = ".htpasswd"
```

See [Config-Driven Proxy](/proxy/config-driven/) for the full `[route.middleware]` reference. Auth config fails closed: an unset/empty `token_env`/`secret_env`, a missing `htpasswd_file`, or a build without the `auth` feature makes that route answer `503 Service Unavailable` (with an error in the startup log) instead of serving it unprotected. Other routes keep working. Bearer tokens are compared in constant time.

## Password hashing (`crypto` feature)

The `crypto` feature (independent of `auth`) adds Argon2id password hashing and secure random tokens:

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["crypto"] }
```

```rust
use rust_web_server::crypto::{hash_password, verify_password, generate_token};

// At registration: store the returned PHC string ($argon2id$v=19$...) as-is.
// The random salt is embedded in it, so no separate salt column is needed.
let hash = hash_password("hunter2")?;

// At login: constant-time comparison; Err only when `hash` isn't a valid PHC string.
if !verify_password(&submitted_password, &hash)? {
    // return 401
}

// Password-reset tokens, email verification codes, API keys:
let reset_token = generate_token(32); // 32 random bytes -> 64-char lowercase hex
```

All three live in `rust_web_server::crypto`; errors are `CryptoError`. Use at least 16 bytes for tokens and 32 bytes for high-value secrets such as API keys.

---

# OAuth2 / OIDC SSO

<https://rws8.tech/features/sso/>

The `sso` feature adds full OAuth 2.0 / OIDC support: authorization-code + PKCE flow, session management, and asymmetric JWT verification via a live JWKS endpoint. The `sso-server` feature additionally lets `rws` act as its own OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server, issuing tokens instead of delegating to an external IdP.

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["sso"] }
```

## Quick start

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::session::SessionStore;
use rust_web_server::sso::{OidcAuth, OidcConfig};

let sessions = Arc::new(SessionStore::new(86_400)); // 24 h TTL
let config   = OidcConfig::google(
    "my-client-id",
    "my-client-secret",
    "https://example.com/auth/callback",
);
let app = App::new().wrap(OidcAuth::new(config, sessions));
```

## Loading config from environment variables

`OidcConfig::from_env()` reads environment variables so credentials stay out of source code:

```bash
RWS_OIDC_PROVIDER=google          # google | github | microsoft | okta | auth0 | keycloak | custom
RWS_OIDC_CLIENT_ID=my-client-id
RWS_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=my-secret
RWS_OIDC_REDIRECT_URI=https://example.com/auth/callback
RWS_OIDC_SCOPES=openid email profile   # space-separated; default: openid email profile
RWS_OIDC_POST_LOGIN_REDIRECT=/dashboard
```

Provider-specific extras:

| Provider | Extra variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `microsoft` | `RWS_OIDC_TENANT_ID` | Tenant GUID, `common`, `organizations`, or `consumers` |
| `okta` | `RWS_OIDC_ISSUER` | Okta org domain, e.g. `dev-12345.okta.com` |
| `auth0` | `RWS_OIDC_ISSUER` | Auth0 domain, e.g. `myapp.us.auth0.com` |
| `keycloak` | `RWS_OIDC_ISSUER` + `RWS_OIDC_TENANT_ID` | Base URL + realm name |
| `custom` | `RWS_OIDC_ISSUER` | OIDC issuer URL for auto-discovery |

```rust
let config = OidcConfig::from_env().expect("OIDC config missing");
```

## Provider presets

All presets accept `(client_id, client_secret, redirect_uri)` unless noted.

```rust
// Google
let cfg = OidcConfig::google("id", "secret", "https://example.com/auth/callback");

// Microsoft Entra ID / Azure AD
let cfg = OidcConfig::microsoft("common", "id", "secret", "https://example.com/auth/callback");

// GitHub OAuth 2.0 (no id_token — uses UserInfo endpoint instead)
let cfg = OidcConfig::github("id", "secret", "https://example.com/auth/callback");

// Okta
let cfg = OidcConfig::okta("dev-12345.okta.com", "id", "secret", "https://example.com/auth/callback");

// Auth0
let cfg = OidcConfig::auth0("myapp.us.auth0.com", "id", "secret", "https://example.com/auth/callback");

// Keycloak
let cfg = OidcConfig::keycloak(
    "https://keycloak.example.com",
    "my-realm",
    "id", "secret",
    "https://example.com/auth/callback",
);

// Auto-discovery from any OIDC-compliant provider
let cfg = OidcConfig::discover("https://provider.example.com", "id", "secret", "https://example.com/auth/callback")?;
```

Chain `.scopes([...])` or `.post_login_redirect(path)` to override the defaults (`openid email profile` — `read:user user:email` for GitHub — and `/`).

## Authorization-code + PKCE flow

```
Browser                App                         Identity Provider
  |                     |                                   |
  |-- GET /any-page --> |                                   |
  |                     | (no session)                      |
  |<-- 302 /auth/login--|                                   |
  |                     |                                   |
  |-- GET /auth/login ->|                                   |
  |                     | generate PKCE verifier+challenge, |
  |                     | state, nonce → save in session    |
  |<-- 302 idp/authorize|                                   |
  |                                                         |
  |------- GET idp/authorize?code_challenge=... ----------->|
  |<--------------------- 302 /auth/callback?code=... ------|
  |                                                         |
  |-- GET /auth/callback?code=... -->|                      |
  |                     | exchange code (with PKCE verifier)|
  |                     |<-------- POST idp/token ----------|
  |                     |----------- id_token+access_token->|
  |                     | verify id_token via JWKS          |
  |                     | store OidcClaims in session       |
  |<-- 302 /dashboard --|                                   |
```

`OidcAuth` intercepts three paths automatically:

| Path | Action |
|---|---|
| `GET /auth/login` | Generates PKCE + state + nonce, redirects to provider |
| `GET /auth/callback` | Validates state, exchanges code, verifies id_token, stores claims |
| `GET /auth/logout` | Destroys session, redirects to `/` |

All other paths check the session. Authenticated requests have claims injected into the `X-Rws-Oidc-Claims` header (JSON) and are forwarded to the next layer. Unauthenticated requests redirect to `/auth/login?return_to=<current-path>`.

## Claims extraction in handlers

```rust
use rust_web_server::sso::OidcAuth;
use rust_web_server::request::Request;
use rust_web_server::response::Response;

fn dashboard(req: &Request) -> Response {
    // Read the full claims object
    if let Some(claims) = OidcAuth::claims(req) {
        let user_id = &claims.sub;
        let email   = claims.email.as_deref().unwrap_or("unknown");
        let name    = claims.name.as_deref().unwrap_or("unknown");
        println!("User {user_id} ({email}) / {name}");
    }

    // Shortcuts
    let sub   = OidcAuth::sub(req);
    let email = OidcAuth::email(req);

    Response::new()
}
```

### `OidcClaims` fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `sub` | `String` | Subject (unique user ID at the provider) |
| `iss` | `String` | Issuer URL |
| `aud` | `Vec` | Intended audience (your client ID) |
| `exp` | `u64` | Expiration as Unix seconds |
| `iat` | `u64` | Issued-at as Unix seconds |
| `nonce` | `Option` | Nonce for replay protection |
| `email` | `Option` | User's email address |
| `email_verified` | `Option<bool>` | Whether the email is verified |
| `name` | `Option` | Full display name |
| `given_name` | `Option` | First name |
| `family_name` | `Option` | Last name |
| `picture` | `Option` | Profile picture URL |
| `locale` | `Option` | User's locale |

## Public path exclusion

Exclude paths from the authentication check (health endpoints, public assets, etc.):

```rust
let app = App::new()
    .wrap(
        OidcAuth::new(config, sessions)
            .exclude("/healthz")
            .exclude("/public/")
    );
```

## Custom paths

```rust
OidcAuth::new(config, sessions)
    .login_path("/login")
    .callback_path("/oauth/callback")
    .logout_path("/logout")
```

## RS256/ES256 JWT verification via JWKS

`JwksCache` fetches the provider's public keys from the JWKS URI and verifies `id_token` JWTs. Key rotation is handled automatically: on a verification failure the cache is refreshed and the verification is retried once.

```rust
use rust_web_server::sso::{JwksCache, VerifyOptions};

let jwks = JwksCache::new("https://accounts.google.com/.well-known/jwks");
let opts = VerifyOptions {
    audience:    "my-client-id",
    issuer:      "https://accounts.google.com",
    leeway_secs: 60,
};
let claims = jwks.verify_jwt(&id_token, &opts)?;
```

`OidcAuth` calls `JwksCache::verify_jwt` internally; you only need to use it directly when processing tokens outside the middleware (e.g. in a mobile API that receives tokens from a separate auth service).

:::note[GitHub does not issue id_tokens]
