```yaml
      RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE: "/run/secrets/key.pem"
      RWS_CONFIG_HTTP_REDIRECT_PORT: "7879"
      RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT: "json"
    volumes:
      - ./certs/cert.pem:/run/secrets/cert.pem:ro
      - ./certs/key.pem:/run/secrets/key.pem:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-fk", "https://localhost:7878/healthz"]
      interval: 15s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 10s
    restart: unless-stopped
```

:::note[SIGHUP hot-reload inside Docker]
Send `docker kill --signal=SIGHUP <container>` to reload TLS certificates, CORS rules, rate limits, and log format without restarting the container. The server's `/admin/config/reload` endpoint does the same over HTTP.
:::

---

# Kubernetes

<https://rws8.tech/deployment/kubernetes/>

## Health endpoints

`rust-web-server` exposes two dedicated health endpoints that map directly to Kubernetes probe semantics:

| Endpoint | Purpose | Probe type |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | Always returns `200 OK` while the process is running | Liveness |
| `GET /readyz` | Returns `200 OK` when ready, `503` during startup and SIGTERM drain | Readiness |

The `SERVER_READY` flag is set to `true` after `Server::setup()` completes and cleared as soon as a shutdown signal is received, so Kubernetes stops routing traffic before in-flight requests finish draining.

## Graceful shutdown

When Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM`, the server:

1. Clears `SERVER_READY` — `/readyz` begins returning `503`, Kubernetes stops sending new traffic.
2. Stops accepting new TCP connections.
3. Waits for all in-flight requests to complete (thread-pool drain on `http1`; tokio task drain on `http2`/`http3`).
4. Exits cleanly.

Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` to at least `30` to give in-flight requests time to complete before Kubernetes sends `SIGKILL`.

:::tip[Helm chart]
The manifests below are also a Helm chart, published with every release (since 18.2.0):

```bash
kubectl create secret tls rws-tls --cert=tls.crt --key=tls.key
helm install my-rws oci://ghcr.io/bohdaq/charts/rws --version 18.2.0
```

It renders the same `Deployment`, `Service`, `PodDisruptionBudget` and `HorizontalPodAutoscaler`, plus an optional `Ingress` and prometheus-operator `ServiceMonitor`; CI installs it into a kind cluster with TLS on and off. Its values are documented in [`helm/rws/README.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/tree/main/helm/rws).
:::

## Deployment YAML

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rws
  labels:
    app: rws
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rws
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rws
      annotations:
        # Prometheus scrape annotations — tells Prometheus to scrape this pod.
        prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
        prometheus.io/path: "/metrics"
        prometheus.io/port: "7878"
        prometheus.io/scheme: "https"   # the pod serves TLS
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: rws
          image: ghcr.io/bohdaq/rws:18
          ports:
            - name: https
              containerPort: 7878
              protocol: TCP
            - name: quic
              containerPort: 7878
              protocol: UDP
          env:
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_IP
              value: "0.0.0.0"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_PORT
              value: "7878"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT
              value: "4"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT
              value: "json"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE
              value: "/tls/tls.crt"
            - name: RWS_CONFIG_TLS_KEY_FILE
              value: "/tls/tls.key"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls
              mountPath: /tls
              readOnly: true
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 7878
              scheme: HTTPS   # the port serves TLS; plain-HTTP probes would fail
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 3
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: 7878
              scheme: HTTPS   # the port serves TLS; plain-HTTP probes would fail
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 2
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "100m"
              memory: "64Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "500m"
              memory: "256Mi"
      volumes:
        - name: tls
          secret:
            secretName: rws-tls
```

Every `RWS_CONFIG_*` variable can come from a ConfigMap or Secret. Settings that name a file, such as `RWS_CONFIG_TLS_CERT_FILE`, take a path, so mount the Secret as a volume (as above) rather than putting its contents in the variable:

```yaml
envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: rws-config   # e.g. RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT, RWS_CONFIG_THREAD_COUNT
```

## Service YAML

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: rws
spec:
  selector:
    app: rws
  ports:
    - name: https
      protocol: TCP
      port: 443
      targetPort: 7878
    - name: quic
      protocol: UDP
      port: 443
      targetPort: 7878
  type: ClusterIP
```

## PodDisruptionBudget

Keep at least two pods running during rolling updates or node drains:

```yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: rws-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rws
```

## HorizontalPodAutoscaler

Scale on CPU utilisation, or on requests per second per pod. rws exports the
counter `rws_requests_total` at `/metrics`; the
[Prometheus Adapter](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/prometheus-adapter)
turns it into the per-pod rate `rws_requests_per_second` in the custom
metrics API. Install it with the rule in
[`helm/prometheus-adapter-values.yaml`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/helm/prometheus-adapter-values.yaml):

```bash
helm install prometheus-adapter prometheus-community/prometheus-adapter \
  -n monitoring -f helm/prometheus-adapter-values.yaml   # set prometheus.url first
kubectl get --raw "/apis/custom.metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/namespaces/default/pods/*/rws_requests_per_second"
```

The rule:

```yaml
rules:
  custom:
    - seriesQuery: 'rws_requests_total{namespace!="",pod!=""}'
      resources:
        overrides:
          namespace: {resource: namespace}
          pod: {resource: pod}
      name:
        matches: "^rws_requests_total$"
        as: "rws_requests_per_second"
      metricsQuery: 'sum(rate(<<.Series>>{<<.LabelMatchers>>}[2m])) by (<<.GroupBy>>)'
```

```yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: rws-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: rws
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
    # Requests per second per pod, from the Prometheus Adapter rule above.
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric:
          name: rws_requests_per_second
        target:
          type: AverageValue
          averageValue: "500"
```

With the Helm chart: `--set autoscaling.enabled=true --set autoscaling.customMetric.enabled=true`.
(Until 18.2.0 this page used an `External` metric named `rws_route_requests_total`, which nothing served.)

## Structured logging for Kubernetes

Access logs are JSON by default (`RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=json`, or `log_format = 'json'` in `rws.config.toml`; `combined` gives Combined Log Format, `off`/`none` disables the access log). Kubernetes log aggregators (Fluentd, Fluent Bit, Vector) can then parse and index each field:

```json
{"time":"2026-07-02T12:00:00Z","remote_addr":"10.0.0.1","method":"GET","path":"/api/users","protocol":"HTTP/1.1","status":200,"bytes":1024}
```

:::note[Log to stdout]
`rust-web-server` writes all access logs to stdout (buffered per thread, written at least every 100 ms). Let the container runtime and your log aggregator handle collection and rotation — this is the Kubernetes-native approach.
:::

## Prometheus scraping

With the `prometheus.io/*` annotations on the pod (`prometheus.io/scheme: "https"` when the pod serves TLS), a Prometheus using annotation-based discovery scrapes `GET /metrics` automatically; with the prometheus-operator, enable the chart's `metrics.serviceMonitor` instead. The endpoint returns server-wide counters and — if `MetricsLayer` is enabled — per-route histograms in Prometheus text format. Circuit-breaker state (`rws_circuit_breaker_state{backend}`) is included automatically. The full metric list is on the [Metrics](/features/metrics/) page.

See the [Observability](/deployment/observability) page for example Grafana queries.

---

# Kubernetes Ingress

<https://rws8.tech/deployment/kubernetes-ingress/>

`KubernetesIngressWatcher` watches the Kubernetes API server for Ingress resources and maintains a live route table in memory. `IngressRouter` implements `Application` and uses that table to forward requests to the correct upstream service.

## How it works

1. `KubernetesIngressWatcher` does a full `GET /apis/networking.k8s.io/v1/namespaces/{ns}/ingresses` on an interval (default 30 s, configurable) as a resync safety net, **and** opens a long-lived `?watch=true` streaming connection alongside it — any `ADDED`/`MODIFIED`/`DELETED` event on that stream triggers an immediate re-list instead of waiting for the next interval. On a quiet cluster the watch connection just sits blocked on a read, costing nothing; if the API server doesn't support watch for some reason, the interval resync alone keeps things working, just at up-to-30s latency instead of near-instant.
2. Each Ingress rule is parsed into an `IngressRule` containing `host`, `path`, `path_type`, `service_name`, `service_port`, and `namespace`.
3. `IngressRouter` matches incoming requests (host header + path, per `path_type` — see [Path matching](#path-matching)) against the live rule table and proxies to `{service_name}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:{service_port}` over HTTP/1.1.

## Environment variables

| Variable | Required | Example | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `RWS_K8S_API_SERVER` | Yes (for `from_env()`) | `http://localhost:8001` | Base URL of the Kubernetes API (plain HTTP) |
| `RWS_K8S_TOKEN` | No | `eyJhbGci…` | Bearer token for API authentication |
| `RWS_K8S_NAMESPACE` | No | `production` | Namespace to watch (default: `default`; use `all` for all namespaces) |

:::note[Two ways to reach the API server]
`from_env()` talks plain `http://` to the Kubernetes API — the simplest option, and the only one that needs no extra Cargo feature. The recommended setup for local development or a sidecar is `kubectl proxy`:

```sh
kubectl proxy &
export RWS_K8S_API_SERVER=http://localhost:8001
export RWS_K8S_TOKEN=
export RWS_K8S_NAMESPACE=default
```

For a pod that wants to talk to the in-cluster API server directly — no sidecar — use [`from_service_account()`](#connecting-directly-from-inside-a-pod) instead, which connects over TLS to `https://kubernetes.default.svc` and requires the `http-client` or `http2` feature.
:::

## Quick start

```rust
use rust_web_server::ingress::{IngressRouter, KubernetesIngressWatcher};
use rust_web_server::server::Server;

fn main() {
    let watcher = KubernetesIngressWatcher::from_env()
        .expect("Set RWS_K8S_API_SERVER before starting");
    watcher.start(); // spawns background polling thread

    let app = IngressRouter::new(watcher);
    let (listener, pool) = Server::setup().unwrap();
    Server::run(listener, pool, app);
}
```

## Configuration options

```rust
let watcher = KubernetesIngressWatcher::from_env()
    .unwrap()
    .namespace("production")     // override namespace
    .ingress_class("rws")        // only watch Ingress objects with spec.ingressClassName: rws
    .poll_interval_secs(15);     // resync every 15 s instead of 30 (watch still runs alongside)

let app = IngressRouter::new(watcher)
    .connect_timeout_ms(2_000)  // TCP connect to upstream (default 5 000 ms)
    .read_timeout_ms(60_000);   // response read timeout   (default 30 000 ms)
```

### IngressClass filtering

On a single-controller cluster, `.ingress_class(...)` doesn't need to be set — the watcher picks up every Ingress object regardless of `spec.ingressClassName` by default, matching the pre-filtering behavior this crate has always had. On a **multi-controller** cluster (e.g. `rws` running alongside `nginx-ingress`), set `.ingress_class("rws")` so this watcher only builds routes from Ingress objects meant for it — an Ingress with no `ingressClassName` at all never matches a configured filter, so it needs one explicitly to be picked up.

## Path matching

`IngressRule::matches` implements the two Kubernetes `pathType` values that carry real routing semantics:

- If `host` is non-empty, the incoming `Host` header must match (case-insensitive).
- Any query string on the request URI is ignored for path matching.
- **`Prefix`** (the default when `pathType` is absent, and how `ImplementationSpecific` is also treated) matches on whole path *segments*, not raw bytes: rule path `/foo` matches `/foo`, `/foo/`, and `/foo/bar`, but **not** `/foobar`.
- **`Exact`** requires the request path to equal the rule's path exactly (ignoring the query string).

The first matching rule wins. Rules are evaluated in the order they are returned by the API server.

Upstream addresses are resolved as:

```
{service_name}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local:{service_port}
```

## RBAC requirements

The pod's service account needs read access to Ingress resources. Apply the following manifests:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress
  namespace: default
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress-reader
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["networking.k8s.io"]
    resources: ["ingresses"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress-reader
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: rws-ingress-reader
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: rws-ingress
    namespace: default
```

## Deployment example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: rws-ingress-controller
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: rws-ingress-controller
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: rws-ingress-controller
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: rws-ingress
      containers:
        - name: rws
          image: your-registry/rust-web-server:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 7878
          env:
            - name: RWS_K8S_API_SERVER
              value: "http://localhost:8001"
            - name: RWS_K8S_TOKEN
              value: ""
            - name: RWS_K8S_NAMESPACE
              value: "default"
        # kubectl proxy sidecar exposes the API over plain HTTP
        - name: kubectl-proxy
          image: bitnami/kubectl:latest
          args: ["proxy", "--port=8001", "--address=127.0.0.1"]
```

## Connecting directly from inside a pod

`from_service_account()` (requires the `http-client` or `http2` feature — both already pull in `rustls`) reads the token, namespace, and CA certificate from the files Kubernetes mounts into every pod at `/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/`, and finds the API server via the `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST`/`KUBERNETES_SERVICE_PORT` environment variables every pod also has injected automatically — the same mechanism every other Kubernetes client library uses. No `kubectl proxy` sidecar needed:

```rust
use rust_web_server::ingress::{IngressRouter, KubernetesIngressWatcher};

let watcher = KubernetesIngressWatcher::from_service_account()
    .expect("not running inside a pod, or the http-client/http2 feature isn't enabled");
watcher.start();

let app = IngressRouter::new(watcher);
```

The connection is TLS, trusting **only** the cluster's own CA certificate (`.../ca.crt`) — not the public root store `http_client` uses elsewhere in this crate, since the API server's certificate is signed by that private, cluster-specific CA. Building without the `http-client`/`http2` feature leaves `from_service_account()` returning a clear error pointing back at the `kubectl proxy` + `from_env()` path above, rather than silently failing at connect time.

```toml
[dependencies]
rust-web-server = { version = "18", features = ["http-client"] }
```

---

# Observability

<https://rws8.tech/deployment/observability/>

## Metrics

### Built-in Prometheus endpoint

`GET /metrics` is always available and returns metrics in the Prometheus text exposition format. No configuration is required.

Server-wide counters updated by the request loop:

| Metric | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `rws_requests_total` | Counter | Total HTTP requests received |
| `rws_errors_total` | Counter | Connections whose handling ended in an error (I/O or application error, or a panicked handler) — not a count of 5xx responses |
| `rws_active_connections` | Gauge | Number of currently open connections |
| `http_server_request_duration_seconds` | Histogram | OpenTelemetry `http.server.request.duration` by method, status, scheme and protocol version — a [native histogram](/features/metrics/#native-histograms) for a protobuf scrape |

### Per-route metrics with MetricsLayer

Add `MetricsLayer` to any application to record per-route counters and latency histograms:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::metrics::MetricsLayer;

let app = App::new().wrap(MetricsLayer);
```

`MetricsLayer` adds:

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rws_route_requests_total` | Counter | `method`, `path`, `status` | Requests per route and status code |
| `rws_route_duration_seconds` | Histogram | `method`, `path` | Response time distribution |

### Circuit breaker state

Present automatically — no `MetricsLayer` or other opt-in needed — for every backend known to [`circuit_breaker::global()`](/proxy/circuit-breaker/):

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rws_circuit_breaker_state` | Gauge | `backend` | `0`=closed, `1`=half_open, `2`=open |

Wire `ReverseProxy::with_circuit_breaker(Arc::new(circuit_breaker::global()))` to get this metric for free alongside [automatic breaker integration](/proxy/circuit-breaker/#automatic-reverseproxy-wiring).

### TLS

`rws_tls_handshakes_total{tls_protocol_version,tls_cipher,tls_group}`, `rws_tls_handshake_failures_total` and `rws_tls_certificate_expiry_timestamp_seconds{name}` — see [TLS metrics](/features/metrics/#tls). Alert on `rws_tls_certificate_expiry_timestamp_seconds - time() < 14 * 86400`.

### Upstreams

Config-file proxies export `rws_upstream_requests_total`, `rws_upstream_request_duration_seconds`, `rws_upstream_retries_total`, `rws_upstream_backend_up` and `rws_upstream_circuit_breaker_state` per `upstream` and `backend` — see [Upstream metrics](/features/metrics/#upstream-metrics).

### OTLP metrics export

`http.server.request.duration` can also be pushed to an OpenTelemetry Collector (or any OTLP/HTTP endpoint: Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Datadog's OTLP intake) — the same data `/metrics` serves, so the two never disagree. The `rws` binary starts the exporter when an endpoint is set:

```bash
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4318   # metrics go to /v1/metrics, spans to /v1/traces
export OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=edge-1                                   # default rws
export OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL=15000                          # ms, default 60000
export OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS="api-key=secret"               # optional, key=value,…
rws
```

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | Collector base URL; `/v1/metrics` and `/v1/traces` are appended |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT` | Full metrics URL, used as is (wins over the base) |
| `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL` | Milliseconds between exports (default `60000`) |
| `OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER` | `none` turns metrics export off |
| `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_HEADERS` | Request headers, `key=value` pairs separated by commas (values percent-decoded) |
| `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `service.name` resource attribute |

Each export is an OTLP/HTTP JSON `ExportMetricsServiceRequest` with cumulative temporality and the convention's explicit buckets, attributes `http.request.method`, `http.response.status_code`, `url.scheme`, `network.protocol.name` and `network.protocol.version`. A last export is sent on SIGTERM/SIGINT. From Rust: `otel::metrics::start(MetricsExportConfig { .. })` or `otel::metrics::start_from_env()`, and `otel::shutdown()` before exit.

### Grafana / PromQL queries

```promql
# Request rate (requests per second over 1 m)
rate(rws_requests_total[1m])

# Error rate
rate(rws_errors_total[1m])

# p99 latency per route
histogram_quantile(0.99, rate(rws_route_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))

# Top routes by request count
topk(10, sum by (path) (rate(rws_route_requests_total[5m])))

# Backends currently tripped open
rws_circuit_breaker_state == 2
```

## Logs

### JSON structured logs (default)

By default the server writes one newline-delimited JSON object per request to stdout:

```json
{"time":"2026-07-02T12:00:00Z","remote_addr":"127.0.0.1","method":"GET","path":"/healthz","protocol":"HTTP/1.1","status":200,"bytes":2}
```

JSON logs are well-suited for ingestion by Loki, Fluentd, Datadog, and other structured-log collectors.

### Combined Log Format

Set `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=combined` (via environment variable or `rws.config.toml`) for Apache Combined Log Format (CLF):

```
127.0.0.1 - - [02/Jul/2026:12:00:00 +0000] "GET /healthz HTTP/1.1" 200 2
```

This format is compatible with GoAccess, AWStats, and most log-analysis tools.

To produce the same line yourself — in your own middleware or a custom server loop — call `Log::combined`:

```rust
use rust_web_server::log::Log;

// request: &Request, response: &Response, peer_addr: &SocketAddr
let line = Log::combined(&request, &response, &peer_addr);
println!("{}", line);
// 192.168.1.1 - - [29/Jun/2026:14:23:05 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 1234
```

`RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=off` writes no access log at all.

### Buffered writes

Access-log lines are buffered per worker thread and written to stdout by a
background thread every 100 ms — at once when a thread's buffer passes
32 KiB, when a thread exits, and when the process exits normally (including
a graceful shutdown on `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`). Writing each line with its own
`write` under the process-wide stdout lock cost about a sixth of a small
request's CPU. A line can therefore appear up to 100 ms after its request;
lines from one thread keep their order, and every line carries its own
timestamp. Code that ends the process some other way can call
`Log::flush_access_log()` first.

### Writing to a file

Set `access_log` (`RWS_CONFIG_ACCESS_LOG`, since 18.1.0) to write the access
log to a file instead of stdout:

```toml
log_format          = "combined"
access_log          = "/var/log/rws/access.log"
access_log_max_size = "100M"    # optional: rotate past 100 MiB
access_log_keep     = 5         # access.log.1 … access.log.5
```

- Lines are appended; the file and its directory must be writable by rws.
- **Rotation by rws:** with `access_log_max_size`, the file is renamed
  `access.log.1` (older ones shift up, the oldest past `access_log_keep` is
  deleted) and a new one is started when the next lines would pass the
  size.
- **Rotation by logrotate:** leave `access_log_max_size` at `0` and have
  logrotate send `SIGUSR1` after moving the file; rws reopens the path
  before its next write:

  ```
  /var/log/rws/access.log {
      daily
      rotate 14
      compress
      delaycompress
      missingok
      notifempty
      postrotate
          systemctl kill -s USR1 rws.service
      endscript
  }
  ```

  Without an access-log file `SIGUSR1` keeps its default action (it ends
  the process), so don't send it to an rws logging to stdout.

### Log aggregation in Kubernetes

The server writes all logs to stdout. Kubernetes log aggregation pipelines pick them up automatically:

```sh
# View logs in real time
kubectl logs -f deployment/my-rws-app

# Ship to Loki via Promtail — no application config required; just label the pod
```


## Tracing

### OtelLayer

`OtelLayer` implements `Middleware` and propagates W3C `traceparent` headers. Add it to your application and configure an OTLP exporter:

```rust
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::core::New;
use rust_web_server::otel::{self, ExporterConfig, OtelLayer, TracingConfig};

otel::setup(TracingConfig {
    service_name: "my-service".to_string(),
    exporter: ExporterConfig::Otlp {
        endpoint: "http://tempo:4318".to_string(),
    },
    ..TracingConfig::default()
});

let app = App::new().wrap(OtelLayer);
```

The layer reads the incoming `traceparent` header, creates a span for each request (a child of the caller's span when one was sent), and exports completed spans to the configured OTLP endpoint. Start nested spans inside a request with `otel::span(name)` / `otel::client_span(name)` — see [Distributed Tracing](/features/tracing/#child-spans).

The `rws` binary adds `OtelLayer` and exports spans by itself when `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` is set — see [Environment variable setup](/features/tracing/#environment-variable-setup).

### Supported backends

- **Grafana Tempo** — point `endpoint` at the OTLP HTTP port (default `4318`)
- **Jaeger** — enable the OTLP receiver and point at port `4318`
- **OpenTelemetry Collector** — use as a fan-out proxy to multiple backends

### Distributed tracing across services

Include the `traceparent` header in outbound requests using the synchronous HTTP client:

```rust
use rust_web_server::http_client::Client;

let response = Client::new()
    .get("http://downstream-service/api/data")
    .header("traceparent", incoming_traceparent)
    .send()?;
```

Inside a traced request rws does this itself: the HTTP client, the proxies and database statements get client spans, and `traceparent` plus [`baggage`](/features/tracing/#baggage) are sent on — see [Automatic client spans and propagation](/features/tracing/#automatic-client-spans-and-propagation).

## Health endpoints

Two health endpoints are built into every server instance without any configuration:

### GET /healthz — liveness

Returns `200 OK` as long as the binary is running. Use this as the Kubernetes liveness probe:

```yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 7878
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
```

### GET /readyz — readiness

Returns `200 OK` during normal operation. Returns `503 Service Unavailable` during graceful shutdown (after `SIGTERM` is received, while in-flight requests are being drained). Use as the Kubernetes readiness probe:

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 7878
  initialDelaySeconds: 3
  periodSeconds: 5
```

The readiness gate ensures the load balancer stops routing new traffic to a pod as soon as it begins draining, giving in-flight requests time to complete before the pod terminates.

---

# systemd

<https://rws8.tech/deployment/systemd/>

On a Linux host without containers, run `rws` as a systemd service. The unit
below runs it as an unprivileged user that can bind ports 80 and 443, sees
the system read-only except for its own state and log directories, and
reloads its configuration on `systemctl reload`.

## Install from a package

Since 18.2.0 rws has `.deb` and `.rpm` packages for x86_64 and arm64, from
signed repositories (so `apt upgrade` / `dnf upgrade` bring new releases) or
from each [GitHub release page](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/releases).
They install the binary as `/usr/bin/rws`, the unit below, a configuration
in `/etc/rws/rws.config.toml` and a placeholder page in `/var/www/rws`,
create the `rws` user, and start the service on port 7878.

Debian, Ubuntu:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://rws8.tech/apt/rws.gpg | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/rws.gpg >/dev/null
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/rws.gpg] https://rws8.tech/apt stable main" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/rws.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install rws
curl localhost:7878/                           # rws is running
```

Fedora, RHEL, Rocky, Alma (packages and repository metadata are signed):

```bash
sudo curl -fsSL -o /etc/yum.repos.d/rws.repo https://rws8.tech/rpm/rws.repo
sudo dnf install rws
```

A downloaded package installs the same way: `sudo apt install ./rws_18.2.0_amd64.deb`,
`sudo dnf install ./rws-18.2.0-1.x86_64.rpm`. The repositories hold the
newest release only; older ones stay on the release pages.

Put your site in `/var/www/rws`, change settings in
`/etc/rws/rws.config.toml` (an upgrade keeps your edits) and apply them with
`sudo systemctl reload rws`. To serve on port 80, set `port = 80` — the unit
already grants the capability.

## Install by hand

```bash
sudo install -m 0755 rws /usr/bin/rws
sudo useradd --system --user-group --no-create-home --home-dir /var/lib/rws --shell /usr/sbin/nologin rws
sudo mkdir -p /etc/rws /var/www/rws
sudo cp rws.config.toml /etc/rws/
sudoedit /etc/systemd/system/rws.service      # the unit below
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now rws
```

## The unit

The packages install this file as `/usr/lib/systemd/system/rws.service`
([`packaging/linux/rws.service`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/packaging/linux/rws.service)):

```ini
[Unit]
Description=rws web server
Documentation=https://rws8.tech
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=rws
Group=rws
WorkingDirectory=/var/www/rws
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_FILE=/etc/rws/rws.config.toml
# ACME certificates and account key in /var/lib/rws (StateDirectory below).
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_ACME_CERT_PATH=/var/lib/rws/cert.pem
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_ACME_KEY_PATH=/var/lib/rws/key.pem
Environment=RWS_CONFIG_ACME_ACCOUNT_KEY_PATH=/var/lib/rws/acme_account.key
ExecStart=/usr/bin/rws
# Re-read the config and certificates without dropping connections.
ExecReload=/bin/kill -HUP $MAINPID
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2s
LimitNOFILE=65536

# Ports 80/443 without root.
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
NoNewPrivileges=yes

# Writable: /var/lib/rws (state) and /var/log/rws (access log) only.
StateDirectory=rws
LogsDirectory=rws
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadOnlyPaths=/var/www/rws /etc/rws
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
ProtectProc=invisible
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
LockPersonality=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
SystemCallArchitectures=native
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallFilter=~@privileged @resources
UMask=0027

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

`systemd-analyze security rws.service` rates it "OK" or better; check it on
your host after installing.

## Access log

Write the access log under `/var/log/rws` (the unit's `LogsDirectory`) in
`/etc/rws/rws.config.toml`:

```toml
access_log = "/var/log/rws/access.log"
```

Rotate it with logrotate, which tells rws to reopen the file with
`systemctl kill -s USR1 rws.service` — see
[Writing to a file](/deployment/observability/#writing-to-a-file) for the
logrotate snippet, or set `access_log_max_size` and let rws rotate it.
Without `access_log`, lines go to stdout and land in the journal
(`journalctl -u rws`).

## Day to day

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Check a config change before applying it | `rws --check /etc/rws/rws.config.toml` |
| Apply it (config, routes, certificates) | `sudo systemctl reload rws` |
| Logs and errors | `journalctl -u rws -f` |
| Reopen the access log | `sudo systemctl kill -s USR1 rws` |
| Restart | `sudo systemctl restart rws` |

---

# Windows

<https://rws8.tech/deployment/windows/>

The `rws.exe` in each release's `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` zip on the
[GitHub release page](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/releases)
runs as it does elsewhere: it serves the current directory on port 7878.

```powershell
Expand-Archive rws-18.2.0-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip C:\rws
cd C:\www
C:\rws\rws-18.2.0-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\rws.exe
```

## As a Windows service

`rws.exe --windows-service=<directory>` runs under the Service Control
Manager (since 18.2.0): it serves `<directory>` and reads
`<directory>\rws.config.toml` if there is one. Stopping the service — or
shutting Windows down — stops rws gracefully, finishing requests in flight.

In an administrator PowerShell:

```powershell
New-Service -Name rws -DisplayName "rws web server" -StartupType Automatic `
  -BinaryPathName '"C:\rws\rws.exe" --windows-service="C:\www"'
Start-Service rws
curl.exe http://localhost:7878/healthz
```

| Task | Command |
|---|---|
| Stop / start | `Stop-Service rws`, `Start-Service rws` |
| Apply a config change | `Restart-Service rws` — there is no SIGHUP on Windows. With `watch = true` rws reloads settings and routes by itself ([Hot reload](/features/hot-reload/)); a new certificate still needs a restart |
| Remove | `Stop-Service rws; sc.exe delete rws` |

The directory is required: a service starts in `C:\Windows\System32`, and
rws serves its working directory. Keep only what should be public in it
(rws never serves `rws.config.toml`, `*.pem` or `*.key`).

A service has no console, so its access log goes nowhere unless you write it
to a file — in `<directory>\rws.config.toml`:

```toml
access_log = 'C:\rws\logs\access.log'
access_log_max_size = 104857600   # rotate at 100 MiB
```

The service runs as LocalSystem by default; to run it as a less privileged
account, set one with `sc.exe config rws obj= "NT AUTHORITY\LocalService"`
and give that account read access to the directory and write access to the
log directory.

---

# WASM Guest Component

<https://rws8.tech/deployment/wasm/>

`rws-wasm-shim` is a separate workspace package that runs the same `App`/`Router`/middleware logic you use natively — but hosted inside a WASM component instead of a `TcpListener`. The host (Wasmtime, Spin, Fastly Compute) owns the listening socket and TLS termination; it calls the guest once per request through the standard [`wasi:http/proxy`](https://github.com/WebAssembly/wasi-http) world.

This is the "Foundation + Phase 1 + most of Phase 2" slice of the project tracked in [`spec/WASM_SHIM.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/spec/WASM_SHIM.md) in the repository — read that file for the full multi-phase plan and every verification detail. Everything on this page was tested against a real `wasmtime serve` process, not just compiled.

## Why not just compile the whole server to WASM?

`rws`'s normal accept loop uses `std::thread` (`ThreadPool`) and `rustls`/`aws-lc-rs` for TLS — neither compiles for `wasm32-wasip2`. Rather than trying to port sockets and TLS into the sandbox, the guest component reuses the existing seam every controller and middleware layer already goes through:

```rust
pub trait Application {
    fn execute(&self, request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result;
}
```

`Request` and `Response` are plain data structs with no socket handle anywhere in them, so the same `App::execute()` call that runs natively behind a `TcpListener` also runs unchanged behind a `wasi:http` incoming request.

## Building and running

```bash
rustup target add wasm32-wasip2   # wasm32-wasip2 is Tier 2 since Rust 1.82
cd rws-wasm-shim
cargo build --release --target wasm32-wasip2
wasmtime serve target/wasm32-wasip2/release/rws_wasm_shim.wasm
```

In another shell:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/
```

The build output (`rws_wasm_shim.wasm`) is already a valid WASM component on this target — no separate `wasm-tools component new` step is needed.

The adapter is a small `Guest::handle` implementation (full version in `rws-wasm-shim/src/lib.rs`):

```rust
use wasip2::exports::http::incoming_handler::Guest;
use wasip2::http::types::{IncomingRequest, ResponseOutparam};
use rust_web_server::app::App;
use rust_web_server::application::Application;
use rust_web_server::core::New;

wasip2::http::proxy::export!(Shim);
struct Shim;

impl Guest for Shim {
    fn handle(request: IncomingRequest, response_out: ResponseOutparam) {
        // translate `request` into a rust_web_server::request::Request,
        // call App::new().execute(&request, &connection), and write the
        // Response back through `response_out`.
    }
}
```

## What runs inside the guest

Only the parts of `rust-web-server` that don't touch a socket or spawn a thread are compiled for `wasm32-wasip2` — everything else is behind `#[cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))]`. This list grew substantially past the initial "core only" slice — outbound HTTP now works, which unblocks everything built on top of it:

| Available in the guest | Native-only (excluded for `wasm32`) |
|---|---|
| `App`, `Router`, `Controller`, extractors | `Server`, `ThreadPool` |
| In-memory middleware (CORS, CSRF, rewrite, IP filter, request ID, in-memory rate limit/cache) | `ReverseProxy`, `H2ReverseProxy`, `GrpcProxy`, `TcpProxy`, `UdpProxy`, `WsProxy` |
| `Response::json`/`::text`, static-file serving (streamed for large files too) | `WebSocket`, `mailer` (raw SMTP — no `wasi:http` equivalent for arbitrary TCP protocols) |
| `http_client::Client` — **both HTTP and HTTPS**, via a `wasi:http` `outgoing-handler` backend (TLS terminated by the host, not `rustls`) | `otel`, `log`, `Scheduler` (background jobs), `redis_protocol`, `circuit_breaker`, `canary`, `service_discovery`'s DNS/etcd/Consul/Docker sources, `ingress`, `timeout`, `proxy_config` (config-driven proxy) |
| `auth` (`BasicAuthLayer`, `JwtLayer`, `ForwardAuthLayer`), `auth-asymmetric`, `csrf`, `crypto`, `webhook`, `rewrite-regex` | `model` (async ORM — needs real DB wire protocols) |
| `sso`, `sso-server`, `sso-saml`, `secrets`, `storage-s3`, `storage-azure` — all work because they only ever used `http_client::Client`, no code changes needed | |

## Three real limitations (confirmed, not theoretical)

All of these were empirically verified against a real `wasmtime serve` process, not inferred from the spec:

1. **Stateful middleware does not survive across requests.** `wasmtime serve` instantiates a **fresh guest per request** — confirmed by making an adapter call a request counter five times per invocation and watching it read back exactly `5` on every single request, never `10` or `15`. `RateLimiter`, `CacheLayer`, in-memory sessions, and metrics counters all silently reset every request under this host. Other hosts (Fastly Compute, Spin) are widely understood to behave the same way for the same isolation reasons, though only `wasmtime serve` was directly tested here. There is no in-crate fix for this — it needs either a host-provided KV binding (the `wasi-keyvalue` proposal, still pre-1.0) or accepting that stateful middleware requires a specific instance-reuse-guaranteeing host.
2. **Filesystem access needs an explicit host grant.** Unlike outbound HTTP (part of the `wasi:http/proxy` world's base contract), filesystem access is opt-in — `wasmtime serve` requires `--dir HOST_DIR::.` to expose any directory to the guest. Without it, static-file controllers silently fall back to `rws`'s built-in embedded default pages for every path, with no error — easy to miss in testing. With `--dir` granted, real files (including a 9 MB file exercised through the streaming code path) serve correctly.
3. **No real client IP or TLS SNI hostname.** The host already accepted the TCP connection and terminated TLS before ever invoking the guest, and the `wasi:http` incoming-request type has no field for either. `ConnectionInfo` gets a placeholder address and `sni_hostname: None`.

## Dependency notes

- The static-file/directory-listing controllers that ship with `App` depend on the [`file-ext`](https://crates.io/crates/file-ext) crate for path handling. `file-ext` 12.1.0 added `wasm32` support (path separator, temp folder, and a `remove_dir_all`-based recursive delete in place of shelling out to `rm`, which has no equivalent in a WASI guest) — an older `file-ext` version will fail to compile for this target.
- `rustls`'s own `aws-lc-rs` crypto-backend feature compiles C/asm that doesn't build for `wasm32-wasip2`. The root `Cargo.toml` moves `rustls`/`webpki-roots` into a `[target.'cfg(not(target_arch = "wasm32"))'.dependencies]` table so enabling `http-client` (or `sso`/`secrets`/`storage-s3`/`storage-azure`, which depend on it) on `wasm32` never pulls that broken dependency in — the wasm32 build gets its TLS from the host instead, via the `outgoing-handler` interface.

## What's still open

- An automated CI job that builds the component and drives a `wasmtime serve` smoke test in scripted form (the manual verification above, scripted).
- Verification against hosts other than `wasmtime serve` (Spin, Fastly Compute) — architecturally expected to behave the same way, but untested.
- A documented, supported answer for stateful middleware under per-request instantiation (a host-provided KV binding, most likely) — currently just a documented limitation, not a workaround.

See `spec/WASM_SHIM.md` in the repository for the complete, itemized history of what was built and verified.

---

# API Reference

<https://rws8.tech/reference/api/>

Full rustdoc documentation is published at [docs.rs/rust-web-server](https://docs.rs/rust-web-server).

This page is a quick-reference index — click through to docs.rs for the complete method-level API. Module paths are relative to `rust_web_server::`; a feature in parentheses means the item is compiled only with that Cargo feature.

## Application layer

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Application` | `application` | Trait implemented by all app types: `execute(&Request, &ConnectionInfo) -> Result`. `runs_inline(request, connection)` (default `false`) lets the async servers run a request on the event loop instead of the blocking pool — only for work that never waits. See [Async handlers](/building-apps/async-handlers/) |
| `AsyncResponse` | `application` (`http2`) | Return type of the optional `Application::execute_async`, awaited on the connection's task instead of holding a blocking-pool thread |
| `Controller` | `controller` | Trait with `is_matching(request, connection)` and `process(request, response, connection)`. See [Controllers](/building-apps/controllers/) |
| `App` | `app` | Zero-config application with all built-in controllers. `App::with_config(ServerConfig)` pins it to a fixed config (no env reads per request — the lock-free pattern for parallel tests) |
| `AppWithState` | `state` | State-aware app with `.get/.post/.put/.patch/.delete` route builders; state shared as `Arc`. Entry point `App::with_state(S)`; `.with_config(ServerConfig)` pins the fallback `App`. See [State](/building-apps/state/) |
| `AsyncAppWithState` | `async_state` (`http2`) | Same with `async fn` handlers. Entry point `App::with_async_state(S)` |
| `Middleware` | `middleware` | Layer trait: `handle(request, connection, next)`. `runs_inline` / `is_passthrough` (default `false`) declare a layer non-blocking or a no-op for a request. See [Middleware](/building-apps/middleware/) |
| `WithMiddleware` | `middleware` | Wraps any `Application` with a layer stack; `app.wrap(layer)`, first-pushed is outermost |
| `Container` | `di` | `TypeId`-keyed dependency injection container: `register::`, `provide::<dyn Trait>`, `*_named`, `get`. Pass it directly to `App::with_state(container)` — not `into_arc()`, which double-wraps. See [Dependency injection](/building-apps/dependency-injection/) |
| `TeraEngine` | `template` (`tera`) | Jinja2-style templates: `from_dir`, `from_raw`; global `template::init(dir)` / `template::render(name, &ctx)` / `template::reload()` (also run on `SIGHUP`). See [Templates](/building-apps/templates/) |

## Macros

| Item | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `routes!` | `macros` | Declarative routing table — builds `AppWithState`, `AsyncAppWithState` or `Router` from `METHOD "path" => handler` lines. See [Routing](/building-apps/routing/) |
| `#[route]`, `#[get]`, `#[post]`, `#[put]`, `#[patch]`, `#[delete]` | crate root (`macros`) | Attribute macros annotating a handler with its method and path |
| `#[derive(FromRequest)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Derives `FromRequest` for a named-field struct, extracting fields in order and stopping at the first error |
| `#[derive(JsonSchema)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Derives `schema::JsonSchema` for a named-field struct or unit enum, following its `#[serde]` renames (18.0.0). See [Typed tools](/mcp/tools/#typed-tools) |
| `#[derive(Validate)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Derives `Validate` from `#[validate(length, range, email, required, url)]` field annotations |
| `#[derive(Config)]` | crate root (`macros`) | Typed env-var binding: generates `load() -> Result`; `#[config(env, default, prefix)]`. See [Config binding](/features/config-binding/) |
| `#[derive(Model)]` | crate root (`macros` + a `model-*` feature) | Maps a struct to a table (`#[table]`, `#[primary_key(auto_increment)]`, `#[column]`, `#[ignore]`) and generates `T::repository(&pool)` / `T::query(&pool)` |

## HTTP primitives

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Request` | `request` | Parsed HTTP request: method, URI, version, headers, body bytes. `request.header(name)` is a case-insensitive, allocation-free lookup; `Request::is_supported_method` checks a method token |
| `Response` | `response` | HTTP response: status code, headers, body as `Vec`. `Response::json(status, bytes)` / `Response::text(status, &str)` are one-line builders; `response.header(name)` looks a header up |
| `STATUS_CODE_REASON_PHRASE` | `response` | Every HTTP status code as a typed constant |
| `Header` | `header` | Name/value pair (`Cow<'static, str>` fields since 18.0.0; build with `Header::new(name, value)`, read via deref); constants for all standard header names. See [Migrating to 18.0](/reference/migrating-18/) |
| `HTTP` | `http` | Version constants; `HTTP::is_supported_version` |
| `MimeType` | `mime_type` | MIME type constants and detection from a file extension |
| `Range` / `ContentRange` | `range` | Byte ranges and the body parts of a `Response` (bytes, files, multipart) |
| `URL` | `url` | Parse and build URLs; percent-encode/decode |
| `FormUrlEncoded` | `body::form_urlencoded` | Parses `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies. See [Forms & uploads](/building-apps/forms-uploads/) |
| `FormMultipartData` | `body::multipart_form_data` | Parses `multipart/form-data` uploads |
| `Json` | `json` (`serde`) | Serde JSON extractor and responder. See [JSON](/building-apps/json/) |
| `CookieJar` | `cookie` | Parses the `Cookie` request header. See [Cookies](/building-apps/cookies/) |
| `SetCookie` | `cookie` | Builds `Set-Cookie` values with all RFC 6265 attributes |
| `signed_cookie` / `verify_signed_cookie` | `cookie` (`crypto`) | HMAC-SHA256 tamper-evident cookie value `"<value>.<hex-signature>"`; verification returns `None` on tampering |
| `encrypted_cookie` / `decrypt_cookie` | `cookie` (`crypto`) | AES-256-GCM confidential cookie value; fresh nonce per call, `None` on tampering or wrong key |

## Routing

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Router` | `router` | Path-pattern router with `:param` and `*wildcard`; `.with_host(name)` restricts it to one virtual host; `.matches(request, connection)` tells whether `handle()` would run a handler |
| `PathParams` | `router` | Extracted path parameters; `.get(name) -> Option<&str>` |
| `ConnectionInfo` | `server` | Client/server IP, port, and SNI hostname per connection |
| `VirtualHostConfig` | `virtual_host` | Per-domain certificate config `{ domain, cert_file, key_file }` for SNI. See [Virtual hosting](/features/virtual-hosting/) |

## Typed extractors and errors

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `FromRequest` | `extract` | Trait for typed extraction from a request, returning a ready error response on failure. See [Extractors](/building-apps/extractors/) |
| `Body` | `extract` | Raw request body bytes (never fails) |
| `Storage::put_stream` / `S3_PART_SIZE` | `storage` | Store a `Read` stream: S3 multipart upload (8 MiB parts), local temp file + rename; default buffers (18.0.0) |
| `request::Body` | `request` | `Request.body` (18.0.0): bytes, or a stream (`Body::stream`, `body_bytes()`, `into_reader()`); derefs to `&[u8]`. Not the `extract::Body` extractor |
| `BodyText` | `extract` | UTF-8 request body (returns 400 on invalid UTF-8) |
| `Query` | `extract` | Parsed query string as `HashMap` |
| `RequestHeaders` | `extract` | All request headers with case-insensitive `.get(name)` |
| `RequestId` | `extract` / `request_id` | The ID `RequestIdLayer` put on the request; empty string without it (never fails) |
| `IntoResponse` | `error` | Trait for mapping error enums to `Response` values. See [Error handling](/building-apps/error-handling/) |
| `AppError` | `error` | Built-in error variants: `BadRequest`, `NotFound`, `Internal`, etc. |
| `Validate` | `validate` | Field-level validation trait. See [Validation](/building-apps/validation/) |
| `ValidationErrors` | `validate` | Collects every validation failure before returning |
| `Validated` | `validate` | Extractor that extracts then validates: 400 on extraction failure, 422 with a JSON error body on validation failure |
| `is_email` / `is_url` | `validate` | Format checks used by the derive; callable directly |

## Server and configuration

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Server` | `server` | TCP listener, thread pool, TLS acceptor, and request loop. `Server::continue_response` / `expectation_failed_response` implement `Expect: 100-continue` / 417 on HTTP/1.1 |
| `server::REQUEST_HEAD_TIMEOUT` | `server` | 30 s: a request head must complete within this of its first byte, else `408` |
| `ServerConfig` | `server_config` | Typed snapshot of per-instance config (CORS, CSP, `client_hints`, `static_cache_control`, log format). `ServerConfig::current()` is the shared per-request snapshot; call `server_config::invalidate()` after a direct `std::env::set_var` |
| `ConfigSnapshot` | `config_reload` | Hot-reloadable values, read with `config_reload::current()`. See [Hot reload](/features/hot-reload/) |
| `config_reload::reload` / `config_reload::on_reload` | `config_reload` | Re-read `rws.config.toml` (also on `SIGHUP` and `POST /admin/config/reload`); register a closure run after every reload |
| `ConfigReport` | `config_check` | Result of `config_check::check_file` / `check_str` (what `rws --check` runs): `errors`, `warnings`, `.is_ok()`, `.render(path)`, `.render_json(path)`. See [Config file](/configuration/config-file/) |
| `get_max_body_size` | `entry_point` | Reads `RWS_CONFIG_MAX_BODY_SIZE_IN_BYTES` (default `0`, unlimited); larger requests get `413` before buffering |
| `get_spa_fallback` / `get_spa_fallback_exclude_prefixes` | `entry_point` | Read `RWS_CONFIG_SPA_FALLBACK*`. See [Static files](/features/static-files/) |
| `FromEnvStr` | `config_binding` | Implement for custom field types used with `#[derive(Config)]` |
| `secrets::resolve` / `resolve_env_vars` | `secrets` (`secrets`) | Resolve `vault://`, `aws-sm://` and `azkv://` references; `Server::setup()` rewrites matching `RWS_*` env vars at startup and fails hard on errors. See [Secrets](/features/secrets/) |
| `SecretsError` | `secrets` (`secrets`) | Error type for secret resolution |
| `StaticResourceController::STREAM_THRESHOLD` | `app::controller::static_resource` | 256 KiB: larger static files are streamed from disk instead of read into memory |
| `StaticResourceController::render_directory_listing` | `app::controller::static_resource` | Renders the listing `App` serves for a directory without `index.html` |
| `DirectoryListingAssetsController` | `app::controller::directory_listing` | Serves the listing's CSS/JS at `/rws-directory-listing.{css,js}` (same-origin, so the default CSP allows them); a file on disk overrides the built-in |

## Middleware

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `RateLimiter` | `rate_limit` | Sliding-window per-key limiter; `rate_limit::global()` for the singleton; `.retry_after()` / `.limits()`. See [Rate limiting](/features/rate-limiting/) |
| `RedisRateLimiter` | `rate_limit` | Fixed-window limiter shared across instances through Redis; `from_env()` |
| `RateLimitLayer` | `middleware` | Enforces the global rate limiter per client IP; `429` with `Retry-After` |
| `CacheLayer` | `cache` | In-memory TTL response cache for GET (`CacheLayer::memory(n).ttl(s).vary_by_header(h)`); skips `no-store`/`private`/`no-cache`, `Range` and out-of-key `Vary` responses. See [Caching](/features/caching/) |
| `MetricsLayer` | `metrics` | Per-route Prometheus counters and latency histograms. See [Metrics](/features/metrics/) |
| `RewriteLayer` | `rewrite` | Request/response header, URI, body, and status rewriting; `.request_uri_regex_rewrite` needs `rewrite-regex`. See [Rewrite](/features/rewrite/) |
| `BasicAuthLayer` | `auth` (`auth`) | HTTP Basic authentication via a closure or `from_htpasswd_file` (plain or rws's `{SHA256}` scheme — not Apache `{SHA}`/`$apr1$`/bcrypt). See [Auth](/features/auth/) |
| `JwtLayer` | `auth` (`auth`) | HS256 Bearer JWT validation; `::rs256`/`::es256` verify against a static public key (`auth-asymmetric`) |
| `ForwardAuthLayer` | `auth::forward` (`auth`) | Delegates allow/deny to an external HTTP service; verbatim pass-through on non-2xx, 502 if unreachable |
| `IpFilter` | `ip_filter` | IPv4/IPv6 address or CIDR allowlist/denylist; `ip_filter::is_valid_entry` checks an entry. See [IP filter](/features/ip-filter/) |
| `Blocklist` | `blocklist` | Runtime IP blocklist: `blocklist::global().block(ip)` / `.unblock` / `.is_blocked` / `.list` / `.clear` |
| `BlocklistLayer` | `blocklist` | Answers `403` for blocked client IPs |
| `MaintenanceLayer` / `MAINTENANCE_MODE` | `maintenance` | While the `AtomicBool` is `true`, answers `503` for everything but `/healthz` and `/readyz` |
| `RequestLog` | `request_log` | In-memory buffer of recent requests (`request_log::global()`, capacity 1000); `.recent(n)` / `.recent_errors(n)` |
| `LogLayer` | `request_log` | Records each request into `RequestLog` |
| `RequestIdLayer` | `request_id` | Correlation-ID middleware — echoes or generates `X-Request-Id` (`generate_request_id()`, UUID-v4-shaped, not crypto-random). See [Request ID](/features/request-id/) |
| `CsrfLayer` | `csrf` (`csrf`) | Double-submit cookie CSRF protection; 403 on mismatch. See [CSRF](/features/csrf/) |
| `CsrfToken` | `csrf` (`csrf`) | Extractor for the current token in a GET handler; implements `Display` |
| `TimeoutLayer` | `timeout` | Wraps a whole `Application` with a deadline (`504`). See [Timeouts](/features/timeouts/) |
| `with_timeout` / `with_timeout_state` / `with_timeout_async` | `timeout` | Per-handler timeouts. The sync ones bound the client's wait but can't cancel the work; `with_timeout_async` (`http2`) cancels the future |
| `FeatureStore` | `feature` | Runtime feature toggles: `feature::global().set(name, bool)` / `.is_enabled` / `.list` |

## Authentication and crypto

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `build_jwt` / `verify_jwt` | `auth` (`auth`) | Sign and verify HS256 JWTs |
| `Claims` | `auth` (`auth`) | Decoded JWT claims: `sub`, `exp`, raw JSON payload |
| `verify_jwt_rs256` / `verify_jwt_es256` | `auth` (`auth-asymmetric`) | Standalone RS256/ES256 verification backing `JwtLayer::rs256`/`::es256` |
| `RsaPublicKey` | `rsa_key` (`auth-asymmetric` / `sso`) | In-crate RSA public key (PEM, SPKI/PKCS#1 DER or components; 2048–8192 bits); `.verify_pkcs1v15_sha256(message, signature)` |
| `hash_password` / `verify_password` | `crypto` (`crypto`) | Argon2id hashing (PHC string, salt embedded) and constant-time verification |
| `generate_token` | `crypto` (`crypto`) | CSPRNG hex token for reset links and API keys |
| `CryptoError` | `crypto` (`crypto`) | Error type for password hashing |
| `verify_webhook_signature` | `webhook` (`webhook`) | Verifies an inbound webhook HMAC for a `WebhookProvider`. See [Webhooks](/features/webhooks/) |
| `WebhookProvider` | `webhook` (`webhook`) | `GitHub`, `Shopify`, `Stripe` (300 s default replay tolerance) |
| `verify_github_signature` / `verify_shopify_signature` / `verify_stripe_signature` / `verify_stripe_signature_with_tolerance` | `webhook` (`webhook`) | Per-provider functions when the provider is known at the call site |

## SSO

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `OidcAuth` | `sso` (`sso`) | OAuth2/OIDC middleware: intercepts `/auth/login`, `/auth/callback`, `/auth/logout`; `OidcAuth::claims(req)` reads the claims. See [SSO](/features/sso/) |
| `OidcConfig` | `sso` (`sso`) | Client configuration; presets `google`, `microsoft`, `github`, `okta`, `auth0`, `keycloak`, and `from_env()` |
| `OidcProvider` | `sso` (`sso`) | Provider endpoints; same presets plus `OidcProvider::discover(issuer)` |
| `OidcClaims` | `sso` (`sso`) | Standard OIDC claims from a verified `id_token` or UserInfo response (no `groups`) |
| `JwksCache` | `sso` (`sso`) | JWKS key cache; `verify_jwt(token, &VerifyOptions)` checks RS256/ES256 signature, `exp`, `iss`, `aud`; refetches once on a key miss |
| `VerifyOptions` | `sso` (`sso`) | `audience`, `issuer`, `leeway_secs` for `JwksCache::verify_jwt` |
| `OidcClient` | `sso` (`sso`) | `authorization_url`, `exchange_code`, `fetch_user_info` |
| `TokenResponse` | `sso` (`sso`) | Token endpoint response returned by `exchange_code` |
| `PkceVerifier` | `sso` (`sso`) | RFC 7636 code verifier; `.challenge()` |
| `PkceChallenge` | `sso` (`sso`) | S256 code challenge for the authorization URL |
| `AuthServer` | `sso` (`sso-server`) | rws as an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server (`/oauth/token`, `/oauth/authorize`, discovery). Tokens are HS256, so `jwks.json` is always empty; `/oauth/authorize` trusts an existing app session, with no built-in login page |
| `AuthServerConfig` | `sso` (`sso-server`) | `issuer`, `signing_secret`, access/refresh token lifetimes, `clients` |
| `ClientStore` | `sso` (`sso-server`) | Registry of OAuth clients: `ClientStore::new().add(client).get(id)` (no `from_env`) |
| `OAuthClient` | `sso` (`sso-server`) | One client; `client_secret: None` is a public PKCE-only client |
| `GrantType` | `sso` (`sso-server`) | `ClientCredentials`, `AuthorizationCode`, `RefreshToken` |
| `SamlSp` | `sso::saml` (`sso-saml`) | SAML 2.0 Service Provider middleware (`/saml/metadata`, `/saml/login`, `/saml/acs`, `/saml/logout`). Verifies RSA-SHA256 signatures byte-exact against the transmitted XML (not full C14N — fails closed), requires exactly one `Assertion`, rejects `EncryptedAssertion`; unsigned HTTP-POST `AuthnRequest`s; local-only logout. See [SAML](/features/saml/) |
| `SamlConfig` | `sso::saml` (`sso-saml`) | `sp_entity_id`, `sp_acs_url`, `idp_metadata`, `sessions` |
| `SamlIdpMetadata` | `sso::saml` (`sso-saml`) | Parsed IdP metadata (`entity_id`, `sso_url`, `signing_key`); `from_file` / `from_url` / `from_str` |
| `AttributeMap` | `sso::saml` (`sso-saml`) | Maps IdP attribute names to claim fields |
| `SamlClaims` | `sso::saml` (`sso-saml`) | `name_id` plus `attributes: HashMap`; read with `SamlSp::claims` / `name_id` / `attr` |

## Real-time protocols

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Sse` | `sse` | `Sse::stream()` → a streaming response and its `SseSender`; `Sse::new()` builds a buffered `text/event-stream` body. See [SSE](/features/sse/) |
| `SseStream` | `sse` | Options for a streaming response: `.buffer(events)`, `.keep_alive(interval)`, `.start()` |
| `SseSender` / `SseClosed` | `sse` | Feeds a streaming response: `send` (waits for room), `try_send`, `send_async` (`http2`), `data`, `comment`; `Err(SseClosed)` once the client is gone |
| `SseEvent` | `sse` | One event: data plus optional `event`, `id`, `retry` |
| `WebSocket` | `websocket` | RFC 6455: `WebSocket::upgrade(request, handler)` for a route, plus the handshake and frame read/write. See [WebSocket](/features/websocket/) |
| `WebSocketConnection` / `WebSocketSender` / `Message` | `websocket` | An upgraded connection: `recv()` → whole `Message::Text`/`Binary` (pings, fragments and the close handshake handled); `sender()` for other threads |
| `Frame` | `websocket` | A WebSocket frame: `Text`, `Binary`, `Ping`, `Pong`, `Close`, `Continuation` |

## MCP

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `Encoding` / `Level` | `compression` | Content codings (`gzip`, `br`, `zstd`) and levels; `negotiate(request, preference)`, `encode`, `apply_compression` (18.1.0). See [Compression](/features/compression/) |
| `JsonSchema` / `ObjectSchema` | `schema` | A type's JSON Schema as text (primitives, `Option`, collections, smart pointers built in); `ObjectSchema` builds an object schema (18.0.0) |
| `McpGateway` / `Upstream` | `mcp::gateway` | One MCP endpoint federating upstream MCP servers: `prefix__tool` names, per-caller `allow` rules, upstream credentials kept server-side (18.0.0). See [MCP gateway](/mcp/gateway/) |
| `InputRequired` / `PromptReply` | `mcp` | MCP 2026-07-28 multi round-trip requests: what a tool (`McpContent::input_required`) or prompt (`.prompt_with_context`) needs from the client — `.elicit`, `.sample`, `.list_roots`, `.state` (signed). See [Asking the client for input](/mcp/tools/#asking-the-client-for-input-mcp-2026-07-28) |
| `TaskContext` / `TaskError` | `mcp` | The MCP Tasks extension: what `McpContext::start_task`'s work runs with (`input`, `is_cancelled`, `status_message`) and how it ends. See [Long-running work: tasks](/mcp/tools/#long-running-work-tasks-mcp-tasks-extension) |
| `McpServer` / `McpIcon` | `mcp` | MCP Streamable HTTP server (`POST /mcp`, JSON-RPC 2.0, plus `GET /mcp` SSE); `.tool` / `.typed_tool` (`serde`) / `.resource` / `.prompt`, `.require_bearer`, `.require_bearer_tokens`, `.require_oauth` (`sso`), `.tool_filter`, `.session_ttl` / `.max_sessions` / `.max_sse_clients`. Entry point `McpServer::new(name, version)` or `app.mcp(name, version)`. See [MCP](/mcp/overview/) |
| `McpContent` | `mcp` | Tool result content: `text`, `json`, `image`, `embedded` |
| `McpContext` | `mcp` | Per-session context for `.tool_with_context` handlers: client info, `auth_claims`, progress, cancellation, `sample`, `list_roots` |
| `ToolAnnotations` | `mcp` | `read_only_hint`, `destructive_hint`, `idempotent_hint`, `open_world_hint` for `.tool_annotated` |

## Proxy

| Type / Trait | Module | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ReverseProxy` | `proxy` | HTTP/1.1 reverse proxy middleware: round-robin with failover (502 when all fail), pooled connections, unbuffered streaming of SSE/chunked/large bodies; `.with_circuit_breaker(Arc<dyn Breaker>)`. See [Reverse proxy](/proxy/reverse-proxy/) |
| `LoadBalancing` | `proxy` | Strategy enum passed to `ReverseProxy::strategy()` |
| `ConnPool` / `Pool` | `proxy` | Per-backend idle-connection pool (`ConnPool = Pool`); `ConnPool::new(max_idle, idle_timeout)`, share with `ReverseProxy::with_pool`. A stale pooled connection is retried once only for idempotent methods |
| `UpstreamTls` | `proxy` | TLS settings for upstreams: a PEM CA file instead of WebPKI and/or a client certificate (`UpstreamTls::new(ca, client)`; `tls_ca_file`, `tls_client_cert` on `ReverseProxy`/`H2ReverseProxy`/`GrpcProxy`, `[[upstream]] tls_ca_file`/`tls_client_cert_file`/`tls_client_key_file`); unloadable → 502 |
| `H2ReverseProxy` | `proxy` (`http2`) | HTTP/2 upstream proxy: `h2://` plain, `h2s://`/`https://` TLS; pooled connections, bodies streamed both ways, trailers kept (18.3.0) |
| `Trailers` | `response` | Trailer fields sent after a body (`Response::trailers`, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3): a shared slot a streamed body's producer fills before it ends (18.3.0) |
| `GrpcWebLayer` | `proxy` (`http2`) | Translates gRPC-web (`application/grpc-web[-text]`) to gRPC for the layers after it and the response back, trailers as the body's last frame (18.3.0). See [gRPC-web](/proxy/grpc-proxy/#grpc-web-from-browsers) |
| `GrpcProxy` | `proxy` (`http2`) | gRPC proxy (wraps `H2ReverseProxy`, filters on `application/grpc*`). See [gRPC proxy](/proxy/grpc-proxy/) |
| `TcpProxy` | `tcp_proxy` | Standalone L4 TCP proxy with round-robin backends. See [TCP proxy](/proxy/tcp-proxy/) |
| `UdpProxy` | `udp_proxy` | Standalone request-reply UDP proxy. See [UDP proxy](/proxy/udp-proxy/) |
| `WsProxy` | `ws_proxy` | WebSocket proxy, `ws://` and `wss://` (`http-client` or `http2`); `with_live_backends` for health-aware selection (503 when empty). See [WebSocket proxy](/proxy/websocket-proxy/) |
| `CanaryLayer` | `canary` | Weighted traffic splitting (smooth weighted round-robin); `Clone` shares state, `.update()` changes weights live. See [Canary](/proxy/canary/) |
| `WeightedBackend` | `canary` | One weighted backend URL |
| `WeightedPool` | `canary` | A weighted group whose members come from a `BackendPool` |
| `CircuitBreaker` | `circuit_breaker` | Per-backend Closed/Open/HalfOpen breaker in memory; `circuit_breaker::global()`. See [Circuit breaker](/proxy/circuit-breaker/) |
| `RedisCircuitBreaker` | `circuit_breaker` | Same state machine shared through Redis; methods return `Result`; `from_env()` |
| `Breaker` | `circuit_breaker` | Object-safe trait over both breakers, taken by `ReverseProxy::with_circuit_breaker` |
| `RetryLayer` | `circuit_breaker` | Re-dispatches a request whose status is retryable (default 502/503/504); push it before the proxy |
| `BackendPool` | `service_discovery` | Backend list refreshed by a background thread. See [Service discovery](/proxy/service-discovery/) |
| `DiscoverySource` | `service_discovery` | `Static`, `EnvPrefix`, `File`, `Dns`, `DnsSrv`, `Consul`, `Docker`, `EtcdWatch` |
| `KubernetesIngressWatcher` | `ingress` | Resyncs and watches Ingress resources; `.from_service_account()` connects in-cluster (`http-client`/`http2`). See [Kubernetes Ingress](/deployment/kubernetes-ingress/) |
| `IngressRouter` | `ingress` | `Application` routing requests by the watched Ingress rules |
| `IngressRule` | `ingress` | One parsed Ingress rule |
| `PathType` | `ingress` | `Exact`, `Prefix`, `ImplementationSpecific` |
| `ProxyConfig` | `proxy_config` | Parsed `[[route]]`/`[[upstream]]` config; `ProxyConfig::is_proxy_mode()`, `.validate(&mut ConfigReport)`. See [Config-driven proxy](/proxy/config-driven/) |
| `ConfigDrivenApp` | `proxy_config` | The app `proxy_config::build_from_file()` returns: first-match router with per-route middleware and per-upstream `strategy` (`round_robin`, `random`, `ip_hash`, `least_connections`); `.with_config(ServerConfig)` |
| `StickyConfig`, `BreakerConfig`, `RetryConfig` | `proxy_config` | An `[[upstream]]`'s `[upstream.sticky]`, `[upstream.circuit_breaker]` and `[upstream.retry]` (fields of `UpstreamConfig`, beside `weights`). See [Weights, stickiness, retries and the circuit breaker](/proxy/config-driven/#weights-stickiness-retries-and-the-circuit-breaker) |
| `ReloadOutcome` | `proxy_config` | Result of `ConfigDrivenApp::reload_from_str` / `reload_from_file` (validated first; the running routes stay on errors) |
