# Troubleshooting

<https://rws8.tech/reference/troubleshooting/>

## Starting the server

### `unable to set up TCP listener: Permission denied (os error 13)`

Ports below 1024 need privileges. Use a higher port (`--port=7878`), or run
with `sudo` / as Administrator. In a container, the release image runs as a
non-root user, so map a high container port to 80/443 instead.

### `unable to set up TCP listener: Address already in use`

Another process holds the port. Find it:

```bash
sudo lsof -i :7878     # macOS and Linux
sudo fuser 7878/tcp    # Linux
```

### `Cannot assign requested address (os error 99)`

The `--ip` you passed isn't assigned to any local interface. List them with
`ip addr` (Linux) or `ifconfig`, or bind to all of them with `--ip=0.0.0.0`.

### `sudo rws` says `command not found`

`~/.cargo/bin` (or `/usr/local/bin`) isn't on root's `PATH`. Use the full
path: `sudo ~/.cargo/bin/rws`.

## Reaching the server

### Other machines can't connect

- Bound to `127.0.0.1`? That only accepts local connections. The default is
  `0.0.0.0`; pass `--ip=0.0.0.0` if you overrode it.
- `Connection refused` from another host with the right IP: a firewall is
  blocking the port.

### Serving on IPv6

`rws --ip=::` listens on IPv6 (and IPv4-mapped addresses). Link-local
`fe80::…` addresses need a zone id that browsers rarely accept; connect with
the machine's IPv4 address or a global IPv6 address instead.

### HTTPS, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 isn't working

No certificate is configured, so `rws` falls back to plain HTTP/1.1. Provide
one ([HTTPS / TLS](/features/https-tls/)) or let `rws` get one
([ACME](/features/acme/)):

```bash
rws --tls-cert-file=/path/to/cert.pem --tls-key-file=/path/to/key.pem
```

### `TLS setup failed: failed to read cert file …`

The path is wrong, the process can't read it, or the file isn't PEM. Both the
certificate (chain) and the key must be PEM.

### The browser warns about the certificate

Self-signed certificates aren't trusted. For local development add yours to
the system trust store (or use `mkcert`); in production use a public CA,
for example through [ACME](/features/acme/).

### Malformed-request errors (`400`)

The server received something that isn't an HTTP request — a port scanner,
TLS sent to a plain-HTTP port, or garbage. The client gets a `400 Bad Request`;
it's safe to ignore.

### A directory shows a file listing

A directory without `index.html` is shown as a listing. Add an `index.html` to
serve that instead.

## Logs and metrics

### I want the Combined Log Format, not JSON

Set `RWS_CONFIG_LOG_FORMAT=combined` (or `log_format = "combined"` in
`rws.config.toml`); `off` disables the access log. JSON is the default. Lines
are buffered and written within 100 ms — see
[Observability](/deployment/observability/).

### Scraping metrics

`GET /metrics` serves Prometheus text format; see [Metrics](/features/metrics/)
for the metric names and a scrape config.

## Kubernetes

### Probes fail with `Connection refused`

The kubelet probes the pod IP, so `rws` must not be bound to `127.0.0.1`.
The default `0.0.0.0` works; check for an `ip = "127.0.0.1"` override.

### `/readyz` returns `503` right after start

Expected: it returns `503` until startup finishes, then `200`. If it stays at
`503`, startup failed — check the logs. Give slow starts an
`initialDelaySeconds`:

```yaml
readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /readyz
    port: 7878
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 5
```

### Requests are dropped on `SIGTERM`

`rws` stops accepting on `SIGTERM` and finishes in-flight requests. Requests
can still arrive while the load balancer hasn't noticed yet; delay
termination with a `preStop` sleep (Kubernetes 1.30+ — the release image has
no shell for an `exec` hook):

```yaml
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    sleep:
      seconds: 5
```

More in [Kubernetes](/deployment/kubernetes/).

## Building from source

### `linker 'cc' not found`

Install a C toolchain (needed by `aws-lc-rs` and other native dependencies):

```bash
sudo apt-get install build-essential        # Debian/Ubuntu
sudo dnf group install "Development Tools"  # Fedora/RHEL
sudo pacman -S base-devel                   # Arch
```

### `found crate … compiled by an incompatible version of rustc`

Stale build artifacts from another toolchain: `cargo clean && cargo build`.

### `error: package … requires rustc 1.88`

The minimum supported Rust version is 1.88: `rustup update stable`.

### `failed open - '…/FETCH_HEAD' is locked: Permission denied`

The Cargo registry was written by `sudo cargo …` once. Fix the ownership
(`sudo chown -R $USER ~/.cargo`) rather than building as root.

---

# Migrating to 18.0

<https://rws8.tech/reference/migrating-18/>

18.0 has a handful of breaking changes; most applications only meet the first and the `Request.body` type. If you are coming from 17.113.0 or earlier, also read [the patch-release changes](#coming-from-171130-or-earlier).

## `Header` fields are `Cow<'static, str>`

`Header { name, value }` used to be two `String`s; now both are
`Cow<'static, str>`, so the standard headers on every response are borrowed
instead of allocated.

```rust
use rust_web_server::header::Header;

// 17.x
let h = Header { name: Header::_LOCATION.to_string(), value: url };

// 18.0 — a &'static str is borrowed, a String is owned
let h = Header::new(Header::_LOCATION, url);
let h = Header::new("X-Static", "fixed");
let h = Header { name: "X-Static".into(), value: "fixed".into() }; // fields are still public
```

Reading:

| 17.x | 18.0 |
|------|------|
| `h.value.as_str()` | `&*h.value` or `h.value.as_ref()` (`as_str` isn't stable on the 1.88 MSRV) |
| `h.value.clone()` (a `String`) | `h.value.to_string()` |
| `h.value.push_str(..)` | `h.value.to_mut().push_str(..)` |
| `h.name == "Content-Type"` | unchanged (`Cow<str>` compares with `&str`) |

To find a request header, prefer `request.header("content-type")` — a
case-insensitive lookup that returns `Option<&Header>` without allocating.

## Default response headers

| Header | 17.x | 18.0 |
|--------|------|------|
| `Accept-CH`, `Critical-CH`, client hints in `Vary` | always | only with `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS=true` |
| `Vary` | `Origin` + the client-hint headers | `Origin` |
| `Cache-Control` on static files | `no-store, …` | `no-cache` (`RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL`) |
| `Last-Modified` on static files | non-standard | standard HTTP date |
| `Date` | — | on every response |
| `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy` | always | only with `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true` |
| `Content-Security-Policy` | `default-src 'self'` unless `RWS_CONFIG_CSP` | `RWS_CONFIG_CSP`, or the default with `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true` |
| `Date-Unix-Epoch-Nanos`, `Last-Modified-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` | always | only with `RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS=true` |
| `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (+ `-Credentials: true`) for any `Origin` | always (`cors_allow_all` defaulted to `true`) | only with `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true` or a listed origin |

What it means:

- **Browsers now keep static files** and revalidate them (`If-None-Match` /
  `If-Modified-Since` → `304`). To get the old behaviour set
  `RWS_CONFIG_STATIC_CACHE_CONTROL=` (empty). For fingerprinted asset names,
  set something like `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. Responses from
  your handlers still default to `no-store, …`.
- **Security headers**: to keep sending `X-Frame-Options`,
  `Referrer-Policy`, `Permissions-Policy` and the default CSP, set
  `RWS_CONFIG_SECURITY_HEADERS=true` (`security_headers = true`). A CSP set
  with `RWS_CONFIG_CSP` is sent either way.
- **Nanosecond timestamps**: clients that read `Date-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` or
  `Last-Modified-Unix-Epoch-Nanos` need `RWS_CONFIG_NANOS_HEADERS=true`
  (`nanos_headers = true`).
- **Client hints**: if your app reads `Sec-CH-*` request headers, set
  `RWS_CONFIG_CLIENT_HINTS=true` (or `client_hints = true` in
  `rws.config.toml`).
- **CORS**: a browser app on another origin that calls `rws` needs its origin
  in `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGINS` (`[cors] allow_origins`), plus
  `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS=true` if it sends cookies. Setting
  `RWS_CONFIG_CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true` restores the old echo-any-origin
  behaviour; avoid it for anything with logins.
- **ACME renewal**: certificates renew at two-thirds of their lifetime (or
  when the CA's renewal information says), not 30 days before expiry; set
  `RWS_CONFIG_ACME_RENEW_BEFORE_DAYS=30` to keep the old margin. Code that
  builds an `AcmeConfig` by hand sets `renew_before_days: None` (or
  `Some(days)`) and `profile: None`.
- **`CacheLayer`** no longer stores `no-cache` responses, responses to `Range`
  requests, or responses whose `Vary` names a request header outside its key.
  Static files are therefore not cached by it (they were never meant to be).

## RSA public keys

`rws` verifies RS256 JWTs and SAML signatures itself now (the `rsa` crate had
an unfixed advisory, RUSTSEC-2023-0071). Two signatures change:

- `auth::verify_jwt_rs256(token, &key)` takes a `&rsa_key::RsaPublicKey`.
- `SamlIdpMetadata.signing_key` is an `rsa_key::RsaPublicKey`.

`JwtLayer::rs256(pem)` and the SSO/JWKS code are unchanged for callers.

```rust
use rust_web_server::rsa_key::RsaPublicKey;

let key = RsaPublicKey::from_public_key_pem(&pem)?; // BEGIN PUBLIC KEY or BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY
let key = RsaPublicKey::from_public_key_der(&der)?; // SPKI
let key = RsaPublicKey::from_components(&n_bytes, &e_bytes)?;
```

Keys under 2048 bits are rejected; a JWKS key that can't be used is skipped.

## `Request.body` is a `Body`

`Request.body` was a `Vec<u8>`; it is a `request::Body`, which can also be a
stream of a body still arriving. It dereferences to `&[u8]`, so reading
code mostly compiles unchanged. What to change:

| 17.x | 18.0 |
|---|---|
| `body: vec![]` | `body: Default::default()` |
| `body: bytes` (a `Vec<u8>`) | `body: bytes.into()` |
| `request.body.clone()` where a `Vec<u8>` is wanted | `request.body.to_vec()` |
| `String::from_utf8(request.body)` | `String::from_utf8(request.body.to_vec())` |
| `request.body = vec` | `request.body = vec.into()` |
| `assert_eq!(b"x".to_vec(), request.body)` | unchanged (`Vec<u8> == Body` works) |

## The `rws` binary runs one runtime per core

The `rws` binary now starts one single-threaded runtime per core, each
accepting on its own `SO_REUSEPORT` socket, like nginx's workers
(`RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME=per-core`, Unix). On fast CPUs this serves more
requests per second; on slower ones it can cost more CPU per small request.
To keep 17.x behaviour, set `runtime = "shared"` in `rws.config.toml` or
`RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME=shared`. Applications built on the library are
unchanged: they stay `shared` unless they set it.

## Coming from 17.113.0 or earlier

18.0 carries the 17.113.1 security fixes and the 17.113.2 conformance fixes.
If you skipped those releases, these refuse or change what you may rely on:

- **Static files:** paths with `..`, dot-files (`.git/`, `.env`; set
  `RWS_CONFIG_SERVE_DOTFILES=true` to serve them), `*.pem`, `*.key` and
  `rws.config.toml` are not served. Request paths are percent-decoded, so a
  file whose name contains a literal `%` is requested as `%25`.
- **ACME** keeps its keys in `.rws/acme/` by default (files at the old
  default paths are moved there on start).
- **The `rws` binary** mounts `/mcp` only when `MCP_TOKEN` is set.
- **HTTP/1.1 requests** without `Host` or with two, with a lower-case method,
  a folded header line or whitespace before a header's colon get `400`; an
  HTTP/1.0 connection closes after each response unless the client sends
  `Connection: keep-alive`.
- **CORS** origins match whole: list each origin, a part of one no longer
  matches.

## Also new in 18.0 (not breaking)

- A request head that doesn't complete within 30 s of its first byte gets
  `408 Request Timeout`.
- `[[upstream]] tls_ca_file` trusts a private CA for `https://` upstreams.
- Inline tables in settings: `rate_limit = { max_requests = 100 }`.

The full list is in [`CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md).

---

# Architecture

<https://rws8.tech/reference/architecture/>

`rws` is one crate: the server, the reverse proxy and the application
framework share one request type and one handler trait. HTTP/1.1 parsing,
routing, middleware, JSON, WebSocket, SSE and the HTTP/2 server are written
in-crate (the `h2` crate is only the proxies' HTTP/2 client); HTTP/3 uses
`h3` + `quinn`, TLS `rustls`.

## Builds

| Build | Runtime | Listeners |
|-------|---------|-----------|
| `http3` (default) | tokio | HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 over TLS (ALPN), HTTP/3 over QUIC on the same port, optional HTTP → HTTPS redirect |
| `http2` | tokio | as above without QUIC |
| `http1` | none — a thread pool | plain HTTP/1.1 |

Without a certificate the async builds serve plain HTTP/1.1 on the same port.

## A request's path

```
TcpListener / QUIC endpoint
  └─ connection task (async builds) or pool thread (http1)
       ├─ TLS handshake, ALPN → HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2      (10 s deadline)
       ├─ read head (≤ 64 KiB, 30 s from its first byte), then the body
       │     (Content-Length or chunked; Expect: 100-continue; body limit → 413)
       ├─ Request::parse → Request + ConnectionInfo (addresses, SNI)
       ├─ Application::execute(&request, &connection) → Response
       │     middleware layers → router / controllers / proxy
       ├─ gzip if the client accepts it and it pays off
       └─ write head + body (one write, writev, sendfile, or chunked stream)
```

- **HTTP/1.1** connections are keep-alive loops with pipelining; one handler
  serves plain TCP and TLS. Every read has a 30 s idle timeout.
- **HTTP/2 and HTTP/3** translate each stream into the same `Request`, call the
  same `Application`, and translate the `Response` back into frames. Large
  bodies stream in 64 KiB chunks within flow-control limits.
- **Where handlers run.** Handlers are synchronous. In the async builds a
  request runs on tokio's blocking pool, unless the application says it is
  cheap (`Application::runs_inline` — `App` does for GET and HEAD), in which
  case it runs on the connection task. Async handlers
  (`App::with_async_state`) and config-file proxy routes without middleware
  are awaited without tying up a thread.

## Applications and middleware

Everything that answers requests implements one trait:

```rust
pub trait Application {
    fn execute(&self, request: &Request, connection: &ConnectionInfo) -> Result;
}
```

- `App` — the built-in controllers (health, metrics, static files, …).
- `App::with_state(S)` / `App::with_async_state(S)` — your routes plus shared state.
- `Router` — path routing with `:params` and `*wildcards`, usable inside any application.
- `McpServer`, `ConfigDrivenApp` (the config-file proxy) — also applications.

Middleware wraps an application (`app.wrap(layer)`); the first layer added is
the outermost. Rate limiting, auth, CORS, caching, metrics, tracing, rewriting
and the reverse proxy itself are all `Middleware`, so one model covers a web
app, a gateway and a mix of both.

## Static files

A GET for a regular file takes a fast path: the open file handle, its size
and modification time, small files' contents (≤ 64 KiB) and their gzip
output are cached per file version, so a hit costs one `fstat`. An edit in
place is served at once (strict mode, the default). Files over 256 KiB
stream from disk; on plain TCP, downloads use `sendfile` with the response
head in the same TCP segment. Responses carry `ETag` and `Last-Modified` and
answer `304` to revalidation.

## Reverse proxy

Upstream HTTP/1.1 connections are pooled per backend (64 idle, 60 s). A
config-file route without middleware is forwarded entirely on the event loop;
others go through the blocking path with the same pool. Responses over 1 MB,
chunked or SSE are streamed through instead of buffered. Health checks,
load-balancing strategies, retries and circuit breakers sit around the pool.
See [Reverse proxy](/proxy/reverse-proxy/) and [Config-driven proxy](/proxy/config-driven/).

## Configuration

Settings are layered — built-in defaults, environment variables,
`rws.config.toml`, command-line flags — and all end up as `RWS_CONFIG_*`
environment variables at startup. Request handling reads a typed snapshot
(`ServerConfig::current()`), rebuilt when the configuration changes; `SIGHUP`
reloads CORS, rate limits, log format, proxy routes and TLS certificates
without a restart. See [Configuration](/configuration/overview/).

---

# Benchmarks

<https://rws8.tech/reference/benchmarks/>

`rws` is measured against Caddy and nginx on the same machine, with the same
files and the same load. The numbers below come from one run (40243377254) of the
[Benchmark workflow](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/.github/workflows/bench.yml)
on a 4-CPU GitHub Actions runner (Linux x86_64), with the load generator on the
same machine.

**Load:** [`oha`](https://github.com/hatoo/oha), 64 keep-alive connections,
20 seconds per scenario after a 2-second warm-up, HTTP/1.1, no compression
(`--disable-compression`: the Caddy and nginx configs don't compress, and
`rws` compresses text by default), access logs off everywhere. `rws` is the
release build (`--features "acme auth mimalloc"`), Caddy 2.11.7, nginx from Ubuntu with
`sendfile`, `open_file_cache` and upstream keep-alive enabled. nginx's
`open_file_cache_valid 1s` trusts a cached file's size and modification time
for a second; `rws` runs with the equivalent `open_file_cache_strict = false`
(its default re-checks them with an `fstat` on every request, so an edit in
place is served at once).

| Scenario | Server | Requests/s | p50 (ms) | p99 (ms) | CPU/request (µs) | Peak memory (MiB) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Static file, 1 KiB | rws | 96,670 | 0.61 | 1.65 | 16.9 | 33.5 |
| | Caddy | 18,592 | 2.73 | 13.49 | 154.4 | 66.1 |
| | nginx | 81,161 | 0.59 | 3.10 | 25.1 | 23.2 |
| Static file, 1 MiB | rws | 9,511 | 6.26 | 14.00 | 209.8 | 33.5 |
| | Caddy | 2,398 | 19.03 | 124.03 | 1,194.7 | 69.4 |
| | nginx | 9,767 | 6.42 | 14.05 | 216.2 | 23.4 |
| Reverse proxy, 1 KiB | rws | 34,260 | 1.79 | 3.89 | 44.6 | 35.5 |
| | Caddy | 13,402 | 4.16 | 14.17 | 190.6 | 66.7 |
| | nginx | 33,942 | 1.74 | 4.51 | 47.1 | 24.2 |

CPU/request is the server's user + system CPU time over the run (including
worker processes) divided by the requests it served.

Every request in every scenario returned `200 OK`.

### Extended scenarios

The same run, with the extended scenarios (`EXTENDED=1`, see
[Reproduce](#reproduce)):

| Scenario | Server | Requests/s | p50 (ms) | p99 (ms) | CPU/request (µs) | Peak memory (MiB) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 26 KiB JS file, gzip | rws | 86,327 | 0.69 | 1.87 | 20.9 | 41.8 |
| | Caddy | 5,729 | 8.51 | 51.96 | 606.3 | 109.2 |
| | nginx | 1,802 | 35.26 | 71.94 | 2,063.6 | 27.3 |
| Static 1 KiB, access log on | rws | 88,643 | 0.66 | 1.81 | 20.2 | 41.6 |
| | Caddy | 15,964 | 2.97 | 18.12 | 191.7 | 65.6 |
| | nginx | 75,518 | 0.62 | 3.16 | 28.6 | 23.2 |
| Static 1 KiB, HTTPS | rws | 70,372 | 0.82 | 2.22 | 25.9 | 49.4 |
| | Caddy | 25,555 | 2.22 | 9.57 | 112.6 | 69.4 |
| | nginx | 63,752 | 0.75 | 3.75 | 33.5 | 41.7 |
| Static 1 KiB, HTTP/2 | rws | 66,141 | 0.90 | 2.44 | 27.4 | 63.7 |
| | Caddy | 13,604 | 4.04 | 14.20 | 216.0 | 66.9 |
| | nginx | 51,416 | 0.84 | 4.46 | 37.9 | 42.2 |
| Static 1 MiB, HTTPS | rws | 1,602 | 35.23 | 49.34 | 923.7 | 65.7 |
| | Caddy | 1,460 | 38.13 | 108.27 | 1,483.6 | 68.0 |
| | nginx | 1,311 | 45.19 | 101.34 | 1,639.9 | 42.3 |

`rws` compresses a static text file once per version and serves the cached
result; nginx and Caddy compress on every request, which is why the gzip row
differs by two orders of magnitude (level 6 everywhere). HTTP/2 is served by
`rws`'s own implementation (since 18.0.0): with the `h2` crate, framing and
HPACK cost more per request than all of nginx's own code, and nginx led this
scenario by 23–41%. Large files over TLS were slow on AMD
EPYC 7763 runners until 18.0.0: rustls copies each record's plaintext into
a buffer 5 bytes past a page boundary, and with the file buffer page-aligned
too, glibc's `rep movsb` ran that copy at 2.8 instead of 40 GB/s (4 KiB
aliasing). The file buffer now starts mid-page; that scenario went from
nginx +9% to `rws` −35 to −50%.

On a 10-core Mac (same tools and configuration, `oha` on the same machine):
1 KiB static — rws 107k, nginx 100k; 1 MiB static — 9.8k vs 9.4k; proxy —
49.0k vs 48.9k requests per second.

## Reading the numbers

- **Against Caddy:** `rws` serves 4.0× (large) to 5.2× (small) as many file
  requests, 2.6× as many proxied and 4.9× as many HTTP/2 requests per
  second, using a quarter to a ninth of the CPU per request, with a p99
  three to nine times lower and about half the memory.
- **Against nginx:** less CPU per request in every scenario — small files
  −33%, large files −3%, proxying −5%, HTTP/2 −28%, HTTPS −23%, large files
  over HTTPS −44%, with an access log −29%, with gzip a hundredth — more
  requests per second in all but large plain files (−3%), and the lower p99
  everywhere. This run used an AMD EPYC runner. On the fastest (Intel)
  runner type nginx keeps 6–8% more plain-HTTP requests per second and
  about the same CPU for large files and proxying (run 40209996636);
  `RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME=per-core` narrows that (run 40242045036). The load
  generator shares the runner's 4 CPUs, so the CPU/request column is the
  comparison to read.
- **Memory:** release builds allocate with mimalloc, which costs about 5%
  less CPU per request than the system allocator but holds more memory —
  34–66 MiB here, against nginx's 23–42. Built without the `mimalloc`
  feature, `rws` peaks at 9–17 MiB.
- The gap depends on the runner's hardware; same-run A/Bs (`base_ref`,
  below) are how changes are judged.
- Shared CI runners are noisy: absolute numbers vary by a factor of two
  between runs. Compare servers within one run, not numbers across runs.
- Compression matters: with `Accept-Encoding: gzip` sent and only `rws`
  compressing, the comparison measures `gzip`, not the servers. Compare like
  for like.

## Why it's fast

- **Open files are reused** (an open-file cache like nginx's): a request for
  a hot file costs one `fstat`; files up to 64 KiB are served from memory,
  and the response head and body go out in one write.
- **Quick requests run on the event loop.** Static files, health checks and
  metrics skip the hand-off to a blocking thread pool, as in nginx. Handlers
  that may block (your routes) still get a pool thread, so a slow handler
  can't stall other connections. See
  [`runs_inline`](/building-apps/middleware/#running-on-the-event-loop-runs_inline).
- **Proxying holds no thread.** Proxy routes without middleware, to HTTP or
  HTTPS backends, wait for the backend on the connection's task, over pooled
  keep-alive connections.
- **One idle timer per connection**, pushed back on each read without a lock.
- **`sendfile` for downloads** over plain HTTP on Linux and macOS: the kernel
  copies file pages straight to the socket, with the response head in the
  same segment (`TCP_CORK` on Linux, `sendfile`'s header vector on macOS).
- **Configuration is a cached snapshot**, not read from the environment on
  every request; a reload replaces it.
- **Few allocations per request.** The standard response headers are
  borrowed `&'static str`s (`Header` fields are `Cow<'static, str>`), so
  attaching them copies nothing; request heads and upstream response heads
  are parsed in one pass over the bytes; numbers are formatted on the stack;
  the file check is one `fstat`.

## Reproduce

Run the workflow from the repository's Actions tab ("Benchmark" → "Run
workflow"), or locally:

```bash
cargo build --release --bin rws --features "acme auth"
RWS=target/release/rws OHA=oha CADDY=caddy NGINX=nginx bench/run.sh
```

`CADDY` and `NGINX` are optional; the proxy scenario needs `NGINX`, which also
serves as the shared backend for every proxy under test. `DURATION` (default
`15s`) and `CONNECTIONS` (default `64`) tune the load. The script prints a
Markdown table and writes `bench-results.md` and `bench-results.json`.

`EXTENDED=1` (on by default in the workflow) adds the paths real deployments
hit that the three scenarios above leave out, each with equivalent settings
on every server: `text-gzip` (a 26 KiB JavaScript file with
`Accept-Encoding: gzip`, gzip level 6 everywhere), `log-1k` (an access log
written to a file), `https-1k` and `h2-1k` (TLS over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2),
and `https-1m` (a 1 MiB file over TLS, where `sendfile` doesn't apply). The
script makes a self-signed certificate with `openssl`, and skips a TLS
scenario for an nginx built without its ssl or http2 module.

## Profile

To see where `rws` spends its CPU, run the workflow with **profile** checked:
it builds with frame pointers and samples `rws` with `perf` during each
scenario, and nginx's workers too (`nginx-<scenario>` reports; the distro
nginx has no symbols, but its kernel time is comparable with `rws`'s). The job summary lists the hottest symbols, and the `bench-profile`
artifact has flat and call-tree reports plus `perf script` output for flame
graphs (`inferno-collapse-perf | inferno-flamegraph`). Locally, on Linux:

```bash
RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes" cargo build --release --bin rws --features "acme auth"
PERF_DIR=perf RWS=target/release/rws OHA=oha NGINX=nginx bench/run.sh
perf report -i perf/static-1k.data --no-children
```

Sampling slows `rws` down, so take throughput numbers from an unprofiled run.

## Compare two builds

Runner hardware differs from run to run (nginx itself varies threefold), so
a change can only be judged against its baseline in the same run. Give the
workflow a **base_ref** (a branch, tag or commit) and it also builds that
ref and benches it as `rws-base`, right after `rws`; locally, set
`RWS_BASE=<binary>`. **base_workers** (`RWS_BASE_WORKERS`) runs `rws-base`
with that many tokio workers — with no base ref, the same build again — to
compare worker counts, and **base_runtime** (`RWS_BASE_RUNTIME`) does the same
for `RWS_CONFIG_RUNTIME` (shared or per-core). (Fewer workers than CPUs raises the measured
requests per second only because the load generator shares the runner's
CPUs; on a dedicated server one worker per core is right.)

---

# Roadmap

<https://rws8.tech/reference/roadmap/>

These features are planned. Each appears as a callout on the relevant docs page.

:::caution[Coming Soon]
**Baggage and automatic child spans**

W3C baggage propagation, and spans created automatically for each database query and outbound call. Child spans already work when started by hand with `otel::span` / `otel::client_span` — see [Distributed Tracing](/features/tracing/#child-spans).
:::

:::caution[Coming Soon]
**Admin UI**

`GET /admin` — a browser-based dashboard showing live metrics, current configuration, and a tail of the access log. Requires authentication.
:::

:::caution[Coming Soon]
**Access log rotation**

Built-in log-file rotation (by size or time) so the server can write logs to disk without an external `logrotate` configuration.
:::

---

**WebAssembly guest component** — shipped. `App`/`Router`/middleware now run inside a `wasi:http/proxy` WASM component (Wasmtime, Spin, Fastly Compute) via the separate `rws-wasm-shim` package. See [WASM Guest Component](/deployment/wasm/). Larger follow-up phases (streaming bodies, outbound HTTP from the guest) remain open — tracked in `spec/WASM_SHIM.md` in the repository.

---

The full ordered list of open work is [`spec/ROADMAP.md`](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/blob/main/spec/ROADMAP.md); track progress and open issues at [github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server](https://github.com/bohdaq/rust-web-server/issues).
